questions.response:
There is no single agreed answer. “God” is a name people use for very different ideas, depending on religion, philosophy, and personal belief.

**In many religious traditions**, God is the ultimate reality: a supreme being who is the source of the universe, often described as eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing, and morally perfect. In Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, God is one personal creator who relates to human beings—through covenant, revelation, prayer, or moral law. Other traditions speak of God differently: as Brahman (the ultimate reality) in some Hindu thought, as a highest deity among many, or in ways that do not map neatly onto a single personal creator.

**In philosophy**, “God” often means whatever would count as the ground of existence or the greatest conceivable being. Classical theism treats God as necessary, uncaused, and the reason anything exists at all. Other views include:
- **Deism**: a creator who does not intervene in the world
- **Pantheism**: God identical with the universe
- **Panentheism**: the universe in God, but God more than the universe

**Outside religion**, some people use “God” metaphorically—for nature, moral order, consciousness, or whatever humans treat as ultimate—while atheists and many agnostics hold that no such being exists, or that the question cannot be settled.

So “What is God?” is less a factual question with one correct definition than a question about what, if anything, is ultimate—and how people have tried to name it. Different answers reflect different experiences, texts, arguments, and ways of life.

questions.question: What are the decrees of God?
questions.reference_answer: The decrees of God are, his eternal purpose, according to the counsel of his will, whereby, for his own glory, he hath foreordained whatsoever comes to pass.

questions.response:
**The decrees of God are His eternal, sovereign purposes by which He freely and unchangeably ordains whatever comes to pass, according to the counsel of His own will.**

This is a technical term in Christian systematic theology, especially Reformed/Calvinist traditions. It refers not primarily to God’s commands or moral laws (often called precepts), but to His comprehensive plan for all history and creation.

### Classic definition
The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), Chapter 3, states it this way:

> God from all eternity, did, by the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely, and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass: yet so, as thereby neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures; nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established.

Key features usually emphasized:
- **Eternal** — decided in eternity, not as a reaction to events in time.
- **Sovereign and free** — grounded in God’s own will, not external necessity.
- **Comprehensive** — covers all things that occur (creation, providence, history, salvation, etc.).
- **Wise and holy** — consistent with God’s character.
- **Compatible with secondary causes** — does not cancel human choices, natural processes, or responsibility; it establishes them.
- **Does not make God the author of sin** — a standard qualification in the tradition.

### Common distinctions
Theologians often speak of the decree as one unified plan that can be considered under aspects such as:
- The decree of creation
- The decree of providence (God’s ongoing governance)
- The decree of election/predestination (regarding salvation)
- Related purposes such as redemption through Christ

Scriptural passages frequently cited in support include Ephesians 1:11 (“works all things according to the counsel of his will”), Romans 8:28–30, Acts 2:23, and Isaiah 46:9–11.

### Broader note
Not all Christian traditions use or emphasize this language the same way. Arminian, Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and other perspectives affirm God’s sovereignty and foreknowledge but differ on the nature, scope, and relation of divine decree to human freedom and contingency. The phrase “decrees of God” is most precise and developed in Reformed confessional theology.

In short: the decrees are God’s eternal plan for everything that happens, executed in time without compromising His holiness or genuine creaturely agency.

questions.response:
**The work of creation** is the act of bringing something into being that was not there before—order, form, life, meaning, or a made thing—out of what was formless, potential, or nothing at all.

It is used in a few related ways:

- **In theology** (especially Christian thought), it names God’s act of making the world: calling light, matter, life, and human beings into existence, and sustaining them. It is often distinguished from later works such as redemption or judgment. The point is origin and gift: the world is not self-made; it is given.
- **In philosophy and art**, it is the human labor of making: shaping raw material, language, sound, or idea into a work that has form and purpose. Creation here is not creation from nothing, but transformation—imposing order, discovering possibility, and finishing something that can stand on its own.
- **More broadly**, it is any generative work that adds reality rather than merely rearranging what already exists: a poem, a building, a scientific theory, a child raised, a community formed. The “work” is both the effort and the result.

What these senses share is that creation is not passive. It is deliberate bringing-forth: from chaos to cosmos, from silence to speech, from potential to a finished thing.

questions.response:
**Sin** is a religious and moral idea: an act, attitude, or state that violates what a tradition holds to be divine law, sacred order, or the right relationship between people and God (or the ultimate good).

### In major traditions
- **Christianity:** Sin is turning away from God—missing the mark of love of God and neighbor. It includes specific wrong acts and a deeper condition of brokenness (often called original sin in many churches). Forgiveness is tied to repentance and grace, especially through Christ.
- **Judaism:** Sin (*chet*, “missing the mark”) is failing to keep the commandments and harming the covenant with God and other people. Emphasis is on repentance (*teshuvah*), repair, and return.
- **Islam:** Sin is disobedience to Allah’s commands. Sins vary in gravity; sincere repentance (*tawbah*) and God’s mercy are central.
- **Other traditions:** Related ideas appear elsewhere—wrong action that creates suffering or imbalance (for example, unskillful action in Buddhism, or *adharma* in Hindu thought)—though “sin” as offense against a personal God is most characteristic of the Abrahamic faiths.

### Common distinctions
- **Act vs. state:** A particular wrong deed versus a lasting condition of alienation or corruption.
- **Against God vs. against others:** Many traditions treat harm to people as also an offense against God.
- **Mortal/venial or major/minor:** Some systems rank sins by seriousness and intent.

### Outside religion
In secular use, “sin” is often metaphorical: a serious moral failing, or simply something strongly disapproved of (“a sin to waste food”). Philosophers may discuss wrongdoing, guilt, and responsibility without a divine lawgiver.

So, briefly: **sin is moral or spiritual failure as defined by a religious (or moral) standard**—especially disobedience to God or violation of what that tradition treats as sacred duty. Exact meaning depends on the tradition.

**We are made partakers of the redemption purchased by Christ by the effectual application of it to us by his Holy Spirit.**

This is the classic answer given in the Westminster Shorter Catechism (Q. 29). In Reformed theology it means that Christ’s finished work—his obedience, death, and resurrection that purchased redemption—is not automatically or mechanically applied to everyone. The Holy Spirit effectually applies that redemption to particular people, bringing them into actual possession of its benefits.

The Spirit does this especially by working faith in us and thereby uniting us to Christ in effectual calling (see the following catechism question, Q. 30). Through that union, the benefits Christ purchased—justification, adoption, sanctification, and the rest—are conveyed to believers. Scripture points in the same direction: the Spirit regenerates and indwells (John 3:5–8; Titus 3:5–6), convicts and draws (John 16:8–14), and seals believers as Christ’s own (Ephesians 1:13–14; Romans 8:9–11, 14–17).

In short: redemption is purchased by Christ alone; we share in it only as the Spirit applies it to us, uniting us to him by faith.

questions.response:
**True faith** is usually understood as more than agreeing with an idea. It is trust that shapes how a person lives.

Across many traditions, a few marks tend to separate “true” faith from habit, performance, or mere opinion:

- **Trust, not just assent.** Believing *that* something is true is weaker than relying on it when it costs something. Faith shows up in dependence, loyalty, and hope under pressure—not only in correct statements.
- **Sincerity.** It is inward, not mainly for status, fear, or display. Outward practice without inner conviction is often treated as empty.
- **Lived consistency.** Belief and conduct are meant to cohere. Many traditions judge faith by love, justice, humility, and perseverance more than by intensity of feeling or volume of words.
- **Openness to being corrected.** True faith is confident enough to act, but not so closed that evidence, conscience, or deeper understanding cannot refine it. Blind stubbornness is often distinguished from faithful trust.
- **Relationship or commitment, not a mood.** In religious settings it is typically directed toward God (or the ultimate), and it includes obedience, prayer, or devotion over time—not a single emotional peak.

Different traditions name this differently. In much of Christianity, faith is trusting God’s character and promises, and a “dead” faith that never bears love is treated as incomplete. In Islam, *iman* joins heart-belief, confession, and action. Other paths stress devotion, right intention, or alignment with what is ultimately real. Philosophers sometimes describe faith as a committed trust that goes beyond what can be fully proved, without requiring one to ignore reason.

So a working definition: **true faith is sincere, enduring trust in what one takes to be ultimately real or worthy—trust that organizes one’s hopes, choices, and character, rather than a label, a feeling, or a set of unexamined opinions.**

What counts as “true” still depends on the standard you use: a particular scripture, moral fruit, intellectual honesty, or personal integrity. If you have a tradition or contrast in mind (faith vs. works, faith vs. doubt, religious vs. secular trust), the answer can be narrowed further.

That line is the opening of the Apostles’ Creed. Saying it is a confession of Christian faith, not a scientific claim or a private opinion. In traditional Christian teaching it means roughly this:

**“I believe”** — not only “I think this is probably true,” but “I trust and commit myself to this.” Faith here is personal allegiance as well as conviction.

**“in God”** — there is one God, not many; the God of Israel whom Christians worship, not a vague force or an idea.

**“the Father”** — God is personal and relational, the source and origin of all things, and (in Christian doctrine) the first person of the Trinity: Father of the Son, and by adoption Father of those who belong to Christ. “Father” names care and authority, not maleness in a biological sense.

**“almighty”** — God is sovereign. Nothing is outside God’s power or final purpose. Classical theology still holds that God does not do what is contrary to God’s own nature (for example, what is evil or absurd); “almighty” means supreme power, not arbitrary chaos.

**“Creator of heaven and earth”** — everything that exists, seen and unseen, depends on God for its being. God is not part of the universe and did not shape it out of some rival eternal stuff; creation is God’s free act. “Heaven and earth” is a way of saying “all reality,” not only the sky and the ground.

So the sentence affirms one personal, all-powerful God who is the origin of everything, addressed as Father. Later lines of the Creed go on to speak of the Son and the Holy Spirit; this first line is the foundation those lines rest on.

I don’t hold beliefs of my own. That is the meaning the phrase carries for those who say it as Christians.

questions.response:
**Providence of God** is the theological idea that God continually sustains, governs, and cares for creation—not only as its origin, but as its ongoing guide.

In classical Christian thought (and in related forms in Judaism and Islam), it usually includes several related claims:

- **Preservation**: God keeps the world in existence and maintains the order of nature. Creation is not left to run on its own after being made.
- **Governance**: God directs history and events toward his purposes. Nothing falls wholly outside his knowledge or rule.
- **Provision and care**: God supplies what creatures need and watches over them—sometimes in ordinary ways (through natural processes and human action), sometimes in ways believers call special or miraculous.

Theologians often distinguish:

- **General providence** — God’s care over the whole created order (seasons, laws of nature, the course of nations).
- **Special providence** — God’s particular care for individuals, the people of God, or decisive moments in salvation history.

A common further distinction is between God’s **permission** of evil and his **ordination** of good: providence is not usually taken to mean that God directly wills every evil act, but that he remains sovereign even over a world in which free creatures do wrong, and can bring good out of suffering.

How providence relates to human freedom, chance, and the problem of evil is debated. Some traditions stress meticulous divine control; others emphasize concurrence (God works through secondary causes and free agents) or a more open future. The core idea, across those differences, is that the world is not abandoned: it is held, ordered, and cared for by God.

So “providence” names both God’s foresight and his active provision—his wise, purposeful involvement in everything that happens.

questions.response:
**Jesus is the unique, eternal Son by nature; believers are children of God by adoption and grace.**

In Scripture, Jesus is called God’s “only begotten” (or “one and only”) Son—most famously in John 3:16, and also in John 1:14, 18; 3:18; and 1 John 4:9. The underlying Greek term (*monogenēs*) stresses uniqueness: He is the one-of-a-kind Son. This points to His eternal relationship with the Father. He is not a created being who later became a son; He is eternally begotten of the Father, sharing the same divine nature (see John 1:1–3, 14; Hebrews 1:1–5; and the classic creedal language that the Son is “begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father”). His sonship is therefore essential and unshared.

By contrast, human beings become children of God through faith in Christ. John 1:12 says that those who receive Him are given the right to become children of God. This sonship is by adoption and new birth, not by nature in the same sense as Christ’s (Romans 8:14–17; Galatians 4:4–7; Ephesians 1:5). Believers are brought into God’s family by grace, united to the Son, and made heirs with Him—but they do not share His eternal, divine generation or His unique status as the incarnate Word.

So the title “only begotten Son” safeguards the distinction: Christ is the Son in a way no creature ever is or can be, while our status as God’s children is a gracious gift that depends entirely on Him.

The line “he descended into hell” (Latin *descendit ad inferna* / *ad inferos*) belongs to the Apostles’ Creed. It was not part of the earliest Roman baptismal creed; it appears in some Western creeds by the late 4th century (notably the creed of Aquileia, as Rufinus notes around 400) and became standard in the received Western text of the Apostles’ Creed centuries later.

It was added to spell out what the burial already implied: that Christ truly died and his soul entered the realm of the dead (Sheol/Hades), not merely that his body was placed in a tomb. The wording rests on passages such as Acts 2:27–31, Ephesians 4:9, and 1 Peter 3:18–19, and it underwrote the later tradition of the “harrowing of hell”—Christ’s victory over death and the liberation of the righteous dead. “Hell” here traditionally means the abode of the dead, not the place of final punishment; many modern versions therefore say “he descended to the dead.”

Interpretations still differ (some stress only the reality of death and burial; others stress a triumphant descent), but the clause’s inclusion was meant to complete the creed’s account of Christ’s passion and to affirm that death did not hold him.

1. **It secures our justification.** By rising, Christ conquered death and confirmed that his death fully paid for sin. God therefore counts his righteousness to those united to him by faith (Rom. 4:25; 1 Cor. 15:17–20; 1 Pet. 1:3).

3. **It guarantees our future resurrection.** His bodily resurrection is the pledge and firstfruits of the glorious resurrection of all who belong to him (Rom. 8:11; 1 Cor. 15:20–23; Phil. 3:20–21).

In short, the resurrection validates the cross, renews believers in the present, and assures them of life with God forever.

Our good works cannot be our righteousness before God—or any part of it—because the righteousness that can stand in his judgment must be perfectly complete and fully conformed to his law, while even our best works remain imperfect and stained by sin.

God’s standard is not “mostly good” or “sincere effort.” His law demands whole-hearted, unbroken obedience in thought, word, and deed (Deut. 6:5; Matt. 5:48; James 2:10). One failure renders a person guilty of breaking the whole. Scripture is blunt that no one meets this: “None is righteous, no, not one” (Rom. 3:10), and “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23). Even the works believers do after regeneration are mixed with remaining sin, selfish motives, and incompleteness. Isaiah’s verdict still applies: “all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment” (Isa. 64:6). They may be genuinely good in a relative, creaturely sense and pleasing to God as the fruit of faith, but they are never pure enough to constitute the righteousness he requires for acceptance.

Second, assurance would collapse, because we could never know whether we had done enough or done it well enough. The gospel instead offers an alien righteousness: Christ’s own perfect obedience and atoning death, credited to the believer by faith alone (2 Cor. 5:21; Phil. 3:9; Rom. 5:19). That righteousness is already complete; nothing we add can improve it, and nothing we lack can diminish it.

Good works remain necessary—they are the inevitable fruit of union with Christ, the path of gratitude, and the evidence of living faith (Eph. 2:10; James 2:14–26; Heidelberg Catechism Q. 86–91). questions.response:
**Sacraments** are sacred rites in Christianity understood as outward signs of God’s grace. Traditions differ on how many there are and exactly how they work.

### Common definition
A classic description (associated with Augustine and later theology) is that a sacrament is a **visible sign of invisible grace**—a ritual act, usually involving words and physical elements (water, bread, wine, oil), through which God is believed to give grace.

### Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches
These churches recognize **seven sacraments**, all traced to Christ and entrusted to the Church:

1. **Baptism** — initiation into the Christian life  
2. **Confirmation** (Orthodox: **Chrismation**) — strengthening by the Holy Spirit  
3. **Eucharist** (Holy Communion) — sharing in Christ’s body and blood  
4. **Penance / Reconciliation** — forgiveness of sins after baptism  
5. **Anointing of the Sick** — healing and comfort for the ill or dying  
6. **Holy Orders** — ordination of bishops, priests, and deacons  
7. **Matrimony** — the covenant of marriage  

In Catholic teaching they are “efficacious signs of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church.”

### Protestant churches
Most Protestant traditions recognize **two sacraments** (sometimes called **ordinances**), because they see only these as clearly instituted by Jesus in the New Testament:

- **Baptism**
- **The Lord’s Supper** (Eucharist / Communion)

Views of what they do vary: some hold that they truly convey grace; others see them mainly as signs, seals, or acts of obedience and remembrance.

In short: sacraments are the Church’s central ritual means of receiving and signifying God’s grace, with Catholics and Orthodox counting seven and most Protestants counting two.

questions.question: What difference is there between the Lord's supper and the papal mass?
questions.reference_answer: The Lord's supper testifies to us, first, that we have complete forgiveness of all our sins through the one sacrifice of Jesus Christ, which He Himself accomplished on the cross once for all; and, second, that through the Holy Spirit we are grafted into Christ, who with His true body is now in heaven at the right hand of the Father, and this is where He wants to be worshipped. But the mass teaches, first, that the living and the dead do not have forgiveness of sins through the suffering of Christ unless He is still offered for them daily by the priests; and, second, that Christ is bodily present in the form of bread and wine, and there is to be worshipped. Therefore the mass is basically nothing but a denial of the one sacrifice and suffering of Jesus Christ, and an accursed idolatry.

questions.response:
The main differences are theological, not merely ceremonial. They concern what the rite *is*, what happens to the bread and wine, and whether it is a sacrifice.

### Roman Catholic Mass
In Catholic teaching (defined especially at the Council of Trent and reaffirmed since), the Mass is:
- A true **sacrifice**: the same sacrifice of Christ on the cross, made present again in an unbloody manner and offered by the priest to God. It is propitiatory (it applies the merits of Christ’s sacrifice for the living and the dead).
- Involves **transubstantiation**: at the words of consecration, the substance of the bread and wine becomes the body and blood of Christ, while the appearances remain. Christ is therefore really, truly, and substantially present and may be adored in the consecrated elements.
- Requires an ordained priest acting *in persona Christi*. The faithful participate, but the sacrificial offering is the priest’s act.
- Understood as both sacrifice and sacrament; receiving Communion is part of the Mass but not the whole of it.

“Papal Mass” usually just means the Roman rite as authorized and regulated under the papacy (as distinct from Eastern Catholic liturgies or Protestant rites), not a wholly different theology.

### The Lord’s Supper (classic Protestant view)
Reformation churches rejected the Mass as a sacrifice and taught the Supper as:
- A **memorial and means of grace**, not a re-offering of Christ. Christ’s sacrifice was once for all (Hebrews 7–10); the Supper proclaims and applies it, it does not repeat or continue it as a propitiatory sacrifice.
- **Real presence** understood differently by tradition:
  - Lutheran: Christ’s body and blood are truly present “in, with, and under” the bread and wine (sacramental union), received by mouth, without transubstantiation or a sacrificial offering.
  - Reformed: Christ is truly present and received by faith through the Holy Spirit; the elements remain bread and wine and are not locally or substantially changed into Christ’s body.
  - Many evangelicals/Zwinglian traditions: primarily a memorial meal of remembrance, thanksgiving, and proclamation, with spiritual blessing for believers.
- Presided over by a minister, but not dependent on a sacrificing priesthood. It is a communion of the church with Christ and with one another.
- Both kinds (bread and cup) are given to the congregation.

### Core contrasts
| Point | Catholic Mass | Protestant Lord’s Supper |
|---|---|---|
| Is it a sacrifice? | Yes — re-presentation of Calvary, propitiatory | No — remembrance and participation in the one finished sacrifice |
| Presence | Transubstantiation; substantial change | Real spiritual/sacramental presence, or memorial; no transubstantiation |
| Who offers it? | Ordained priest | Congregation with a minister; priesthood of believers |
| Purpose | Sacrifice + sacrament; benefits applied to living and dead | Communion, remembrance, strengthening of faith, proclamation of Christ’s death |

These are not minor liturgical preferences. They reflect different readings of the New Testament (especially the institution narratives, John 6, and Hebrews) and of the early church’s practice. Catholic and Protestant Christians can describe one another’s positions accurately while still holding that the other side is mistaken on these points.

questions.response:
The strict preaching of the Ten Commandments does not assume anyone can keep them perfectly in this life. Scripture is clear that no one does (Romans 3:10–23; James 2:10; 1 John 1:8). Their strictness serves other purposes.

They function as a mirror. By holding up God’s perfect standard of love for Him and neighbor, they expose the depth of human sinfulness and the impossibility of self-justification. That conviction is meant to drive people away from reliance on their own obedience and toward the forgiveness and righteousness found only in Christ, who alone fulfilled the law (Matthew 5:17; Galatians 3:24; Romans 10:4).

They also keep believers dependent. Even those united to Christ still fall short. Continual confrontation with the commandments fosters ongoing repentance, eager prayer for the Spirit’s renewing work, and gradual growth in conformity to God’s image—perfection being reserved for the life to come, not achieved here.

In short, the law is preached strictly because God’s holiness is strict, sin is serious, and the gospel is the only sufficient answer. The commandments diagnose the disease; they do not supply the cure.

questions.response:
It appears, to many, through the world’s dependence, order, and the structure of reason and conscience—not as a laboratory demonstration, but as the best account of why there is something rather than nothing, and why that something is intelligible and morally charged.

A few of the classic lines of appearance:

- **Contingency and cause.** Things that exist but need not exist (you, stars, laws that could have been otherwise) seem to require a ground that does not itself depend on anything else. An infinite regress of dependent things explains none of them. That independent ground is what classical theism means by God.
- **Order and fitness.** The universe is not a chaos of brute facts. It is lawful, mathematically describable, and strikingly fit for complex life. Design-like order is the ordinary way we read purpose when we meet it elsewhere; many take the same reading of nature as a whole (fine-tuning of constants, the emergence of mind) to point beyond blind mechanism.
- **Mind and morality.** Consciousness, truth-seeking, and the sense that some things are really right or wrong—not merely preferred—are odd if reality is only matter in motion. A source that is itself mind and good makes better sense of why rational and moral creatures exist and why their judgments can track reality.
- **The limits of “it just is.”** Every alternative (brute fact, infinite regress, self-causing universe) also asks for a kind of faith. The theistic reading is that the appearance of dependence, order, and value is not an illusion but a sign.

None of this compels assent the way a proof in geometry does. People weigh the same appearances and conclude differently—some find God the most coherent explanation, others find the appearances better explained without one, or find the problem of evil decisive against a good God. The question “how doth it appear” is therefore answered by tracing those signs and then judging, honestly, whether they hold.

There is no single agreed answer. “God” is a name people use for very different ideas, depending on tradition, philosophy, and personal experience.

In many monotheistic religions—Judaism, Christianity, and Islam among them—God is the one supreme being: creator of the universe, eternal, all-powerful and all-knowing, and in some sense personal (a “who,” not merely a force). Details differ sharply: whether God is triune, how God relates to scripture and law, what God requires of people, and whether God intervenes in history.

Other traditions use the word, or something like it, differently:
- **Polytheistic** views speak of many gods, often with limited domains.
- **Pantheism** identifies God with the universe or nature itself.
- **Panentheism** holds that the divine includes the universe but is more than it.
- **Deism** posits a creator who does not intervene.
- Some **Hindu** and other Asian traditions speak of Brahman, Ishvara, or deities in ways that do not map cleanly onto Western “God.”
- **Philosophical** uses treat God as a necessary being, first cause, ground of moral value, or ultimate reality—sometimes without religious worship attached.

Nonreligious views reject the claim that any such being exists. On those accounts, “God” names a human idea: a projection, a cultural symbol, a moral ideal, or a mistaken explanation of the world. Agnostic positions hold that we do not, or cannot, know.

So “what God is” is not a settled fact the way the charge of an electron is. It is a contested concept. People answer it from revelation, tradition, argument, experience, or the absence of those. questions.response:
The Fall (Adam and Eve’s disobedience in Genesis 3) is understood in traditional Christian teaching to have brought sin, death, and alienation from God upon the whole human race.

Core consequences drawn from Scripture and historic doctrine include:

- **Loss of communion with God** and original righteousness. Humanity was driven from Eden and cut off from unhindered fellowship with the Creator (Genesis 3:23–24).
- **Sin and a corrupted nature** passed to all descendants. “Sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men” (Romans 5:12). This is often called original sin: a bent will, guilt, and inability to restore oneself.
- **Physical and spiritual death**, plus liability to judgment. The warning “you shall surely die” was fulfilled in mortality and in separation from God; apart from redemption, this includes eternal punishment (Genesis 2:17; Romans 6:23).
- **Misery in this life**: pain in childbearing, toilsome labor, a cursed ground that yields thorns, conflict, shame, and the frustration of a creation now “subjected to futility” (Genesis 3:16–19; Romans 8:20–22). Disease, sorrow, and natural evil are traced theologically to this rupture.
- **Enslavement under God’s wrath and curse** until grace intervenes. Catechisms such as the Westminster Shorter Catechism summarize the estate of fallen humanity as loss of communion with God, subjection to his wrath and curse, and exposure to all the miseries of this life, to death, and to hell.

Christian hope locates the remedy not in human effort but in the “second Adam,” Jesus Christ, whose obedience and death undo the Fall’s condemnation for those united to him (Romans 5:15–21; 1 Corinthians 15:21–22). Different traditions weight these points differently, but the misery of the Fall is consistently sin, death, suffering, and estrangement from God.

questions.response:
The “second covenant” is the new covenant mediated by Jesus Christ (Jer. 31:31–34; Luke 22:20; Heb. 8–10), set over against the first (Mosaic) covenant. God’s grace is manifested in it chiefly in these ways:

- **In the person and work of Christ himself.** “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). He is the mediator who fulfills the law’s demands, bears its curse, and secures an eternal inheritance for his people (Heb. 9:15; Gal. 3:13–14).

- **In full and final forgiveness.** Under the new covenant God promises, “I will forgive their wickedness and will remember their sins no more” (Jer. 31:34; Heb. 8:12; 10:17–18). This rests on Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice, not on repeated animal offerings.

- **In inward renewal by the Spirit.** God writes his law on the heart and gives a new heart and Spirit so that obedience flows from transformed desire rather than mere external command (Jer. 31:33; Ezek. 36:26–27; Rom. 8:3–4; 2 Cor. 3:3–6).

- **In direct, personal knowledge of God and free access to him.** All covenant members “will know the Lord” (Jer. 31:34), and believers draw near with confidence through Christ’s blood (Heb. 4:16; 10:19–22).

- **In an unconditional, everlasting bond.** The new covenant is enacted on better promises and cannot be broken by human failure in the way the Sinai covenant could; its blessings are secured by Christ’s obedience and intercession (Heb. 7:22–25; 8:6; 13:20).

In short, grace appears not as a mere mitigation of law but as God’s free, effective gift of Christ, forgiveness, the Spirit, and eternal life to all who believe.

The catechism answers:

> They who, having never heard the gospel, know not Jesus Christ, and believe not in him, cannot be saved, be they never so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature, or the laws of that religion which they profess; neither is there salvation in any other, but in Christ alone, who is the Savior only of his body the church.

### Biblical grounding typically cited for this view
- Salvation is exclusively through Christ: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6); “there is salvation in no one else” (Acts 4:12).

It shows God’s existence, power, and moral law, yet leaves people under condemnation apart from the gospel.

In this framework, Christ is the only Savior, and he saves his people (the church) through the means he has appointed—chiefly the preaching of the Word and the response of faith.

Not all Christians hold this strict exclusivist position. Some affirm **inclusivism**: people may be saved by Christ’s work even without explicit knowledge of him (e.g., through a sincere response to whatever light they have, or by God’s sovereign application of Christ’s atonement). There is no single agreed answer. “God” is a name people use for whatever they take to be ultimate—often a supreme being, sometimes a more abstract ground of reality.

**Common theistic ideas**
- In Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, God is usually understood as one, personal, eternal creator who is all-powerful, all-knowing, and morally perfect, and who relates to the world and to people.
- Other traditions speak of many gods (polytheism), of God as identical with the universe (pantheism), or of a divine reality that includes the world but is more than it (panentheism).

**Philosophical sketches**
Philosophers have described God as a necessary being (something that must exist), a first cause or prime mover, the ground of being, perfect goodness, or the source of moral and rational order. These are arguments and definitions, not proofs everyone accepts.

**Other views**
Atheists hold that no such being exists. Agnostics hold that we do not or cannot know. Some people use “God” metaphorically—for love, nature, conscience, or the mystery of existence—without meaning a supernatural person.

So “What is God?” is partly a question of definition and partly a question of belief. Traditions answer it through scripture, practice, and experience; philosophy answers it through argument; many people answer it by saying the word points beyond what we can fully grasp. Which of those approaches matters most depends on what you are asking—definition, evidence, or personal meaning.

questions.response:
**The decrees of God** are a classic concept in Christian systematic theology (especially Reformed/Calvinist traditions): God’s eternal, sovereign purpose by which He has freely and unchangeably ordained everything that comes to pass.

### Classic definition
The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), Chapter 3, states it this way:

> God from all eternity, by the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely and unchangeably ordained whatsoever comes to pass; yet so as thereby neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures, nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established.

Similar ideas appear in other confessions (e.g., the Belgic Confession, Canons of Dort) and in theologians such as Calvin, Turretin, and Hodge.

### Main features usually included
- **Eternal**: The decree is not a reaction in time but part of God’s timeless counsel.
- **Comprehensive**: It covers all events—creation, history, human choices, salvation, and final judgment—without exception.
- **Wise, holy, and free**: Grounded in God’s perfect knowledge, goodness, and sovereign will, not necessity or external constraint.
- **Unchangeable**: What God has purposed will certainly occur; the decree is not revised by events.
- **Compatible with secondary causes**: Human responsibility, free agency (in the sense of acting according to one’s nature and desires), and natural processes are real and are the means by which the decree is carried out. God is not said to be the author of sin; He permits and governs it for His purposes without being its moral cause.
- **Particular aspects**: Within the one decree, theology often distinguishes elements such as the decree of election/predestination (choosing some for salvation in Christ), reprobation (passing over others), and the broader decree of providence that governs all creation.

### Related distinctions
Theologians sometimes speak of God’s **decretive will** (what He has sovereignly ordained will happen) versus His **preceptive will** (what He commands humans to do). These can differ in appearance—people disobey commands—yet both fall under His ultimate purpose. The decrees are also closely tied to doctrines of providence (God’s ongoing governance) and predestination.

### Broader context
Not all Christian traditions use the language of “decrees” in the same strong sense. Arminian, Lutheran, Catholic, and Eastern Orthodox theologies affirm God’s sovereignty, foreknowledge, and providence but often differ on the extent of unconditional ordination, the relation of divine will to human free will, and how election is understood. The term is most precise and central in the Reformed tradition.

In short, the decrees express the conviction that nothing occurs outside God’s eternal, wise, and holy plan, while human moral responsibility remains intact. For primary sources, see the Westminster Confession Chapter 3, the Canons of Dort, or standard Reformed systematic theologies.

questions.question: How do we know there is a God?

questions.response:
There isn’t a single proof that settles the question for everyone. People who believe in God usually point to a mix of philosophical arguments, personal experience, and trust in a tradition—not to a laboratory demonstration. Whether those reasons are enough is something reasonable people still disagree about.

Common lines of thought include:

- **Cosmological arguments.** Why is there something rather than nothing? Some argue that the universe’s existence, or its beginning, needs a cause that is not itself part of the universe—often called God.
- **Design or fine-tuning.** The universe’s laws and constants look strikingly suited to life. Some take that as a sign of intention; others say we only notice the conditions that allow observers, or that unknown physics may explain it.
- **Moral arguments.** If objective right and wrong exist, some argue they need a grounding beyond human preference. Critics reply that morality can be grounded in reason, human nature, or social life without God.
- **Experience and testimony.** Many people report a sense of presence, answered prayer, or moral transformation, and trust religious texts and communities. These are powerful for those who have them, but hard to transfer as public evidence.
- **Ontological and other abstract arguments.** Some try to show that the very idea of a greatest conceivable being implies existence. These are highly contested even among believers.

None of these is universally accepted. Critics raise the problem of evil and suffering, the success of natural explanations, disagreements among religions, and the possibility that “God” is a name for what we don’t yet understand. Believers often answer that God is not a scientific hypothesis in the ordinary sense, and that faith involves trust as well as argument.

So “how do we know?” depends on what kind of knowing you accept. If you require the kind of evidence used in science, many conclude we don’t know. If you allow philosophical reasoning, moral intuition, or religious experience, some conclude belief is rational—even if not proven. Both stances are live options; the question is which standards of evidence you find compelling, and whether you’ve examined the strongest versions of the arguments on each side.

questions.question: How do we know that the Bible is the Word of God?
questions.reference_answer: The Bible evidences itself to be God's Word by the heavenliness of its doctrine, the unity of its parts, its power to convert sinners and to edify saints; but the Spirit of God only, bearing witness by and with the Scriptures in our hearts, is able fully to persuade us that the Bible is the Word of God.

questions.response:
Christians do not usually claim the Bible can be proved the way a lab result is proved. They argue that a set of historical, textual, and theological considerations make it reasonable to receive it as God’s word—and that the Spirit confirms that conviction in believers. Here is the main case, stated plainly.

### What the claim means
“Word of God” does not mean every sentence was dictated in the same way, or that the Bible is a science textbook. Classic Christian teaching (for example, 2 Timothy 3:16 and 2 Peter 1:20–21) holds that God so guided the human authors that what they wrote is trustworthy revelation: God’s message in human words, centered on who God is and what he has done, especially in Jesus.

### Lines of argument Christians rely on

**1. Jesus’ own stance**  
The Gospels present Jesus treating the Old Testament as God’s word (“Scripture cannot be broken,” John 10:35; “it is written”). He also commissioned apostles and promised the Spirit would teach them (John 14–16). If Jesus is who he claimed to be, his view of Scripture carries unique weight. That pushes the question back to whether the resurrection and his self-claims hold up historically—which is why Christian apologetics spends so much time there.

**2. The resurrection as the hinge**  
The New Testament writers tie their authority to having seen the risen Jesus (1 Corinthians 15; Acts 1–2). If Jesus rose, his endorsement of the Scriptures and of the apostolic witness is not merely religious opinion. Historians debate the details, but the early, public claim of resurrection, the empty-tomb tradition, and the sudden origin of the church are the facts any alternative explanation has to account for.

**3. The character of the text itself**  
- Many authors, centuries, and genres, yet a single storyline: creation, fall, covenant, exile, Messiah, church, new creation.  
- The Old Testament is quoted and fulfilled in the New in ways the writers treat as intentional, not accidental.  
- Moral and theological depth that has shaped cultures for millennia, including sharp self-criticism of God’s own people—unusual for pure propaganda.

**4. Historical and manuscript grounding**  
The Bible is not a late legend floating free of history. We have a very large manuscript tradition for the New Testament compared with other ancient works, early quotations in the church fathers, and archaeological and historical points of contact (places, officials, customs) that generally fit the first-century setting. That supports *reliability as ancient testimony*; it does not by itself prove inspiration. Christians treat reliable human testimony about God’s acts as the vehicle of revelation.

**5. Prophecy and coherence**  
Believers point to predictions and patterns (for example, servant and kingdom themes in Isaiah, Micah’s Bethlehem, the broad shape of Daniel and the prophets) that they see fulfilled in Jesus. Critics reply that some “fulfillments” are reread in light of Jesus, or are vague. The Christian claim is cumulative: the pattern fits Jesus better than rival centers of history, not that every verse is a crystal-clear prediction.

**6. The church’s reception and the Spirit’s witness**  
The canon was not invented by a single council out of nowhere. Books were received because churches already treated them as apostolic and life-giving; later councils recognized that reception. John Calvin and many others add that ultimate certainty is not a bare syllogism but the Holy Spirit persuading the reader that God is speaking (the “internal testimony”). Arguments remove obstacles; they do not replace faith.

### What this does *not* prove
- It does not force agreement the way a mathematical proof does. People of good will study the same evidence and remain unconvinced; other religions offer parallel claims for their scriptures.  
- Difficulties remain: violence in some Old Testament narratives, apparent tensions between passages, the long process of canon recognition, and the gap between “reliable history” and “God-breathed.” Christians answer these in different ways (genre, progressive revelation, textual criticism), but they are real questions, not trivia.  
- Personal transformation and cultural influence are supporting signs, not standalone proof—other movements have changed lives too.

### A short way to put it
We “know” in the Christian sense by a convergence: Jesus’ authority, the resurrection claim, the unity and historical rootedness of the writings, the church’s long reception of them, and the Spirit’s convincing work in those who read them as addressed to them. Historical study can show that the Bible is a serious, early, and remarkably preserved witness to Israel’s faith and to Jesus. Calling it the Word of God is the further judgment that in that witness God himself has spoken—and that judgment is held by faith, open to examination, not by coercion.

If you want to go deeper, the most useful next step is usually one concrete strand: the historical case for the resurrection, how the New Testament uses the Old, or how a particular difficult passage is handled.

questions.response:
In Christian theology—especially Reformed and confessional Protestant traditions—the decrees of God are His eternal, sovereign purposes by which He has freely and unchangeably ordained everything that comes to pass.

A classic statement appears in the Westminster Confession of Faith (3.1): God, “from all eternity, did, by the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely, and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass.” These decrees are understood as:

- **Eternal** — settled before creation, not reactions to events in time.
- **Wise and holy** — flowing from God’s perfect knowledge and character.
- **Sovereign and efficacious** — they certainly accomplish what God intends (creation, providence, redemption, and final judgment).
- **Comprehensive** — covering all events, while not removing secondary causes or human responsibility.

Scriptural themes often cited include God’s working “all things according to the counsel of his will” (Ephesians 1:11), His foreknowledge and predestination (Romans 8:29–30), and the certainty of events such as the crucifixion (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28).

Theologians commonly distinguish God’s **decretive will** (what He has ordained will happen) from His **preceptive will** (what He commands creatures to do). Not every tradition uses the language of “decrees” in the same exhaustive sense; some emphasize God’s desires, permissions, or responses within history more than a single eternal plan that fixes every detail. The core idea, however, is that history unfolds according to God’s purposeful counsel rather than by chance.

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about the holy scripture?
questions.reference_answer: Although the light of nature, and the works of creation and providence, do so far manifest the goodness, wisdom, and power of God, as to leave men inexcusable; yet are they not sufficient to give that knowledge of God, and of his will, which is necessary unto salvation; therefore it pleased the Lord, at sundry times, and in divers manners, to reveal himself, and to declare that his will unto his Church; and afterwards, for the better preserving and propagating of the truth, and for the more sure establishment and comfort of the Church against the corruption of the flesh, and the malice of Satan and of the world, to commit the same wholly unto writing; which maketh the holy Scripture to be most necessary; those former ways of God's revealing his will unto his people being now ceased. Under the name of holy Scripture, or the Word of God written, are now contained all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which are these: Of the Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, The Song of Songs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi; Of the New Testament: The Gospels according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, John. The Acts of the Apostles, Paul's Epistles to the Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, The Epistle to the Hebrews, The Epistle of James, The First and Second Epistles of Peter, The First, Second, and Third Epistles of John, The Epistle of Jude, The Revelation. All which are given by inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life. The books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon of the Scripture; and therefore are of no authority in the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved, or made use of, than other human writings. The authority of the holy Scripture, for which it ought to be believed and obeyed, dependeth not upon the testimony of any man or church, but wholly upon God (who is truth itself), the Author thereof; and therefore it is to be received, because it is the Word of God. We may be moved and induced by the testimony of the Church to an high and reverent esteem of the holy Scripture; and the heavenliness of the matter, the efficacy of the doctrine, the majesty of the style, the consent of all the parts, the scope of the whole (which is to give all glory to God), the full discovery it makes of the only way of man's salvation, the many other incomparable excellencies, and the entire perfection thereof, are arguments whereby it doth abundantly evidence itself to be the Word of God; yet, notwithstanding, our full persuasion and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our hearts. The whole counsel of God, concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man's salvation, faith, and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men. Nevertheless we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word; and that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the Church, common to human actions and societies, which are to be ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence, according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed. All things in Scripture are not alike plain in themselves, nor alike clear unto all; yet those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed, for salvation, are so clearly propounded and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of the ordinary means, may attain unto a sufficient understanding of them. The Old Testament in Hebrew (which was the native language of the people of God of old), and the New Testament in Greek (which at the time of the writing of it was most generally known to the nations), being immediately inspired by God, and by his singular care and providence kept pure in all ages, are therefore authentical; so as in all controversies of religion the Church is finally to appeal unto them. But because these original tongues are not known to all the people of God who have right unto, and interest in the Scriptures, and are commanded, in the fear of God, to read and search them, therefore they are to be translated into the vulgar language of every nation unto which they come, that the Word of God dwelling plentifully in all, they may worship him in an acceptable manner, and, through patience and comfort of the Scriptures, may have hope. The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself; and therefore, when there is a question about the true and full sense of any scripture (which is not manifold, but one), it must be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly. The Supreme Judge, by which all controversies of religion are to be determined, and all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of men, and private spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), in Chapter 1, “Of the Holy Scripture,” teaches the following.

**Necessity.** The light of nature and the works of creation and providence show God’s goodness, wisdom, and power enough to leave people without excuse, but they are not enough for the knowledge of God and his will that is needed for salvation. God therefore revealed himself and his will to the church and committed that revelation wholly to writing, so that the truth would be better preserved and spread, and the church more surely established and comforted.

**Canon.** “Holy Scripture” means the books of the Old and New Testaments, which the Confession lists. They are given by inspiration of God to be the rule of faith and life. The Apocrypha are not divinely inspired and are not part of the canon; they have no authority in the church beyond other human writings.

**Authority.** Scripture’s authority does not rest on any person or church, but wholly on God, its author. It is to be received because it is the Word of God. Full persuasion of its infallible truth and divine authority comes from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in the heart. The church’s testimony may move people to regard Scripture highly, and its heavenly character, doctrines, style, consistency, scope, and other excellencies are arguments that it is the Word of God, but full assurance is the Spirit’s work.

**Sufficiency.** The whole counsel of God concerning everything necessary for his glory, human salvation, faith, and life is either expressly set down in Scripture or deducible from it by good and necessary consequence. Nothing is to be added by new revelations of the Spirit or by human traditions. The Spirit’s inward illumination is still necessary for a saving understanding of what is revealed. Some circumstances of worship and church government, common to human societies, are to be ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence, according to the general rules of the Word.

**Clarity.** Not everything in Scripture is equally plain or equally clear to everyone. What must be known, believed, and observed for salvation is set forth clearly enough, in one place or another, that both the learned and the unlearned, using ordinary means, may reach a sufficient understanding.

**Text and translation.** The Old Testament in Hebrew and the New Testament in Greek, being immediately inspired by God and kept pure in all ages by his care, are authentic. The church is finally to appeal to them in controversies of faith. Because not everyone knows those languages, Scripture is to be translated into the common languages of every nation.

**Interpretation and final authority.** The infallible rule for interpreting Scripture is Scripture itself. When the true and full sense of a passage is in question—and that sense is one, not many—it is to be sought in other places that speak more clearly. The supreme judge in all religious controversies, and the standard by which councils, ancient writers, human doctrines, and private spirits are to be examined, is the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture.

The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), in Chapter 2, “Of God, and of the Holy Trinity,” teaches the following.

**One God.** There is only one living and true God. He is infinite in being and perfection: a most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions. He is immutable, immense, eternal, incomprehensible, almighty, most wise, most holy, most free, and most absolute. He is most loving, gracious, merciful, long-suffering, abundant in goodness and truth, and forgiving of sin; he rewards those who diligently seek him. He is also most just and terrible in his judgments, hates all sin, and will by no means clear the guilty.

**God’s self-sufficiency and sovereignty.** God has all life, glory, goodness, and blessedness in and of himself. He does not need any creature he has made, nor does he derive glory from them; he only manifests his own glory in, by, unto, and upon them. He is the sole fountain of all being—of whom, through whom, and to whom are all things—and has sovereign dominion over them. His knowledge is infinite, infallible, and independent of the creature, so that nothing is contingent or uncertain to him. He is most holy in all his counsels, works, and commands, and worship, service, and obedience are due to him from angels, humans, and every other creature.

**The Trinity.** In the unity of the Godhead there are three persons, of one substance, power, and eternity: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Ghost. The Father is of none, neither begotten nor proceeding; the Son is eternally begotten of the Father; the Holy Ghost eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son.

In short, the Confession affirms classical Christian monotheism and the Nicene doctrine of the Trinity: one divine essence in three coequal, coeternal persons, distinguished by their relations of origin (unbegotten, begotten, and proceeding).

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about god's eternal decree?
questions.reference_answer: God from all eternity did, by the most wise and holy counsel of his own will, freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass; yet so as thereby neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures, nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established. Although God knows whatsoever may or can come to pass upon all supposed conditions, yet hath he not decreed anything because he foresaw it as future, or as that which would come to pass upon such conditions. By the decree of God, for the manifestation of his glory, some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life, and others fore-ordained to everlasting death. These angels and men, thus predestinated and fore-ordained, are particularly and unchangeably designed; and their number is so certain and definite that it can not be either increased or diminished. Those of mankind that are predestinated unto life, God, before the foundation of the world was laid, according to his eternal and immutable purpose, and the secret counsel and good pleasure of his will, hath chosen in Christ, unto everlasting glory, out of his mere free grace and love, without any foresight of faith or good works, or perseverance in either of them, or any other thing in the creature, as conditions, or causes moving him thereunto; and all to the praise of his glorious grace. As God hath appointed the elect unto glory, so hath he, by the eternal and most free purpose of his will, fore-ordained all the means thereunto. Wherefore they who are elected, being fallen in Adam, are redeemed by Christ, are effectually called unto faith in Christ by his Spirit working in due season; are justified, adopted, sanctified, and kept by his power through faith unto salvation. Neither are any other redeemed by Christ, effectually called, justified, adopted, sanctified, and saved, but the elect only. The rest of mankind God was pleased, according to the unsearchable counsel of his own will, whereby he extendeth or withholdeth mercy as he pleaseth, for the glory of his sovereign power over his creatures, to pass by, and to ordain them to dishonor and wrath for their sin, to the praise of his glorious justice. The doctrine of this high mystery of predestination is to be handled with special prudence and care, that men attending the will of God revealed in his Word, and yielding obedience thereunto, may, from the certainty of their effectual vocation, be assured of their eternal election. So shall this doctrine afford matter of praise, reverence, and admiration of God; and of humility, diligence, and abundant consolation to all that sincerely obey the gospel.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), Chapter 3 (“Of God’s Eternal Decree”), teaches the following.

**God ordains all that comes to pass.** From eternity, by the wise and holy counsel of his own will, God freely and unchangeably ordained whatever happens. This does not make God the author of sin, does not force the will of creatures, and does not remove the liberty or contingency of secondary causes; rather, it establishes them.

**The decree is not based on foresight.** God knows everything that could happen under any conditions, but he has not decreed anything because he foresaw it as future or as what would follow from such conditions.

**Election and reprobation.** For the display of his glory, God predestined some people and angels to everlasting life and foreordained others to everlasting death. Those so designated are particularly and unchangeably fixed, and their number cannot be increased or diminished.

**Election is of free grace.** Those chosen for life were chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world, according to God’s eternal purpose and the good pleasure of his will, out of mere free grace and love—not because of foreseen faith, good works, perseverance, or anything else in the creature. Election is to the praise of his glorious grace.

**Means as well as ends.** God also foreordained the means to that glory. The elect, fallen in Adam, are redeemed by Christ, effectually called by the Spirit, justified, adopted, sanctified, and kept by God’s power through faith unto salvation. Only the elect are so redeemed and saved.

**The non-elect.** The rest of mankind God was pleased, according to the unsearchable counsel of his will, to pass by and to ordain to dishonor and wrath for their sin, to the praise of his glorious justice—extending or withholding mercy as he pleases.

**How the doctrine should be used.** This “high mystery” is to be handled with special care, so that people attend to God’s revealed will, obey it, and from the certainty of their effectual calling gain assurance of election. Rightly held, the doctrine leads to praise, reverence, and admiration of God, and to humility, diligence, and consolation for those who sincerely obey the gospel.

In short, the Confession teaches an unconditional, particular decree that includes both election and reprobation, preserves human responsibility and secondary causes, and is meant to humble and comfort believers rather than to encourage speculation or presumption.

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about providence?
questions.reference_answer: God, the great Creator of all things, doth uphold, direct, dispose, and govern all creatures, actions, and things, from the greatest even to the least, by his most wise and holy providence, according to his infallible fore-knowledge and the free and immutable counsel of his own will, to the praise of the glory of his wisdom, power, justice, goodness, and mercy. Although in relation to the foreknowledge and decree of God, the first cause, all things come to pass immutably and infallibly, yet by the same providence he ordereth them to fall out, according to the nature of second causes, either necessarily, freely, or contingently. God, in his ordinary providence, maketh use of means, yet is free to work without, above, and against them, at his pleasure. The almighty power, unsearchable wisdom, and infinite goodness of God so far manifest themselves in his providence that it extendeth itself even to the first fall, and all other sins of angels and men, and that not by a bare permission, but such as hath joined with it a most wise and powerful bounding, and otherwise ordering and governing of them, in a manifold dispensation, to his own holy ends; yet so as the sinfulness thereof proceedeth only from the creature, and not from God; who, being most holy and righteous, neither is nor can be the author or approver of sin. The most wise, righteous, and gracious God doth oftentimes leave for a season his own children to manifold temptations and the corruption of their own hearts, to chastise them for their former sins, or to discover unto them the hidden strength of corruption and deceitfulness of their hearts, that they be humbled; and to raise them to a more close and constant dependence for their support unto himself, and to make them more watchful against all future occasions of sin, and for sundry other just and holy ends. As for those wicked and ungodly men whom God, as a righteous judge, for former sins, doth blind and harden, from them he not only withholdeth his grace, whereby they might have been enlightened in their understandings and wrought upon in their hearts, but sometimes also withdraweth the gifts which they had, and exposeth them to such objects as their corruption makes occasion of sin; and withal, gives them over to their own lusts, the temptations of the world, and the power of Satan; whereby it comes to pass that they harden themselves, even under those means which God useth for the softening of others. As the providence of God doth, in general, reach to all creatures, so, after a most special manner, it taketh care of his Church, and disposeth all things to the good thereof.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith treats providence in Chapter 5 (“Of Providence”). Its teaching can be summarized as follows.

**God governs everything.** God, as Creator, upholds, directs, disposes, and governs all creatures, actions, and things—from the greatest to the least—by his wise and holy providence, according to his infallible foreknowledge and the free, unchangeable counsel of his will, for the praise of his wisdom, power, justice, goodness, and mercy.

**First cause and second causes.** In relation to God’s decree, all things come to pass immutably and infallibly. At the same time, providence orders events according to the nature of secondary causes, so that they occur necessarily, freely, or contingently. Divine sovereignty does not cancel creaturely freedom or ordinary causation.

**Means, and freedom beyond means.** In ordinary providence God uses means, yet he is free to work without, above, or against them as he pleases (miracles and extraordinary acts included).

**Sin is bounded, not authored.** Providence extends even to the fall and to all other sins of angels and humans—not by bare permission only, but with a wise and powerful limiting, ordering, and governing of them toward God’s holy ends. The sinfulness itself comes only from the creature. God, being most holy and righteous, is neither the author nor the approver of sin.

**Why believers are sometimes left to temptation.** God often, for a season, leaves his own children to temptations and the corruption of their hearts: to chasten them for former sins, to show them the deceitfulness of their hearts so they may be humbled, to drive them to closer dependence on him, and to make them more watchful against future sin—and for other just and holy ends.

**Hardening of the wicked.** As a righteous judge, God sometimes blinds and hardens the ungodly for former sins: withholding grace, sometimes withdrawing gifts they had, exposing them to occasions their corruption turns into sin, and giving them over to their own lusts, the world’s temptations, and Satan’s power. They harden themselves even under means God uses to soften others.

**Special care of the church.** Providence reaches all creatures in general, but in a most special way it cares for the church and disposes all things for its good.

In short, the Confession teaches an exhaustive, purposeful divine government of all things that works through ordinary causes, never makes God the author of sin, disciplines believers, judges the wicked, and especially serves the good of the church.

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about god's covenant with man?
questions.reference_answer: The distance between God and the creature is so great that although reasonable creatures do owe obedience unto him as their Creator, yet they could never have any fruition of him as their blessedness and reward but by some voluntary condescension on God's part, which he hath been pleased to express by way of covenant. The first covenant made with man was a covenant of works, wherein life was promised to Adam, and in him to his posterity, upon condition of perfect and personal obedience. Man by his fall having made himself incapable of life by that covenant, the Lord was pleased to make a second, commonly called the covenant of grace: wherein he freely offered unto sinners life and salvation by Jesus Christ, requiring of them faith in him that they may be saved, and promising to give unto all those that are ordained unto life his Holy Spirit, to make them willing and able to believe. This covenant of grace is frequently set forth in the Scripture by the name of a testament, in reference to the death of Jesus Christ the testator, and to the everlasting inheritance, with all things belonging to it, therein bequeathed. This covenant was differently administered in the time of the law and in the time of the gospel: under the law it was administered by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the paschal lamb, and other types and ordinances delivered to the people of the Jews, all fore-signifying Christ to come, which were for that time sufficient and efficacious, through the operation of the Spirit, to instruct and build up the elect in faith in the promised Messiah, by whom they had full remission of sins and eternal salvation; and is called the Old Testament. Under the gospel, when Christ the substance was exhibited, the ordinances in which this covenant is dispensed are the preaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper; which, though fewer in number, and administered with more simplicity and less outward glory, yet in them it is held forth in more fulness, evidence, and spiritual efficacy, to all nations, both Jews and Gentiles; and is called the New Testament. There are not, therefore, two covenants of grace differing in substance, but one and the same under various dispensations.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), Chapter 7 (“Of God’s Covenant with Man”), teaches the following.

**Why a covenant is needed.** The distance between God and creatures is so great that, although rational creatures owe God obedience as Creator, they could never enjoy him as their blessedness and reward except by God’s voluntary condescension. God has been pleased to express that condescension by way of covenant.

**Covenant of works.** The first covenant with man was a covenant of works. Life was promised to Adam, and in him to his posterity, on condition of perfect and personal obedience.

**Covenant of grace.** By the fall, man made himself incapable of life under that first covenant. God was then pleased to make a second covenant, commonly called the covenant of grace. In it he freely offers sinners life and salvation by Jesus Christ, requires faith in Christ for salvation, and promises to give his Holy Spirit to all ordained to eternal life, so that they are made willing and able to believe.

**Testament.** Scripture often calls this covenant of grace a testament, with reference to the death of Christ the testator and to the everlasting inheritance, with all that belongs to it, bequeathed in it.

**One covenant, two administrations.** The covenant of grace was administered differently under the law and under the gospel, but it is one covenant in substance.

- Under the law (the “old testament”), it was administered by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the paschal lamb, and other types and ordinances given to the Jews, all pointing forward to Christ. Through the Spirit these were, for that time, sufficient and effective to instruct and build up the elect in faith in the promised Messiah, through whom they had full remission of sins and eternal salvation.
- Under the gospel (the “new testament”), when Christ the substance was exhibited, the ordinances are the preaching of the Word and the sacraments of baptism and the Lord’s Supper. These are fewer, simpler, and less outwardly glorious, yet they set forth the covenant with more fullness, clarity, and spiritual efficacy to all nations, Jews and Gentiles alike.

There are therefore not two covenants of grace differing in substance, but one and the same covenant under different dispensations.

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about christ the mediator?
questions.reference_answer: It pleased God, in his eternal purpose, to choose and ordain the Lord Jesus, his only-begotten Son, to be the Mediator between God and man, the Prophet, Priest, and King; the Head and Saviour of his Church, the Heir of all things, and Judge of the world; unto whom he did, from all eternity, give a people to be his seed, and to be by him in time redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified. The Son of God, the second person in the Trinity, being very and eternal God, of one substance, and equal with the Father, did, when the fulness of time was come, take upon him man's nature, with all the essential properties and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin: being conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost in the womb of the Virgin Mary, of her substance. So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, the Godhead and the manhood, were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion. Which person is very God and very man, yet one Christ, the only mediator between God and man. The Lord Jesus, in his human nature thus united to the divine, was sanctified and anointed with the Holy Spirit above measure; having in him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, in whom it pleased the Father that all fulness should dwell; to the end that, being holy, harmless, undefiled, and full of grace and truth, he might be thoroughly furnished to execute the office of a mediator and surety. Which office he took not unto himself, but was thereunto called by his Father, who put all power and judgment into his hand, and gave him commandment to execute the same. This office the Lord Jesus did most willingly undertake, which, that he might discharge, he was made under the law, and did perfectly fulfill it; endured most grievous torments immediately in his soul, and most painful sufferings in his body; was crucified, and died; was buried, and remained under the power of death, yet saw no corruption. On the third day he arose from the dead, with the same body in which he suffered; with which also he ascended into heaven, and there sitteth at the right hand of his Father, making intercession; and shall return to judge men and angels at the end of the world. The Lord Jesus, by his perfect obedience and sacrifice of himself, which he through the eternal Spirit once offered up unto God, hath fully satisfied the justice of his Father, and purchased not only reconciliation, but an everlasting inheritance in the kingdom of heaven, for all those whom the Father hath given unto him. Although the work of redemption was not actually wrought by Christ till after his incarnation, yet the virtue, efficacy, and benefits thereof were communicated unto the elect, in all ages successively from the beginning of the world, in and by those promises, types, and sacrifices, wherein he was revealed, and signified to be the seed of the woman which should bruise the serpent's head, and the Lamb slain from the beginning of the world, being yesterday and today the same, and forever. Christ, in the work of mediation, acteth according to both natures; by each nature doing that which is proper to itself; yet, by reason of the unity of the person, that which is proper to one nature is sometimes, in Scripture, attributed to the person denominated by the other nature. To all those for whom Christ hath purchased redemption he doth certainly and effectually apply and communicate the same; making intercession for them, and revealing unto them, in and by the Word, the mysteries of salvation; effectually persuading them by his Spirit to believe and obey; and governing their hearts by his Word and Spirit; overcoming all their enemies by his almighty power and wisdom, in such manner and ways as are most consonant to his wonderful and unsearchable dispensation.
