questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith treats Christ the Mediator in Chapter 8 (“Of Christ the Mediator”). Its teaching can be summarized as follows.

**Eternal appointment.** In God’s eternal purpose, the Lord Jesus, the only begotten Son, was chosen and ordained as Mediator between God and man—Prophet, Priest, and King; Head and Savior of the church; heir of all things; and Judge of the world. From eternity the Father gave him a people to be redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified.

**Person: true God and true man.** The Son, the second person of the Trinity, very and eternal God, of one substance and equal with the Father, in the fullness of time took a true human nature, with its essential properties and common infirmities, yet without sin. He was conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the virgin Mary, of her substance. Two whole, perfect, and distinct natures—Godhead and manhood—are inseparably joined in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion. He is very God and very man, yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and man.

**Anointing and calling.** In his human nature, united to the divine, he was sanctified and anointed with the Holy Spirit above measure, with all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, so that all fullness dwells in him. Holy, harmless, undefiled, and full of grace and truth, he was fitted to be Mediator and Surety. He did not take this office to himself; the Father called him to it, put all power and judgment in his hand, and commanded him to execute it. He undertook it willingly.

**Obedience, suffering, and exaltation.** To discharge the office he was made under the law and fulfilled it perfectly. He endured grievous torments in soul and painful sufferings in body, was crucified, died, was buried, and remained under the power of death, yet saw no corruption. On the third day he rose with the same body in which he suffered, ascended into heaven, sits at the Father’s right hand making intercession, and will return to judge men and angels at the end of the world.

**Satisfaction and purchase.** By his perfect obedience and the sacrifice of himself, offered once through the eternal Spirit, he fully satisfied the Father’s justice and purchased not only reconciliation but an everlasting inheritance in the kingdom of heaven for all whom the Father has given him.

**Benefits before the incarnation.** Although redemption was actually wrought only after the incarnation, its virtue, efficacy, and benefits were communicated to the elect in every age from the beginning of the world, through the promises, types, and sacrifices in which he was revealed—the seed of the woman and the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world—the same yesterday, today, and forever.

**Both natures in one person.** In mediation he acts according to both natures, each doing what is proper to itself; yet, because of the unity of the person, what belongs to one nature is sometimes in Scripture attributed to the person named by the other nature.

**Application of redemption.** To all for whom he purchased redemption he certainly and effectually applies and communicates it: interceding for them, revealing the mysteries of salvation in and by the Word, effectually persuading them by his Spirit to believe and obey, governing their hearts by Word and Spirit, and overcoming all their enemies by his almighty power and wisdom, in ways fitting his wise and unsearchable dispensation.

In short, the Confession presents Christ as the God-man, eternally appointed and willingly obedient, whose once-for-all work fully satisfies divine justice and whose ongoing mediation effectually saves all the Father has given him.

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about effectual calling?
questions.reference_answer: All those whom God hath predestinated unto life, and those only, he is pleased, in his appointed and accepted time, effectually to call, by his Word and Spirit, out of that state of sin and death, in which they are by nature, to grace and salvation by Jesus Christ; enlightening their minds, spiritually and savingly, to understand the things of God; taking away their heart of stone, and giving unto them an heart of flesh; renewing their wills, and by his almighty power determining them to that which is good, and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ; yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by his grace. This effectual call is of God's free and special grace alone, not from anything at all foreseen in man; who is altogether passive therein, until, being quickened and renewed by the Holy Spirit, he is thereby enabled to answer this call, and to embrace the grace offered and conveyed in it. Elect infants, dying in infancy, are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who worketh when, and where, and how he pleaseth. So also are all other elect persons who are incapable of being outwardly called by the ministry of the Word. Others, not elected, although they may be called by the ministry of the Word, and may have some common operations of the Spirit, yet they never truly come unto Christ, and therefore cannot be saved: much less can men, not professing the Christian religion, be saved in any other way whatsoever, be they never so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature and the law of that religion they do profess; and to assert and maintain that they may is very pernicious, and to be detested.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), Chapter 10 (“Of Effectual Calling”), teaches that effectual calling is God’s sovereign, gracious work by which he brings the elect to salvation in Christ. Its main points are:

- God effectually calls only those he has predestined to life, and he does so at the time he appoints. By his Word and Spirit he draws them out of their natural state of sin and death into grace and salvation through Jesus Christ.
- In this call he enlightens their minds to understand the things of God, removes their “heart of stone” and gives them a “heart of flesh,” renews their wills, and by his almighty power determines them to what is good, effectually drawing them to Christ. They come freely, because his grace makes them willing.
- This call is of God’s free and special grace alone, not based on anything foreseen in the person. Until quickened and renewed by the Holy Spirit, the person is passive; only then is he or she enabled to answer the call and embrace the grace offered in it.
- Elect infants who die in infancy, and other elect persons incapable of being outwardly called by the ministry of the Word, are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when, where, and how he pleases.
- Those not elected may be outwardly called by the Word and may experience some common operations of the Spirit, yet they never truly come to Christ and therefore cannot be saved. The Confession also rejects the idea that people outside the Christian religion can be saved by the light of nature or by diligence in another religion.

In short, effectual calling is presented as an irresistible, regenerating work of the Spirit that applies redemption to the elect, distinct from a merely external or common call.

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about justification?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God effectually calleth he also freely justifieth; not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous: not for anything wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ's sake alone; nor by imputing faith itself, the act of believing, or any other evangelical obedience to them, as their righteousness; but by imputing the obedience and satisfaction of Christ unto them, they receiving and resting on him and his righteousness by faith; which faith they have not of themselves, it is the gift of God. Faith, thus receiving and resting on Christ and his righteousness, is the alone instrument of justification; yet is it not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love. Christ, by his obedience and death, did fully discharge the debt of all those that are thus justified, and did make a proper, real, and full satisfaction to his Father's justice in their behalf. Yet inasmuch as he was given by the Father for them, and his obedience and satisfaction accepted in their stead, and both freely, not for anything in them, their justification is only of free grace; that both the exact justice and rich grace of God might be glorified in the justification of sinners. God did, from all eternity, decree to justify all the elect, and Christ did, in the fulness of time, die for their sins, and rise again for their justification: nevertheless, they are not justified until the Holy Spirit doth, in due time, actually apply Christ unto them. God doth continue to forgive the sins of those that are justified; and although they can never fall from the state of justification, yet they may by their sins fall under God's fatherly displeasure, and not have the light of his countenance restored unto them, until they humble themselves, confess their sins, beg pardon, and renew their faith and repentance. The justification of believers under the Old Testament was, in all these respects, one and the same with the justification of believers under the New Testament.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith treats justification in Chapter 11 (“Of Justification”). Its teaching can be summarized as follows.

**What justification is.** God freely justifies those whom he effectually calls. Justification is not the infusion of righteousness into a person, but God’s pardoning their sins and accounting and accepting them as righteous. It is not based on anything wrought in them or done by them, but for Christ’s sake alone. Faith itself, the act of believing, or any other evangelical obedience is not imputed as their righteousness. What is imputed is the obedience and satisfaction of Christ. They receive and rest on Christ and his righteousness by faith—and that faith is not of themselves; it is the gift of God.

**Faith as the instrument.** Faith, receiving and resting on Christ and his righteousness, is the sole instrument of justification. Yet it is never alone in the person justified: it is always accompanied by all other saving graces, and it is not a dead faith but works by love.

**Ground in Christ’s work and free grace.** By his obedience and death, Christ fully discharged the debt of those who are justified and made a proper, real, and full satisfaction to the Father’s justice on their behalf. Because Christ was given by the Father for them, and his obedience and satisfaction were accepted in their place—freely, not for anything in them—their justification is only of free grace, so that both God’s exact justice and his rich grace are glorified in the justification of sinners.

**Decree, accomplishment, and application.** From all eternity God decreed to justify the elect. Christ, in the fullness of time, died for their sins and rose again for their justification. They are not justified, however, until the Holy Spirit, in due time, actually applies Christ to them.

**Continuing forgiveness and perseverance.** God continues to forgive the sins of those who are justified. They can never fall from the state of justification, though by their sins they may fall under God’s fatherly displeasure and lose the light of his countenance until they humble themselves, confess their sins, seek pardon, and renew their faith and repentance.

**Old and New Testaments.** The justification of believers under the Old Testament was, in all these respects, the same as the justification of believers under the New Testament.

In short, the Confession teaches forensic justification by grace alone, through faith alone, on the ground of Christ’s imputed righteousness alone—distinct from sanctification, yet never separated from a living faith that works by love.

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about the perseverance of the saints?
questions.reference_answer: They whom God hath accepted in his Beloved, effectually called and sanctified by his Spirit, can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace; but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved. This perseverance of the saints depends, not upon their own free will, but upon the immutability of the decree of election, flowing from the free and unchangeable love of God the Father; upon the efficacy of the merit and intercession of Jesus Christ; the abiding of the Spirit and of the seed of God within them; and the nature of the covenant of grace: from all which ariseth also the certainty and infallibility thereof. Nevertheless they may, through the temptations of Satan and of the world, the prevalency of corruption remaining in them, and the neglect of the means of their preservation, fall into grievous sins; and for a time continue therein: whereby they incur God's displeasure, and grieve his Holy Spirit; come to be deprived of some measure of their graces and comforts; have their hearts hardened, and their consciences wounded; hurt and scandalize others, and bring temporal judgments upon themselves.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) teaches the perseverance of the saints in Chapter 17. In summary:

1. Those whom God has accepted in Christ, effectually called, and sanctified by the Spirit cannot totally or finally fall away from the state of grace. They will certainly persevere to the end and be eternally saved.

2. This perseverance does not depend on their own free will, but on the unchangeable decree of election, the free and unchangeable love of God the Father, the merit and intercession of Christ, the abiding of the Spirit and the seed of God in them, and the nature of the covenant of grace. From these the certainty and infallibility of perseverance arise.

3. Nevertheless, believers may, through temptation, remaining corruption, and neglect of the means of grace, fall into grievous sins and continue in them for a time. In doing so they incur God’s displeasure, grieve the Holy Spirit, lose some measure of graces and comforts, harden their hearts, wound their consciences, harm others, and bring temporal judgments on themselves—yet they are not finally lost.

The chapter thus affirms both the certainty of final salvation for the elect and the real possibility of serious, temporary lapses.

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about the last judgment?
questions.reference_answer: God hath appointed a day wherein he will judge the world in righteousness by Jesus Christ, to whom all power and judgment is given of the Father. In which day, not only the apostate angels shall be judged, but likewise all persons, that have lived upon earth, shall appear before the tribunal of Christ, to give an account of their thoughts, words, and deeds; and to receive according to what they have done in the body, whether good or evil. The end of God's appointing this day, is for the manifestation of the glory of his mercy in the eternal salvation of the elect; and of his justice in the damnation of the reprobate, who are wicked and disobedient. For then shall the righteous go into everlasting life, and receive that fulness of joy and refreshing which shall come from the presence of the Lord: but the wicked, who know not God, and obey not the gospel of Jesus Christ, shall be cast into eternal torments, and be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power. As Christ would have us to be certainly persuaded that there shall be a day of judgment, both to deter all men from sin, and for the greater consolation of the godly in their adversity: so will he have that day unknown to men, that they may shake off all carnal security, and be always watchful, because they know not at what hour the Lord will come; and may be ever prepared to say, Come, Lord Jesus, come quickly. Amen.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), Chapter 33 (“Of the Last Judgment”), teaches the following.

God has appointed a day when he will judge the world in righteousness by Jesus Christ, to whom the Father has given all power and judgment. On that day the fallen angels and every person who has ever lived will appear before Christ’s tribunal, give an account of their thoughts, words, and deeds, and receive according to what they have done in the body, whether good or evil.

The purpose of that day is to display God’s glory: his mercy in the eternal salvation of the elect, and his justice in the damnation of the reprobate. The righteous will enter everlasting life and the fullness of joy in the Lord’s presence; the wicked, who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of Jesus Christ, will be cast into eternal torments and punished with everlasting destruction away from the presence of the Lord and the glory of his power.

Christ wants people to be sure that a day of judgment will come, both to deter sin and to comfort the godly in adversity. He also keeps the day unknown, so that people will not grow careless, will stay watchful, and will always be ready to say, “Come, Lord Jesus.”

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the means by which we know god?
questions.reference_answer: We know God by two means: First, by the creation, preservation, and government of the universe, since that universe is before our eyes like a beautiful book in which all creatures, great and small, are as letters to make us ponder the invisible things of God: God's eternal power and divinity, as the apostle Paul says in Romans 1:20. All these things are enough to convict humans and to leave them without excuse. Second, God makes himself known to us more clearly by his holy and divine Word, as much as we need in this life, for God's glory and for our salvation.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 2 (The Means by Which We Know God). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (Article 2) teaches that we know God by two means:

1. **Creation (general revelation)**: By the creation, preservation, and government of the universe, which is like a book in which all creatures lead us to see God’s eternal power and divinity (cf. Rom. 1:20). This is enough to leave people without excuse.

2. **Scripture (special revelation)**: More clearly and fully by His holy and divine Word, as far as is necessary for His glory and our salvation in this life.

In short, nature reveals that God exists and is powerful, while Scripture reveals Him savingly and sufficiently for faith and life.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the sufficiency of scripture?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that this Holy Scripture contains the will of God completely and that everything one must believe to be saved is sufficiently taught in it. For since the entire manner of service which God requires of us is described in it at great length, no one- even an apostle or an angel from heaven, as Paul says- (Gal. 1:8) ought to teach other than what the Holy Scriptures have already taught us. For since it is forbidden to add to the Word of God, or take anything away from it, (Deut. 12:32, Rev. 22:18-19) it is plainly demonstrated that the teaching is perfect and complete in all respects. Therefore we must not consider human writings- no matter how holy their authors may have been- equal to the divine writings; nor may we put custom, nor the majority, nor age, nor the passage of times or persons, nor councils, decrees, or official decisions above the truth of God, for truth is above everything else. For all human beings are liars by nature and more vain than vanity itself. Therefore we reject with all our hearts everything that does not agree with this infallible rule, as we are taught to do by the apostles when they say, "Test the spirits to see whether they are from God," (1 John 4:1) and also, "Do not receive into the house or welcome anyone who comes to you and does not bring this teaching." (2 John 10)

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561) addresses the sufficiency of Scripture in Article 7. It teaches that Holy Scripture fully contains the will of God and sufficiently teaches everything necessary for salvation. The whole manner of service God requires is set out in it, so no one—not even an apostle or an angel—may teach anything beyond what Scripture already teaches. Because it is forbidden to add to or take away from God’s Word, its teaching is perfect and complete.

Human writings, however holy their authors, are not equal to the divine writings. Custom, majority opinion, antiquity, councils, decrees, or official decisions must not be placed above the truth of God. Whatever does not agree with this infallible rule is to be rejected.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the creation of all things?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that the Father, when it seemed good to him, created heaven and earth and all other creatures from nothing, by the Word- that is to say, by the Son. God has given all creatures their being, form, and appearance and their various functions for serving their Creator. Even now God also sustains and governs them all, according to his eternal providence and by his infinite power, that they may serve humanity, in order that humanity may serve God. God has also created the angels good, that they might be messengers of God and serve the elect. Some of them have fallen from the excellence in which God created them into eternal perdition; and the others have persisted and remained in their original state, by the grace of God. The devils and evil spirits are so corrupt that they are enemies of God and of everything good. They lie in wait for the church and every member of it like thieves, with all their power, to destroy and spoil everything by their deceptions. So then, by their own wickedness they are condemned to everlasting damnation, daily awaiting their torments. For that reason we detest the error of the Sadducees, who deny that there are spirits and angels, and also the error of the Manicheans, who say that the devils originated by themselves, being evil by nature, without having been corrupted.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 12 (The Creation of All Things). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561) treats the creation of all things mainly in Article 12, with related teaching in Articles 13 and 14.

**Article 12 — Creation** teaches that:

- The Father created heaven, earth, and all creatures **out of nothing**, by the Word—that is, by his Son—as it seemed good to him.
- He gave every creature its being, shape, form, and particular offices so that it might serve its Creator.
- He still upholds and governs all things by his eternal providence and infinite power, for the service of humanity, so that people may serve God.
- He created the angels good, to be his messengers and to serve the elect. Some fell from that excellence into everlasting perdition; others, by God’s grace, remained steadfast.
- Devils and evil spirits are corrupt enemies of God and of every good thing, hostile especially to the church, and are destined for eternal damnation—not because they were created evil, but because they fell.
- The confession rejects the Sadducees, who deny spirits and angels, and the Manichees, who teach that devils originated of themselves and are wicked by nature rather than by corruption.

**Related articles:** Article 13 says God did not abandon creation after making it, but rules and governs it by his providence. Article 14 teaches that God created man good, in his own image, able to conform to his will, and that man fell by disobedience.

In short, creation is the free work of the triune God (Father by the Son), from nothing, ordered to God’s glory and humanity’s service of God, and continually upheld—not a self-originating or dualistic cosmos.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the doctrine of god's providence?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that this good God, after creating all things, did not abandon them to chance or fortune but leads and governs them according to his holy will, in such a way that nothing happens in this world without God's orderly arrangement. Yet God is not the author of, and cannot be charged with, the sin that occurs. For God's power and goodness are so great and incomprehensible that God arranges and does his works very well and justly even when the devils and the wicked act unjustly. We do not wish to inquire with undue curiosity into what God does that surpasses human understanding and is beyond our ability to comprehend. But in all humility and reverence we adore the just judgments of God, which are hidden from us, being content to be Christ's disciples, so as to learn only what God shows us in the Word, without going beyond those limits. This doctrine gives us unspeakable comfort since it teaches us that nothing can happen to us by chance but only by the arrangement of our gracious heavenly Father, who watches over us with fatherly care, sustaining all creatures under his lordship, so that not one of the hairs on our heads (for they are all numbered) nor even a little bird can fall to the ground without the will of our Father. (Matt. 10:29-30) In this thought we rest, knowing that God holds in check the devils and all our enemies, who cannot hurt us without divine permission and will. For that reason we reject the damnable error of the Epicureans, who say that God does not get involved in anything and leaves everything to chance.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 13 (The Doctrine of God's Providence). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561) treats God’s providence chiefly in Article 13.

It teaches that the good God who created all things did not abandon them to fortune or chance. He rules and governs them according to his holy will, so that nothing in the world happens apart from his orderly arrangement. At the same time, God is not the author of sin and cannot be charged with it: his power and goodness are such that he orders his work justly even when devils and wicked people act unjustly.

The article warns against prying with undue curiosity into what exceeds human understanding. Believers are to adore God’s hidden judgments in humility and to learn only what Christ shows in his Word.

This doctrine is presented as a source of comfort: nothing befalls us by chance, but only by the arrangement of our gracious heavenly Father, who watches over us with fatherly care. Not a hair of the head nor a sparrow falls apart from his will, and he restrains enemies so that they cannot harm his people without his permission. The confession therefore rejects the Epicurean error that God is uninvolved and leaves all things to chance.

(The surrounding articles on creation and the fall supply context, but the explicit doctrine of providence is Article 13.)

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the creation and fall of humanity?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that God created human beings from the dust of the earth and made and formed them in his image and likeness- good, just, and holy; able by their will to conform in all things to the will of God. But when they were in honor they did not understand it (Ps. 49:20) and did not recognize their excellence. But they subjected themselves willingly to sin and consequently to death and the curse, lending their ear to the word of the devil. For they transgressed the commandment of life, which they had received, and by their sin they separated themselves from God, who was their true life, having corrupted their entire nature. So they made themselves guilty and subject to physical and spiritual death, having become wicked, perverse, and corrupt in all their ways. They lost all their excellent gifts which they had received from God, and retained none of them except for small traces which are enough to make them inexcusable. Moreover, all the light in us is turned to darkness, as the Scripture teaches us: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it." (John 1:5) Here John calls the human race "darkness." Therefore we reject everything taught to the contrary concerning human free will, since humans are nothing but the slaves of sin and cannot do a thing unless it is given them from heaven. (John 3:27) For who can boast of being able to do anything good by oneself, since Christ says, "No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father who sent me"? (John 6:44) Who can glory in their own will when they understand that "the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God"? (Rom. 8:7) Who can speak of their own knowledge in view of the fact that "those who are unspiritual do not receive the gifts of God's Spirit"? (1 Cor. 2:14) In short, who can produce a single thought, knowing that we are not able to think a thing about ourselves, by ourselves, but that "our competence is from God"? (2 Cor. 3:5) And therefore, what the apostle says ought rightly to stand fixed and firm: God works within us both to will and to do according to his good pleasure. (Phil. 2:13) For there is no understanding nor will conforming to God's understanding and will apart from Christ's involvement, as he teaches us when he says, "Apart from me you can do nothing." (John 15:5)

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 14 (The Creation and Fall of Humanity). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561) treats the creation and fall of humanity mainly in Articles 14, 15, and 17, with creation more broadly in Article 12.

**Creation (Article 14).** God created man from the dust of the earth and made him in his own image and likeness: good, righteous, and holy, and able to will what agrees with God’s will. Humanity was created in honor and excellence, not already fallen or defective.

**The fall (Article 14).** Man did not remain in that state. He willfully listened to the devil, transgressed the commandment of life, and subjected himself to sin, death, and the curse. By that disobedience he separated himself from God, who was his true life, and corrupted his whole nature, so that he became liable to both bodily and spiritual death. He lost the excellent gifts he had received, retaining only slight remains—enough to leave him without excuse, but not enough to restore him. The confession therefore denies that fallen people have a free will able to do what is truly good: they are enslaved to sin, cannot come to Christ unless drawn by the Father, and can neither will nor do any spiritual good apart from God’s work in them.

**Original sin (Article 15).** Through Adam’s disobedience, original sin extends to all mankind. It is a corruption of the whole nature and a hereditary disease, present even in infants in the womb, and the root of every actual sin. It is so vile before God that it is enough to condemn all people. Baptism does not abolish or wholly eradicate it; sin still flows from that source. For believers it is not imputed unto condemnation—God forgives it by grace—but they still feel its power and long to be delivered from “this body of death.” The confession rejects the Pelagian claim that sin comes only by imitation.

**Recovery (Article 17).** After the fall, when man had made himself miserable, God in mercy sought him out when he fled in terror, and comforted him with the promise that the seed of the woman would bruise the serpent’s head—pointing ahead to Christ.

In short: humanity was created good and in God’s image, fell by willful disobedience, and is now wholly corrupted by original sin, unable to save itself, yet not abandoned—God promised a Redeemer.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the doctrine of original sin?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that by the disobedience of Adam original sin has been spread through the whole human race. (Rom. 5:12-13) It is a corruption of the whole human nature- an inherited depravity which even infects small infants in their mother's womb, and the root which produces in humanity every sort of sin. It is therefore so vile and enormous in God's sight that it is enough to condemn the human race, and it is not abolished or wholly uprooted even by baptism, seeing that sin constantly boils forth as though from a contaminated spring. Nevertheless, it is not imputed to God's children for their condemnation but is forgiven by his grace and mercy- not to put them to sleep but so that the awareness of this corruption might often make believers groan as they long to be set free from the body of this death. (Rom. 7:24) Therefore we reject the error of the Pelagians who say that this sin is nothing else than a matter of imitation.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 15 (The Doctrine of Original Sin). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561) treats original sin in Article 15 (building on the account of the fall in Article 14). Its teaching can be summarized as follows:

- Through Adam’s disobedience, original sin extends to all mankind. It is a corruption of the whole human nature and a hereditary disease, so that even infants in the womb are infected by it.
- This corruption is the root that produces every kind of actual sin. It is so vile before God that it is sufficient, by itself, to condemn the whole human race.
- Baptism does not abolish or wholly eradicate it. Sin continues to flow from this source, “as water from a fountain.”
- For the children of God, however, this corruption is not imputed unto condemnation; by God’s grace and mercy it is forgiven. Believers are not to rest securely in sin, but to groan under it and long to be delivered from “this body of death.”
- The confession explicitly rejects the Pelagian claim that sin arises only by imitation.

In short, original sin is universal, total, hereditary, condemnable in itself, and only partially subdued (not removed) in this life, yet forgiven for believers.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the doctrine of election?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that- all Adam's descendants having thus fallen into perdition and ruin by the sin of Adam- God showed himself to be as he is: merciful and just. God is merciful in withdrawing and saving from this perdition those who, in the eternal and unchangeable divine counsel, have been elected and chosen in Jesus Christ our Lord by his pure goodness, without any consideration of their works. God is just in leaving the others in their ruin and fall into which they plunged themselves.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561) addresses election primarily in Article 16. It teaches that, after the fall of Adam’s posterity into ruin, God shows himself both merciful and just: merciful in delivering and preserving from perdition all whom he has elected in Christ Jesus according to his eternal and unchangeable counsel of mere goodness, without regard to their works; and just in leaving others in the fall and perdition into which they have plunged themselves.

In short, election is unconditional, grounded solely in God’s sovereign good pleasure, accomplished in Christ, and paired with a just passing over of the non-elect.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the righteousness of faith?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that for us to acquire the true knowledge of this great mystery the Holy Spirit kindles in our hearts a true faith that embraces Jesus Christ, with all his merits, and makes him its own, and no longer looks for anything apart from him. For it must necessarily follow that either all that is required for our salvation is not in Christ or, if all is in him, then those who have Christ by faith have his salvation entirely. Therefore, to say that Christ is not enough but that something else is needed as well is a most enormous blasphemy against God- for it then would follow that Jesus Christ is only half a Savior. And therefore we justly say with Paul that we are justified "by faith alone" or "by faith apart from works." (Rom. 3:28) However, we do not mean, properly speaking, that it is faith itself that justifies us- for faith is only the instrument by which we embrace Christ, our righteousness. But Jesus Christ is our righteousness in making available to us all his merits and all the holy works he has done for us and in our place. And faith is the instrument that keeps us in communion with him and with all his benefits. When those benefits are made ours, they are more than enough to absolve us of our sins.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 22 (The Righteousness of Faith). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response: The Belgic Confession (1561) treats this mainly in Articles 22–23. It teaches that sinners are justified by faith alone, apart from works, but that faith itself is not the righteousness that justifies. Faith is only the instrument by which we embrace Christ and all his merits. Jesus Christ is our righteousness: his obedience and holy works, done for us and in our place, are imputed to us, and in him we have complete salvation. Our blessedness before God therefore consists in the forgiveness of sins and the gift of righteousness by grace, through the redemption that is in Christ—not in any merit of our own. Resting on that imputed obedience alone frees the conscience; relying even slightly on ourselves or any other creature would leave us condemned.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the last judgement?
questions.reference_answer: Finally we believe, according to God's Word, that when the time appointed by the Lord is come (which is unknown to all creatures) and the number of the elect is complete, our Lord Jesus Christ will come from heaven, bodily and visibly, as he ascended, with great glory and majesty, to declare himself the judge of the living and the dead. He will burn this old world, in fire and flame, in order to cleanse it. Then all human creatures will appear in person before the great judge- men, women, and children, who have lived from the beginning until the end of the world. They will be summoned there "with the archangel's call and with the sound of God's trumpet." (1 Thess. 4:16) For all those who died before that time will be raised from the earth, their spirits being joined and united with their own bodies in which they lived. And as for those who are still alive, they will not die like the others but will be changed "in the twinkling of an eye" from perishable to imperishable. (1 Cor. 15:51-53) Then the books (that is, the consciences) will be opened, and the dead will be judged according to the things they did in the world, (Rev. 20:12) whether good or evil. Indeed, all people will give account of all the idle words they have spoken, (Matt. 12:36) which the world regards as only playing games. And then the secrets and hypocrisies of all people will be publicly uncovered in the sight of all. Therefore, with good reason the thought of this judgment is horrible and dreadful to wicked and evil people. But it is very pleasant and a great comfort to the righteous and elect, since their total redemption will then be accomplished. They will then receive the fruits of their labor and of the trouble they have suffered; their innocence will be openly recognized by all; and they will see the terrible vengeance that God will bring on the evil ones who tyrannized, oppressed, and tormented them in this world. The evil ones will be convicted by the witness of their own consciences, and shall be made immortal- but only to be tormented in "the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." (Matt. 25:41) In contrast, the faithful and elect will be crowned with glory and honor. The Son of God will profess their names (Matt. 10:32) before God his Father and the holy and elect angels; all tears will be wiped from their eyes; (Rev. 7:17) and their cause- at present condemned as heretical and evil by many judges and civil officers- will be acknowledged as the cause of the Son of God. And as a gracious reward the Lord will make them possess a glory such as the human heart could never imagine. So we look forward to that great day with longing in order to enjoy fully the promises of God in Christ Jesus, our Lord.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 37 (The Last Judgement). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession treats the last judgment in **Article 37**. Its teaching can be summarized as follows.

**Christ will return as judge.** At a time known only to God, when the number of the elect is complete, the Lord Jesus Christ will come from heaven bodily and visibly, as he ascended, in glory and majesty, to judge the living and the dead. This present world will be purged by fire.

**All people will appear.** Every human being—men, women, and children, from the beginning of the world to its end—will stand in person before the judge. The dead will be raised, their souls reunited with their own bodies; those still alive will be changed “in the twinkling of an eye.” All are summoned by the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God.

**Judgment is according to works, and nothing is hidden.** The “books” (understood as consciences) will be opened. People will be judged for what they have done, good or evil, and will give account even for idle words. Secrets and hypocrisy will be exposed before all.

**The outcome differs for the wicked and the elect.** For the wicked the judgment is dreadful: they are convicted by their own consciences and consigned to everlasting torment in the fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For the righteous and elect it is a comfort: their redemption is completed, their innocence is publicly acknowledged, their suffering is vindicated, Christ confesses their names before the Father and the angels, their tears are wiped away, and they receive a glory beyond human imagination.

**The church is to long for that day.** Believers are to look forward to it so that they may fully enjoy the promises of God in Christ Jesus.

Article 37 is thus a classic Reformed statement of bodily resurrection, a public final judgment by Christ, everlasting punishment and everlasting glory, and comfort for the persecuted church—not a private or merely spiritual reckoning.

questions.question: What do the Canons of Dort teach about divine predestination in Article 7?
questions.reference_answer:
Election is the unchangeable purpose of God, whereby, before the foundation of the world, He hath out of mere grace, according to the sovereign good pleasure of His own will, chosen, from the whole human race, which had fallen through their own fault from their primitive state of rectitude into sin and destruction, a certain number of persons to redemption in Christ, whom He from eternity appointed the Mediator and Head of the elect, and the foundation of salvation.

This elect number, though by nature neither better nor more deserving than others, but with them involved in one common misery, God hath decreed to give to Christ, to be saved by Him, and effectually to call and draw them to His communion by His Word and Spirit, to bestow upon them true faith, justification and sanctification; and having powerfully preserved them in the fellowship of His Son, finally, to glorify them for the demonstration of His mercy and for the praise of His glorious grace, as it is written: "According as He hath chosen us in Him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before Him in love: having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to Himself, according to the good pleasure of His will, to the praise of the glory of His grace, wherein He hath made us accepted in the beloved" (Eph. 1:4-6). And elsewhere: "Whom He did predestinate, them He also called: and whom He called, them He also justified: and whom He justified them He also glorified" (Rom. 8:30).

Article 7 of the First Head of Doctrine in the Canons of Dort teaches that election is God’s unchangeable purpose, formed before the foundation of the world. Out of mere grace and according to the sovereign good pleasure of his will, God chose a definite number of people from the fallen human race for redemption in Christ, whom he appointed from eternity as Mediator and Head of the elect.

Those chosen are not by nature better or more deserving than others; they share the same misery. God decreed to give them to Christ, effectually call and draw them by his Word and Spirit, grant them true faith, justification, and sanctification, preserve them in communion with his Son, and finally glorify them—to display his mercy and the riches of his grace. The article cites Ephesians 1:4–6 and Romans 8:30 in support.

questions.question: What do the Canons of Dort teach about divine predestination in Article 9?
questions.reference_answer: This election was not founded upon foreseen faith, and the obedience of faith, holiness, or any other good quality or disposition in man, as the prerequisite, cause or condition on which it depended; but men are chosen to faith and to the obedience of faith, holiness, etc.; therefore election is the fountain of every saving good, from which proceeds faith, holiness, and the other gifts of salvation, and finally eternal life itself, as its fruits and effects, according to that of the apostle: "He hath chosen us [not because we were but] that we should be holy, and without blame, before Him in love" (Eph. 1:4).

scoring.rubric: Must reflect the teaching of Canons of Dort, Head 1 (Divine Predestination), Article 9. Should align with Reformed soteriology.

questions.response:
**Article 9 of the First Head of Doctrine** (Divine Election and Reprobation) teaches that election is unconditional and is the source of salvation’s benefits, not their result.

In substance it says:

- Election is **not** based on foreseen faith, obedience, holiness, or any other good quality or disposition in the person chosen, as if those were a prerequisite, cause, or condition.
- People are chosen **unto** faith, obedience, holiness, and the rest—not because God foresaw those things in them.
- Election is therefore the **fountain** (source) of every saving good. Faith, holiness, the other gifts of salvation, and finally eternal life flow from it as fruits and effects.
- It appeals to Ephesians 1:4: God chose us so that we would be holy and blameless before him in love—not because we already were.

So Article 9 rejects the idea that God elects on the basis of foreseen faith or merit, and affirms that faith and holiness are results of election, not its ground.

questions.response:

questions.response:
**Article 1 of the Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine** of the Canons of Dort teaches that man was created good in God’s image, but by his own free will fell into total corruption.

In substance it says:

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about the holy scriptures?
questions.reference_answer: The Holy Scripture is the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving Knowledge, Faith and Obedience; Although the light of Nature, and the works of Creation and Providence do so far manifest the goodness, wisdom and power of God, as to leave men unexcusable; yet are they not sufficient to give that knowledge of God and His will, which is necessary unto Salvation. Therefore it pleased the Lord at sundry times, and in divers manners, to reveal himself, and to declare that His will unto his Church; and afterward for the better preserving, and propagating of the Truth, and for the more sure Establishment, and Comfort of the Church against the corruption of the flesh, and the malice of Satan, and of the World, to commit the same wholly unto writing; which maketh the Holy Scriptures to be most necessary, those former ways of Gods revealing his will unto his people being now ceased. Under the Name of Holy Scripture or the Word of God written; are now contained all the Books of the Old and New Testament which are these: Of the Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, The Song of Songs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. Of the New Testament: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, The Acts of the Apostles, Pauls Epistle to the Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Phillippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, to Titus, to Philemon, the Epistle to the Hebrews, the Epistle of James, the First and Second Epistles of Peter, the First, Second and Third Epistles of John, the Epistle of Jude, the Revelation. The Books commonly called Apocrypha not being of Divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon (or rule) of the Scripture, and therefore are of no authority to the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved or made use of, then other humane writings. The Authority of the Holy Scripture for which it ought to be believed dependeth not upon the testimony of any man, or Church; but wholly upon God (who is truth it self) the Author thereof; therefore it is to be received, because it is the Word of God. We may be moved and induced by the testimony of the Church of God, to an high and reverent esteem of the Holy Scriptures; and the heavenliness of the matter, the efficacy of the Doctrine, and the Majesty of the stile, the consent of all the parts, the scope of the whole (which is to give all glory to God) the full discovery it makes of the only way of mans salvation, and many other incomparable Excellencies, and intire perfections thereof, are arguments whereby it doth abundantly evidence it self to be the Word of God; yet notwithstanding; our full perswasion, and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our Hearts. The whole Councel of God concerning all things necessary for his own Glory, Mans Salvation, Faith and Life, is either expressely set down or necessarily contained in the Holy Scripture; unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new Revelation of the Spirit, or traditions of men.Nevertheless we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God, to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word, and that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the Church common to humane actions and societies; which are to be ordered by the light of nature, and Christian prudence according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed. All things in Scripture are not alike plain in themselves, nor alike clear unto all; yet those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed for Salvation, are so clearly propounded, and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of ordinary means, may attain to a sufficient understanding of them. The Old Testament in Hebrew, (which was the Native language of the people of God of old) and the New Testament in Greek (which at the time of the writing of it was most generally known to the Nations being immediately inspired by God, and by his singular care and Providence kept pure in all Ages, are therefore authentical; so as in all controversies of Religion the Church is finally to appeal unto them But because these original tongues are not known to all the people of God, who have a right unto, and interest in the Scriptures, and are commanded in the fear of God to read and search them, therefore they are to be translated into the vulgar language of every Nation, unto which they come, that the Word of God dwelling plentifully in all, they may worship him in an acceptable manner, and through patience and comfort of the Scriptures may have hope. The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture it self: And therefore when there is a question about the true and full sense of any Scripture (which is not manifold but one) it must be searched by other places that speak more clearly. The supream judge by which all controversies of Religion are to be determined, and all Decrees of Councels, opinions of antient Writers, Doctrines of men, and private Spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit, into which Scripture so delivered, our faith is finally resolved.

questions.response:
The 1689 London Baptist Confession (Second London Confession), Chapter 1, “Of the Holy Scriptures,” teaches the following.

**Sufficiency and necessity.** Scripture is the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of saving knowledge, faith, and obedience. The light of nature and God’s works in creation and providence show enough of God’s goodness, wisdom, and power to leave people without excuse, but they are not enough for the knowledge of God and his will that salvation requires. God therefore revealed himself and his will, and afterward committed that revelation wholly to writing so the truth would be preserved and the church better guarded against corruption. With those earlier modes of revelation ended, the written Scriptures are most necessary.

**Canon.** “Holy Scripture” means the books of the Old and New Testaments in the Protestant canon (Genesis through Malachi; Matthew through Revelation), given by inspiration of God as the rule of faith and life. The Apocrypha are not divinely inspired, are not part of the canon, and have no authority in the church beyond that of other human writings.

**Authority.** Scripture’s authority does not rest on any person or church, but wholly on God its author. It is to be received because it is the Word of God. The church’s testimony, the heavenliness of its matter, the power of its doctrine, the majesty of its style, the agreement of its parts, its aim of giving all glory to God, and its clear account of the only way of salvation are strong evidences that it is God’s Word. Full persuasion and assurance of its infallible truth and divine authority, however, come from the inward work of the Holy Spirit bearing witness by and with the Word.

**Completeness.** The whole counsel of God about everything necessary for his glory and for human salvation, faith, and life is either expressly stated in Scripture or necessarily contained in it. Nothing is to be added by new revelations of the Spirit or by human traditions. The Spirit’s inward illumination is still necessary for a saving understanding of what is revealed. Some circumstances of worship and church government, common to human societies, are to be ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence according to the general rules of the Word.

**Clarity.** Not everything in Scripture is equally plain or equally clear to everyone. What must be known, believed, and observed for salvation is set out clearly enough, in one place or another, that both the learned and the unlearned, using ordinary means, may reach a sufficient understanding.

**Text and translation.** The Old Testament in Hebrew and the New Testament in Greek, immediately inspired by God and by his care and providence kept pure in all ages, are authentic. In controversies of religion the church is finally to appeal to them. Because not everyone knows those languages, and because God’s people have a right to the Scriptures and are commanded to read and search them, they are to be translated into the common language of every nation.

**Interpretation and final authority.** The infallible rule for interpreting Scripture is Scripture itself. Where the true and full sense of a passage is in question—and that sense is one, not many—it is to be sought in other places that speak more clearly. The supreme judge of all religious controversies, councils, ancient writers, human doctrines, and private spirits is the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit; faith is finally resolved into that Scripture.

In short, the confession treats the Protestant canon as God’s inspired, sufficient, clear, and self-authenticating Word, to be translated, read, and interpreted by Scripture itself, and as the final standard for faith and life.

questions.response:
The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith (Second London Confession), Chapter 2, “Of God and of the Holy Trinity,” teaches classical Christian theism and the doctrine of the Trinity. In substance it follows the Westminster Confession, with Baptist wording.

**One God.** There is only one living and true God. He exists of himself, is infinite in being and perfection, and cannot be fully comprehended by anyone but himself. He is a most pure spirit—invisible, without body, parts, or passions—and alone has immortality. He is immutable, immense, eternal, incomprehensible, almighty, most holy, most wise, most free, and most absolute. He works all things according to the counsel of his own immutable and righteous will, for his own glory. He is loving, gracious, merciful, long-suffering, abundant in goodness and truth, and forgiving of sin, yet also just and terrible in judgment, hating all sin and not clearing the guilty.

**God’s self-sufficiency and sovereignty.** All life, glory, goodness, and blessedness are in God himself. He does not need any creature he has made, nor does he derive glory from them; he only manifests his own glory in, by, unto, and upon them. He is the sole fountain of all being—“of whom, through whom, and to whom are all things”—and has sovereign dominion over all creatures. His knowledge is infinite, infallible, and independent of the creature, so nothing is contingent or uncertain to him. He is most holy in all his counsels, works, and commands. Angels and humans owe him worship, service, and obedience as creatures to their Creator, and whatever else he requires of them.

**The Trinity.** In this one divine and infinite Being there are three subsistences: the Father, the Word (or Son), and the Holy Spirit. They are of one substance, power, and eternity. Each has the whole divine essence, yet the essence is undivided. The Father is of none, neither begotten nor proceeding; the Son is eternally begotten of the Father; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. All three are infinite and without beginning, so there is but one God—not divided in nature and being, but distinguished by personal properties and relations. The confession calls this doctrine of the Trinity the foundation of all communion with God and of comfortable dependence on him.

In short: one God in three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—equal in essence, power, and eternity, distinguished only by their eternal relations, and worthy of all worship as the self-existent, sovereign Creator.

- God has also decreed the means by which the elect are saved (redemption by Christ, effectual calling, justification, adoption, sanctification, and preservation). Only the elect are redeemed, called, justified, and saved in this way.
- The doctrine is to be handled with care, so that those who obey the gospel may find in it grounds for assurance, humility, praise, and comfort rather than presumption or despair.

The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith addresses divine providence in Chapter 5 (“Of Divine Providence”). Its teaching, which closely follows the Westminster Confession on this point, can be summarized as follows:

- God, as the good Creator, upholds, directs, disposes, and governs all creatures and things—from the greatest to the least—by his wise and holy providence, according to his infallible foreknowledge and the free, immutable counsel of his will, for the praise of his glory.
- In relation to God’s decree as first cause, all things come to pass immutably and infallibly; nothing occurs by chance or outside his providence. At the same time, he orders events to occur according to the nature of secondary causes, whether necessarily, freely, or contingently.
- God ordinarily works through means, yet remains free to work without, above, or against them as he pleases.
- His providence extends even to the fall and to sinful actions of angels and humans. This is not bare permission: he wisely and powerfully bounds, orders, and governs them toward his holy ends. Yet the sinfulness of those acts proceeds only from the creatures, not from God, who is neither the author nor the approver of sin.
- God sometimes leaves his own people for a season to temptations and the corruptions of their hearts—for chastisement, to humble them, to drive them to greater dependence on him, and for other just ends—so that whatever befalls the elect is appointed for his glory and their good.
- As righteous judge, God may blind and harden the wicked for former sins: withholding grace, withdrawing gifts, giving them over to their own lusts and to Satan, so that they harden themselves under the very means that soften others.
- While providence extends to all creatures, it takes special care of the church and disposes all things for its good.

In short, the confession affirms exhaustive divine sovereignty over all events while insisting that God is not the author of sin and that secondary causes (including free human actions) remain real.

Moreover Man having brought himself under the curse of the Law by his fall, it pleased the Lord to make a Covenant of Grace wherein he freely offereth unto Sinners, Life and Salvation by Jesus Christ, requiring of them Faith in him, that they may be saved; and promising to give unto all those that are ordained unto eternal Life, his holy Spirit, to make them willing, and able to believe. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (Second London Baptist Confession) treats God’s covenant mainly in Chapter 7, “Of God’s Covenant.” Its teaching can be summarized as follows.

God is so far above creatures that, although they owe him obedience as Creator, they could never have earned the reward of life on their own. Any such arrangement depends on God’s voluntary condescension, which he has been pleased to express by way of covenant.

After the fall brought humanity under the curse of the law, God made a covenant of grace. In it he freely offers sinners life and salvation through Jesus Christ, requires faith in Christ for salvation, and promises to give his Holy Spirit to all who are ordained to eternal life so that they are made willing and able to believe.

That covenant of grace is revealed in the gospel: first to Adam in the promise of salvation through the seed of the woman, then by further steps, until it is fully disclosed in the New Testament. It rests on an eternal covenant transaction between the Father and the Son concerning the redemption of the elect. Only by the grace of this covenant has anyone descended from fallen Adam ever been saved. Fallen people are utterly unable to be accepted with God on the terms under which Adam stood in innocence.

In short, the confession centers salvation on the covenant of grace, grounded in the eternal covenant of redemption, rather than on any continuing ability of fallen humanity to meet the original terms of life with God. (Related material appears elsewhere—for example, in its account of the law and in its rejection of infant baptism—but Chapter 7 is the direct statement on God’s covenant.)

questions.reference_answer: It pleased God in his eternal purpose, to chuse and ordain the Lord Jesus his only begotten Son, according to the Covenant made between them both, to be the Mediator between God and Man; the Prophet, Priest and King; Head and Saviour of his Church, the heir of all things, and judge of the world: Unto whom he did from all Eternity give a people to be his seed, and to be by him in time redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified. The Son of God, the second Person in the Holy Trinity, being very and eternal God, the brightness of the Fathers glory, of one substance and equal with him: who made the World, who upholdeth and governeth all things he hath made: did when the fullness of time was come take unto him mans nature, with all the Essential properties, and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin: being conceived by the Holy Spirit in the Womb of the Virgin Mary, the Holy Spirit coming down upon her, and the power of the most High overshadowing her, and so was made of a Woman, of the Tribe of Judah, of the Seed of Abraham, and David according to the Scriptures: So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, were inseparably joined together in one Person: without conversion, composition, or confusion: which Person is very God, and very Man; yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and Man. The Lord Jesus in his humane nature thus united to the divine, in the Person of the Son, was sanctified, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, above measure; having in him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in whom it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell: To the end that being holy, harmless, undefiled, and full of Grace, and Truth, he might be throughly furnished to execute the office of a Mediator, and Surety; which office he took not upon himself, but was thereunto called by his Father; who also put all power and judgement in his hand, and gave him Commandement to execute the same. This office the Lord Jesus did most willingly undertake, which that he might discharge he was made under the Law, and did perfectly fulfill it, and underwent the punishment due to us, which we should have born and suffered, being made Sin and a Curse for us: enduring most grievous sorrows in his Soul; and most painful sufferings in his body; was crucified, and died, and remained in the state of the dead; yet saw no corruption: on the third day he arose from the dead, with the same body in which he suffered; with which he also ascended into heaven: and there sitteth at the right hand of his Father, making intercession; and shall return to judge Men and Angels, at the end of the World. The Lord Jesus by his perfect obedience and sacrifice of himself, which he through the Eternal Spirit once offered up unto God, hath fully satisfied the Justice of God, procured reconciliation, and purchased an Everlasting inheritance in the Kingdom of Heaven, for all those whom the Father hath given unto him. Although the price of Redemption was not actually paid by Christ, till after his Incarnation, yet the vertue, efficacy, and benefit thereof were communicated to the Elect in all ages successively, from the beginning of the World, in and by those Promises, Types, and Sacrifices, wherein he was revealed, and signified to be the Seed of the Woman, which should bruise the Serpents head; and the Lamb slain from the foundation of the World: Being the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. Christ in the work of Mediation acteth according to both natures, by each nature doing that which is proper to it self; yet by reason of the Unity of the Person, that which is proper to one nature, is sometimes in Scripture attributed to the Person denominated by the other nature. To all those for whom Christ hath obtained eternal redemption, he doth certainly, and effectually apply, and communicate the same; making intercession for them, uniting them to himself by his spirit, revealing unto them, in and by the word, the mystery of salvation; perswading them to believe, and obey; governing their hearts by his word and spirit, and overcoming all their enemies by his Almighty power, and wisdom; in such manner, and wayes as are most consonant to his wonderful, and unsearchable dispensation; and all of free, and absolute Grace, without any condition foreseen in them, to procure it. This office of Mediator between God and Man, is proper onely to Christ, who is the Prophet, Priest, and King of the Church of God; and may not be either in whole, or any part thereof transfer'd from him to any other. This number and order of Offices is necessary; for in respect of our ignorance, we stand in need of his prophetical Office; and in respect of our alienation from God, and imperfection of the best of our services, we need his Priestly office, to reconcile us, and present us acceptable unto God: and in respect our averseness, and utter inability to return to God, and for our rescue, and security from our spiritual adversaries, we need his Kingly office, to convince, subdue, draw, uphold, deliver, and preserve us to his Heavenly Kingdome.

questions.response:
The 1689 London Baptist Confession treats this in Chapter 8, “Of Christ the Mediator.” Its teaching can be summarized as follows.

**Who the Mediator is.** In God’s eternal purpose, and according to the covenant between the Father and the Son, the Lord Jesus—God’s only begotten Son—was chosen and ordained as the one mediator between God and man. He is prophet, priest, and king; head and savior of the church; heir of all things; and judge of the world. From eternity the Father gave him a people to be redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified.

**His person.** The Son, truly and eternally God and equal with the Father, took a full human nature in the fullness of time—conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary—yet without sin. Two whole, perfect, and distinct natures (divine and human) are inseparably joined in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion. He is truly God and truly man, one Christ, the only mediator between God and man.

**His equipping.** In his human nature, united to the divine, he was sanctified and anointed with the Holy Spirit above measure, with all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. The Father called him to the mediatorial office and put all power and judgment in his hand. He did not take the office on himself.

**His work.** He willingly undertook the office, was made under the law, fulfilled it perfectly, and bore the punishment due to his people—made sin and a curse for them. He suffered in soul and body, was crucified, died, and remained dead without seeing corruption. He rose on the third day in the same body, ascended, sits at the Father’s right hand making intercession, and will return to judge men and angels.

**The benefit of his work.** By his perfect obedience and once-for-all sacrifice he fully satisfied God’s justice, procured reconciliation, and purchased an everlasting inheritance for all the Father gave him. Though the price was paid only after the incarnation, its virtue reached the elect in every age through promises, types, and sacrifices that pointed to him. He is “the same yesterday, and today, and for ever.”

**How he applies redemption.** To those for whom he obtained redemption he certainly and effectually applies it: interceding for them, uniting them to himself by the Spirit, revealing salvation in the Word, persuading them to believe and obey, governing them by Word and Spirit, and overcoming their enemies—all of free and absolute grace, not because of any condition foreseen in them.

**Offices that cannot be transferred.** Mediation belongs to Christ alone and may not be given, in whole or in part, to anyone else. The three offices answer human need: the prophetic office for ignorance, the priestly office for alienation from God and the imperfection of even our best service, and the kingly office for inability to return to God and for rescue from spiritual enemies.

In short, the confession teaches that Christ alone, as God and man in one person, was eternally appointed mediator; that he accomplished redemption by obedience and sacrifice; and that he effectually applies that redemption to the elect as prophet, priest, and king.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about effectual calling?

This Effectual Call is of God's free, and special grace alone, not from any thing at all foreseen in man, nor from any power, or agency in the Creature, coworking with his special Grace, the Creature being wholly passive therein, being dead in sins and trespasses, until being quickned & renewed by the holy Spirit, he is thereby enabled to answer this call, and to embrace the Grace offered and conveyed in it; and that by no less power, then that which raised up Christ from the dead. Elect Infants dying in infancy, are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit; who worketh when, and where, and how he pleaseth: so also are all other elect persons, who are uncapable of being outwardly called by the Ministry of the Word. Others not elected, although they may be called by the Ministry of the word, and may have some common operations of the Spirit, yet not being effectually drawn by the Father, they neither will, nor can truly come to Christ; and therefore cannot be saved: much less can men that receive not the Christian Religion be saved; be they never so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature, and the Law of that Religion they do profess.

It teaches that God effectually calls those he has predestined to life, at his appointed time, by his Word and Spirit. He brings them out of their natural state of sin and death into grace and salvation in Christ: spiritually enlightening their minds, replacing a heart of stone with a heart of flesh, renewing their wills, and powerfully drawing them to Christ—so that they come freely, made willing by grace.

This call is of God’s free and special grace alone. It does not rest on anything foreseen in the person, nor on any power or cooperation in the creature. Those called are wholly passive until the Holy Spirit quickens and renews them (being dead in sin), after which they are enabled to answer the call and embrace the grace offered in it—by the same power that raised Christ from the dead.

Those not elected may be called outwardly by the Word and may experience common operations of the Spirit, yet, not being effectually drawn by the Father, they neither will nor can truly come to Christ and therefore cannot be saved.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about justification?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God Effectually calleth, he also freely justifieth, not by infusing Righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting, and accepting their Persons as Righteous; not for any thing wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ's sake alone, not by imputing faith it self, the act of beleiving, or any other evangelical obedience to them, as their Righteousness; but by imputing Christs active obedience unto the whole Law, and passive obedience in his death, for their whole and sole Righteousnnss, they receiving, and resting on him, and his Righteousness, by Faith; which faith they have not of themselves, it is the gift of God. Faith thus receiving and resting on Christ, and his Righteousness, is the alone instrument of Justification: yet it is not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving Graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love. Christ by his obedience, and death, did fully discharge the debt of all those that are justified; and did by the sacrifice of himself, in the blood of his cross, undergoing in their stead, the penalty due unto them: make a proper, real and full satisfaction to Gods justice in their behalf: yet in asmuch as he was given by the Father for them, and his Obedience and Satisfaction accepted in their stead, and both freely, not for any thing in them; their Justification is only of Free Grace, that both the exact justice and rich Grace of God, might be glorified in the Justification of sinners. God doth continue to Forgive the sins of those that are justified, and although they can never fall from the state of justication; yet they may by their sins fall under Gods Fatherly displeasure; and in that condition, they have not usually the light of his Countenance restored unto them, untill they humble themselves, confess their sins, beg pardon, and renew their faith, and repentance. The Justification of Believers under the Old Testament was in all these respects, one and the same with the justification of Believers under the New Tement.

questions.response:
The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith (Chapter 11, “Of Justification”) teaches a classic Reformed account of justification. In summary:

- God freely justifies those he effectually calls by pardoning their sins and accepting them as righteous for Christ’s sake alone—not by infusing righteousness into them, and not on the basis of anything they do or any righteousness wrought in them.
- The ground of justification is the imputation of Christ’s righteousness: his active obedience to the whole law and his passive obedience in death. Faith itself, the act of believing, or any other evangelical obedience is not imputed as that righteousness.
- Faith is the sole instrument by which sinners receive and rest on Christ and his righteousness. It is the gift of God, and though it is never alone in the justified person (it is accompanied by other saving graces and works by love), justification is by faith alone.
- Christ fully discharged the debt of the justified by his obedience and death, making a real and full satisfaction to God’s justice in their place. Because he was given by the Father and his work accepted freely, justification is of free grace, so that both God’s justice and his grace are glorified.
- God decreed from eternity to justify the elect; Christ died for their sins and rose for their justification; yet they are not personally justified until the Spirit applies Christ to them in due time.
- Those who are justified can never fall from that state, though they may fall under God’s fatherly displeasure for sin and ordinarily do not regain the light of his countenance until they repent, confess, and renew faith.
- Justification of believers was the same in substance under the Old Testament as under the New.

The chapter is forensic and Christ-centered: pardon plus imputation of Christ’s obedience, received by faith alone, grounded in his satisfaction, and applied by the Spirit—consistent with the broader Reformed confessional tradition on this point.
