questions.question: What Bible passages teach the doctrine of election?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Eph 1:4-5, Rom 8:29-30, Rom 9:11-13
questions.response:
The doctrine of election (God’s choosing of people for salvation) is drawn mainly from these New Testament passages, along with a few Old Testament texts about Israel. Christians disagree on how to read them—especially whether election is unconditional and individual, or conditioned on foreseen faith, or primarily corporate—so the list below is the set of texts most often cited, not a settled interpretation.

### Central New Testament passages

**Ephesians 1:3–14**  
Paul says God “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” and “predestined us for adoption” according to the purpose of his will (esp. vv. 4–5, 11). This is the most direct “election” language in Paul.

**Romans 8:28–30**  
Those whom God foreknew he also predestined, called, justified, and glorified. Often called the “golden chain.”

**Romans 9:6–24**  
God’s choice of Jacob over Esau “before they were born,” “not because of works but because of him who calls,” and the potter/clay image of vessels of mercy and wrath. This chapter is the main battleground text for the doctrine.

**Romans 11:5–7**  
A remnant “chosen by grace,” not by works; the elect obtained what Israel sought, while the rest were hardened.

**John 6:37–44, 65**  
“All that the Father gives me will come to me.” “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” Jesus ties coming to him to the Father’s giving and drawing.

**John 10:26–29**  
“You do not believe because you are not among my sheep.” The sheep are given by the Father and cannot be snatched away.

**John 15:16**  
“You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you…”

**Acts 13:48**  
“As many as were appointed to eternal life believed.”

**2 Thessalonians 2:13–14**  
“God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth,” and called you through the gospel.

**2 Timothy 1:9**  
God “saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began.”

**1 Peter 1:1–2**  
Addressed to those “elect” (or “chosen”) “according to the foreknowledge of God the Father.”

**1 Peter 2:9**  
“You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood…” (corporate language applied to the church).

### Other texts often linked to the doctrine

- **Matthew 22:14** — “Many are called, but few are chosen.”
- **Matthew 24:22, 24, 31** and **Mark 13:20, 22, 27** — “the elect” in the end-times discourse.
- **Colossians 3:12** — “God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved.”
- **Revelation 13:8; 17:8** — names written in the book of life “from the foundation of the world” (cited by some as supporting election before time).
- **Deuteronomy 7:6–8** — Israel chosen not because it was greater than other nations, but because the Lord loved them and kept his oath. Often treated as the Old Testament pattern behind New Testament election language.
- **Isaiah 41–45** and related “servant” texts — God choosing Israel (and the servant) for his purposes.

### How these are usually grouped

| Emphasis | Passages most often cited |
|---|---|
| Choice before creation / before works | Eph 1:4–5; Rom 9:11–13; 2 Tim 1:9; 2 Thess 2:13 |
| God’s initiative in calling and drawing | John 6:37–44, 65; John 15:16; Acts 13:48 |
| The chain from foreknowledge to glory | Rom 8:29–30 |
| A remnant chosen by grace | Rom 11:5–7 |
| The church as a chosen people | 1 Pet 1:1–2; 1 Pet 2:9; Col 3:12 |

### A note on interpretation

These verses are agreed to be about God’s choosing. What they *teach* as a doctrine is disputed:

- **Reformed / Calvinist** readings take them as unconditional election of individuals to salvation, grounded in God’s will rather than foreseen faith.
- **Arminian and many Catholic and Eastern readings** stress foreknowledge (Rom 8:29; 1 Pet 1:2), human response, and often a corporate or conditional sense of election.
- Some read the language as primarily about **Israel and the church as a people**, not a fixed list of individuals.

If you want, I can walk through one passage (for example Romans 9 or Ephesians 1) in more detail, or compare how two traditions handle the same verses.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach the perseverance of the saints?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: John 10:28-29, Rom 8:38-39, Phil 1:6
questions.response:
Scripture teaches the perseverance of the saints (that those truly united to Christ by faith will be kept by God and continue in faith to the end) in several places. The doctrine is not that professing believers can live however they want and still be saved, but that God preserves his elect so that they persevere.

Key passages include:

- **John 6:37–40** — Jesus says all the Father gives him will come to him, and he will lose none of them but raise them up on the last day. The Father’s will is that everyone who looks to the Son and believes has eternal life.
- **John 10:27–29** — “My sheep hear my voice… I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father… is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand.”
- **Romans 8:28–39** — Those God foreknew he predestined, called, justified, and glorified. Nothing in creation “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
- **Philippians 1:6** — “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.”
- **Ephesians 1:13–14** — Believers are sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, “who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it.”
- **1 Peter 1:3–5** — God has caused believers to be born again to a living hope and an inheritance “kept in heaven for you, who by God’s power are being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.”
- **Jude 1, 24–25** — Believers are “kept for Jesus Christ,” and God “is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory.”
- **1 John 2:19** — Those who permanently depart show they “were not of us, for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us.”

Related texts often cited alongside these include 1 Corinthians 1:8–9, 1 Thessalonians 5:23–24, Hebrews 7:25, and 2 Timothy 1:12. Together they present perseverance as the fruit of God’s preserving grace, not human self-sufficiency.

Other passages (for example, warnings in Hebrews 6 and 10, or calls to continue in the faith) are read by advocates of this doctrine as means God uses to keep his people, or as distinguishing true faith from temporary profession, rather than as teaching that the regenerate can finally fall away. Different Christian traditions weigh those warning texts differently.

questions.question: What verses support the doctrine of total depravity?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 3:10-12, Eph 2:1-3, Gen 6:5
questions.response:
Total depravity (also called total inability) is the teaching that sin has corrupted every part of human nature, so that apart from God’s grace people cannot turn to God or do what is spiritually good. These passages are the ones most often cited in support of it. Wording below is from the King James Version.

**Universal corruption of the heart**
- Genesis 6:5 — “every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.”
- Genesis 8:21 — “the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth.”
- Jeremiah 17:9 — “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?”
- Mark 7:21–23 — evil thoughts and deeds come “from within, out of the heart of man.”

**Sin from the beginning of life**
- Psalm 51:5 — “Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.”
- Psalm 58:3 — “The wicked are estranged from the womb: they go astray as soon as they be born.”

**No one righteous or seeking God**
- Romans 3:10–12 (quoting the Psalms) — “There is none righteous, no, not one: There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. They are all gone out of the way… there is none that doeth good, no, not one.”
- Romans 3:23 — “all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
- Isaiah 64:6 — “all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags.”

**Inability, not only unwillingness**
- Romans 8:7–8 — “the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be. So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God.”
- 1 Corinthians 2:14 — “the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God… neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.”
- John 6:44 — “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him.”
- John 6:65 — “no man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father.”

**Spiritual death and slavery to sin**
- Ephesians 2:1–3 — “dead in trespasses and sins,” living “in the lusts of our flesh,” and “by nature the children of wrath.”
- John 8:34 — “Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.”
- Romans 6:16–20 — people are described as slaves of sin until set free.
- Titus 3:3 — “foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures.”

**Sin entering through Adam**
- Romans 5:12 — “by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned.”
- Romans 5:19 — “by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners.”

These texts are read by Reformed writers as teaching that sin touches mind, will, and affections, and that coming to Christ depends on God’s drawing and regenerating grace (often linked with John 3:3–8 and Ezekiel 36:26–27). Other Christian traditions accept the universality and seriousness of sin in many of these verses but deny that they prove total inability of the will. The doctrine is an interpretation of these passages, not a phrase the Bible itself uses.

questions.question: Which passages teach justification by faith alone?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 3:28, Eph 2:8-9, Gal 2:16
questions.response:
**Romans 3:21–28, Romans 4, Galatians 2:16, Galatians 3, Ephesians 2:8–9, and related texts (such as Philippians 3:9 and Titus 3:5–7) are the main passages used to teach justification by faith apart from works.**

These texts, especially in Paul, present justification (being declared righteous before God) as received through faith in Christ, not by works of the law or human merit. The classic Reformation reading (“faith alone” / *sola fide*) treats the repeated contrast with works as excluding works as a contributing cause or ground of justification. Key points from the passages:

- **Romans 3:21–28** states that righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe, and that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. Boasting is excluded.
- **Romans 4** (especially vv. 1–8, 22–25) uses Abraham: his faith was counted as righteousness before circumcision or law-keeping; God justifies the ungodly who believe, not the one who works for a wage.
- **Galatians 2:16** (and the surrounding argument in Galatians 2–3) says a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Christ; the same point is repeated for emphasis, and “the righteous shall live by faith” (quoting Habakkuk 2:4) is set against justification by the law.
- **Ephesians 2:8–9** says salvation is by grace through faith, not a result of works, so that no one may boast (the gift character of grace and faith is stressed).
- **Philippians 3:9** contrasts a righteousness of one’s own based on the law with the righteousness from God that depends on faith.
- **Titus 3:5–7** denies justification or salvation by works done in righteousness and attributes it to God’s mercy, the washing of regeneration, and justification by grace.

Related supporting notes often drawn from these chapters include peace with God through justification by faith (Romans 5:1) and the insistence that the promise rests on grace and is guaranteed to faith (Romans 4:16).

**Important qualifications readers usually note:**
- The phrase “faith alone” is an interpretive summary of the “faith, not works” contrast; the exact wording “faith alone” appears in James 2:24 in a different sense (“not by faith alone”), which Protestants typically read as addressing a dead, non-working profession of faith rather than the ground of justification before God.
- These passages focus on works of the law / meritorious works as the basis of right standing; they do not deny that genuine faith produces obedience and good works (a point Paul and James both affirm in other ways).
- Historic Catholic and Orthodox readings accept justification by grace through faith but reject the “alone” formulation that excludes all cooperation or subsequent works from the broader account of salvation, often appealing to James 2 and other texts alongside Paul.

For the wording itself, consult a standard translation of the passages listed above (Romans 3–5, Galatians 2–3, Ephesians 2, Philippians 3, Titus 3). The doctrine’s classic Protestant statement is that these texts teach sinners are justified by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, apart from works.

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach the doctrine of original sin?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 5:12, Rom 5:18-19, Ps 51:5, Gen 3:6-7
questions.response:
The doctrine of original sin—that Adam’s fall left humanity sinful by nature, not only by later personal acts—is drawn mainly from these passages. Traditions differ on whether that includes inherited guilt, a corrupted nature only, or both.

**The fall**
- **Genesis 3** — Adam and Eve disobey; the consequences (death, curse, exile) fall on them and their descendants.
- **Genesis 6:5; 8:21** — Human inclination is described as evil from youth, not only after deliberate adult choices.

**Inherited condition**
- **Psalm 51:5** — “Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me” (KJV). Often read as sinfulness from the beginning of life, not merely personal crimes.
- **Psalm 58:3** — The wicked are said to go astray from the womb.
- **Job 14:4; 15:14** — No one is clean who is born of a woman; humanity is not righteous by nature.

**Paul’s explicit link to Adam**
- **Romans 5:12–21** — The central text: sin entered through one man, and death through sin, so death spread to all because all sinned. One trespass brought condemnation; one man’s obedience brings justification. This is the passage most often used to teach solidarity with Adam.
- **1 Corinthians 15:21–22** — “For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.”

**Humanity “by nature” under sin**
- **Romans 3:9–23** — All, Jew and Gentile, are under sin; none is righteous; all have sinned.
- **Ephesians 2:1–3** — People are dead in trespasses and sins and are “by nature the children of wrath.”
- **John 3:5–6** — What is born of the flesh is flesh; new birth is required, which many read as implying a condition present from natural birth.

**Related themes (supporting, not the core proof-texts)**
- **Romans 7:14–25** — Indwelling sin even in the regenerate.
- **Genesis 5:3** — Adam’s son is in Adam’s likeness, sometimes linked to transmission of a fallen condition after the image was marred.

**How these are used**
Western theology (Augustine, much of Catholic and Protestant teaching) treats **Romans 5** with **Psalm 51:5** and **Ephesians 2:3** as teaching both a corrupted nature and, in many accounts, guilt imputed from Adam. Eastern Orthodox teaching more often speaks of ancestral sin: inherited mortality and a wounded nature, without Augustine’s strong doctrine of inherited guilt. The texts themselves stress universal sin, death through Adam, and the need for Christ’s new humanity; how “original guilt” versus “original corruption” is parsed is a matter of interpretation, not a single verse that uses the later phrase “original sin.”

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the doctrine of the Trinity?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, 2 Cor 13:14, John 1:1, Gen 1:26
questions.response:
The word “Trinity” does not appear in the Bible. The doctrine—that there is one God who exists eternally as three distinct persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is a later summary of how Christians read a set of biblical claims together: God is one, the Father is God, the Son is God, the Spirit is God, and the three are not the same person.

### One God
- Deuteronomy 6:4: “The LORD our God, the LORD is one.”
- Isaiah 45:5; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6; James 2:19.

### The Father, Son, and Spirit named together
- Matthew 28:19: baptism “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (one “name,” three persons).
- 2 Corinthians 13:14: grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, love of God, and fellowship of the Holy Spirit.
- Matthew 3:16–17: at Jesus’ baptism the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks.
- 1 Peter 1:2; Ephesians 4:4–6.

### The Son identified with God
- John 1:1–3, 14: the Word was with God and was God, and became flesh.
- John 20:28: Thomas calls Jesus “My Lord and my God.”
- Philippians 2:5–11: Christ in the form of God, yet taking human form.
- Colossians 2:9: in Christ “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily.”
- Hebrews 1:1–3, 8: the Son is the radiance of God’s glory; the Father addresses him as God.
- John 10:30 and John 14:9 are often read with these texts (“I and the Father are one”; “whoever has seen me has seen the Father”), though they are also debated.

### The Spirit identified with God, yet distinct
- Acts 5:3–4: lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God.
- John 14:16–17, 26; 15:26; 16:7–15: the Spirit is “another” advocate, sent by the Father and the Son, who teaches and glorifies Christ.
- 1 Corinthians 2:10–11; 2 Corinthians 3:17–18.

### How the doctrine was formed
Early Christians held these lines together: monotheism, worship of Jesus, and the personal work of the Spirit. The formal wording (one essence, three persons; co-equal and co-eternal) was worked out in the early church, especially in the Nicene Creed (325, revised 381) and later creeds, in response to views that denied the full deity of the Son or the Spirit.

Not every group that uses the Bible accepts this reading. Unitarian Christians, Jehovah’s Witnesses, and some others argue that the same texts teach the supremacy of the Father and a lesser status for the Son and Spirit. So the Trinity is a doctrinal conclusion drawn from Scripture, not a single verse that states the formula.

questions.question: What passages affirm the full deity of Jesus Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: John 1:1, John 1:14, Col 2:9, Heb 1:3, Phil 2:6
questions.response:
Christians have long pointed to a cluster of New Testament passages (and a few Old Testament texts read as messianic) as affirming that Jesus is fully God—not merely a great teacher, prophet, or exalted creature. The classic texts include:

**Explicit identification of Jesus as God**
- **John 1:1, 14** — “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God… And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
- **John 20:28** — Thomas addresses the risen Jesus: “My Lord and my God!”
- **Romans 9:5** — Christ is described as “God over all, blessed forever” (wording varies slightly by translation, but the divine ascription is the traditional reading).
- **Titus 2:13** — “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.”
- **Hebrews 1:8** — The Father says of the Son, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (quoting Psalm 45).
- **2 Peter 1:1** — “our God and Savior Jesus Christ.”
- **1 John 5:20** — Jesus Christ is called “the true God and eternal life.”
- **Colossians 2:9** — “In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily.”

**Jesus claims divine prerogatives and identity**
- **John 8:58** — “Before Abraham was, I am,” echoing God’s self-name in Exodus 3:14; the crowd treats it as blasphemy.
- **John 10:30–33** — “I and the Father are one.” His hearers understand this as making himself God.
- **John 5:18–23** — He is accused of making himself equal with God, and he claims to do what only God does (give life, judge).
- **Mark 2:5–7** (and parallels) — He forgives sins, which the scribes say only God can do.
- **Matthew 28:18–20** — All authority in heaven and earth is his; baptism is in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together.
- **Revelation 1:17–18; 22:12–13** — He calls himself “the first and the last” and “the Alpha and the Omega,” titles of God in Isaiah and earlier in Revelation.

**Divine works and worship ascribed to him**
- **Colossians 1:15–17** — He is the image of the invisible God; all things were created through him and for him, and in him all things hold together.
- **John 1:3** and **Hebrews 1:2–3** — Creation and the sustaining of the universe are attributed to the Son; he is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact imprint of his nature.
- **Philippians 2:5–11** — He existed “in the form of God” and did not regard equality with God as something to be exploited; every knee will bow and every tongue confess him as Lord (language drawn from Isaiah 45, which insists that glory belongs to God alone).
- **Hebrews 1:6** — Angels are commanded to worship the Son.
- **Matthew 14:33; John 9:38; Revelation 5:12–14** — Jesus receives worship that, in a Jewish context, belongs to God alone.

**Old Testament texts applied to him**
- **Isaiah 9:6** — The coming child is called “Mighty God, Everlasting Father.”
- **Matthew 1:23** — “Immanuel,” meaning “God with us.”
- **Isaiah 40:3** applied to the forerunner of Jesus (e.g., Mark 1:3) — preparing the way of the Lord (Yahweh).

Taken together, these passages are the main biblical basis for the historic Christian confession that Jesus is fully divine—of the same nature as the Father—while also truly human. Different churches emphasize different texts, and some groups dispute particular translations or interpretations, but the passages above are the ones most often cited for the full deity of Christ.

questions.question: Which Bible passages teach the bodily resurrection of Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Cor 15:3-8, Matt 28:5-6, Luke 24:39, John 20:27
questions.response:
Several New Testament passages present Jesus’ resurrection as bodily—not merely spiritual or symbolic. The clearest ones are below.

### Gospel narratives
- **Matthew 28:1–10, 16–20** — The empty tomb, the angel’s announcement that he has risen, and the risen Jesus meeting the women and the disciples.
- **Mark 16:1–8** (and the longer ending in **16:9–20** in many manuscripts) — The empty tomb and appearances of the risen Jesus.
- **Luke 24** — The empty tomb, the road to Emmaus, and especially **24:36–43**, where Jesus invites the disciples to touch him and eats fish in their presence, stressing that he is not a ghost.
- **John 20–21** — The empty tomb, Jesus showing his hands and side (**20:19–20**), Thomas invited to touch the wounds (**20:24–29**), and the appearance by the Sea of Tiberias (**21**).

### Apostolic teaching
- **Acts 1:3** — Jesus presented himself alive after his suffering “by many proofs,” appearing over forty days.
- **Acts 2:24–32** — Peter’s Pentecost sermon: God raised Jesus, and his flesh did not see corruption (citing Psalm 16).
- **Acts 10:40–41** and **Acts 13:30–37** — Further early preaching that God raised Jesus bodily and that witnesses ate and drank with him.
- **1 Corinthians 15:3–8** — Paul’s summary of the gospel: Christ died, was buried, was raised, and appeared to many, including more than five hundred at once.
- **1 Corinthians 15:12–23, 35–49** — The resurrection as historical and bodily, and the nature of the resurrection body (a transformed physical body, not a mere spirit).
- **Romans 6:4–9** and **Romans 8:11** — Christ raised from the dead; believers united with that resurrection.
- **Philippians 3:20–21** — The risen Christ will transform believers’ lowly bodies to be like his glorious body.
- **1 Peter 1:3** and **1 Peter 3:18** — New birth through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead; put to death in the flesh but made alive.

### Often cited as supporting the same claim
- **Romans 1:3–4**, **Romans 10:9**, **Colossians 2:12**, **1 Thessalonians 4:14**, and **Revelation 1:17–18** (the living one who was dead and is alive forever).

The passages most often used specifically for a **bodily** (not only spiritual) resurrection are **Luke 24:36–43**, **John 20:19–29**, **Acts 1:3** and **10:40–41**, and **1 Corinthians 15**.

questions.question: What Scripture supports the doctrine of substitutionary atonement?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Isa 53:5-6, 2 Cor 5:21, 1 Pet 2:24, Rom 3:25
questions.response:
The doctrine of substitutionary atonement—that Christ died in the place of sinners, bearing the penalty their sin deserved—is drawn especially from these passages.

**Old Testament background**
- **Isaiah 53:4–6, 10–12** — The servant “has borne our griefs” and “was pierced for our transgressions”; “the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all”; “his soul makes an offering for guilt” and he “bore the sin of many.”
- **Leviticus 16** (and related sacrificial laws) — The sin offering and the scapegoat picture guilt being transferred and borne away; the New Testament reads Christ’s death in light of that pattern.

**Jesus’ own words**
- **Mark 10:45** (cf. Matthew 20:28) — “The Son of Man came… to give his life as a ransom for many.”
- **Matthew 26:28** — His blood is “poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.”

**Apostolic teaching**
- **Romans 3:23–26** — All have sinned; God put Christ forward as a propitiation (atoning sacrifice) so that he might be just and the justifier of those who have faith in Jesus.
- **Romans 5:6–8** — “Christ died for the ungodly… while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
- **2 Corinthians 5:21** — “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
- **Galatians 3:13** — “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.”
- **1 Peter 2:24** — “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree.”
- **1 Peter 3:18** — “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God.”
- **Hebrews 9:26–28** — He appeared once “to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” and “was offered once to bear the sins of many.”
- **1 John 2:2; 4:10** — He is the propitiation for our sins; God “sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.”

**Related images**
- **John 1:29** — “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.”
- **1 Corinthians 15:3** — “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures.”

These texts are the main scriptural basis cited for penal or substitutionary atonement. Other Christian traditions stress additional or alternative themes (victory over evil, moral example, recapitulation) and sometimes read the same verses with different emphasis, but the language of bearing sin, ransom, curse, and propitiation is what the substitutionary reading rests on.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the imputation of Christ's righteousness?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 2 Cor 5:21, Rom 4:3-6, Phil 3:9, Rom 5:19
questions.response:
The doctrine of the imputation of Christ’s righteousness is drawn mainly from Paul’s letters, especially where he uses the language of righteousness being “credited” or “counted” to believers through faith, not earned by works.

### Central passages

**Romans 4** is the clearest text. Paul takes Genesis 15:6—“Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness”—and treats that crediting (Greek *logizomai*, often translated “imputed” or “reckoned”) as the pattern of justification:

- Righteousness is credited to the one who believes, apart from works (Romans 4:3–5).
- David is cited for the blessing of the person to whom God credits righteousness apart from works (Romans 4:6–8).
- What was written about Abraham applies to those who believe in the God who raised Jesus (Romans 4:22–25).

**2 Corinthians 5:21** states the exchange in compact form: God made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us, “so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”

**Philippians 3:9** contrasts a righteousness of one’s own, based on the law, with “the righteousness that comes from God on the basis of faith” and is found in Christ.

**Romans 5:12–19** sets Adam and Christ in parallel. Through Adam’s disobedience many were made sinners; through Christ’s obedience many are made righteous (especially 5:18–19). Reformed readers take this as including the crediting of Christ’s obedience to those united to him.

**Romans 3:21–26** says the righteousness of God is revealed apart from the law and comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe, received by faith rather than achieved by works of the law.

Related texts often cited alongside these include 1 Corinthians 1:30 (Christ became for us righteousness), Galatians 2:16 and 3:6–14 (justified by faith, not by works of the law), and Isaiah 53:11 and 61:10 as background for a righteousness given rather than self-produced.

### How the doctrine is understood

In classic Protestant (especially Reformed) teaching, these passages are taken to mean that God counts Christ’s righteousness—his obedience and his atoning death—to the believer, so that the believer is declared righteous before God. The believer’s own works are not the ground of that verdict.

Other Christian traditions accept justification by grace through faith but often read the same texts as teaching that God makes people righteous (an infused or transformative righteousness) rather than merely crediting an alien righteousness. The debate is largely about how to relate “credited as righteousness,” union with Christ, and the new life that follows faith—not about whether those verses exist.

So the biblical case for imputation rests above all on Romans 4’s “credited” language, reinforced by 2 Corinthians 5:21, Philippians 3:9, and the Adam–Christ contrast in Romans 5.

questions.question: What passages describe the process of sanctification?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Thess 4:3, Phil 2:12-13, 2 Cor 3:18, Heb 12:14
questions.response:
Sanctification in Scripture is both a status (believers are set apart in Christ) and an ongoing process (they grow in holiness). Passages that describe the process usually stress God’s work through the Spirit and the word, together with the believer’s active response.

**God’s ongoing work**
- **Philippians 1:6** — God, who began the good work, will bring it to completion.
- **Philippians 2:12–13** — Believers “work out” their salvation because God works in them to will and to act.
- **1 Thessalonians 5:23–24** — God himself sanctifies completely and is faithful to do it.
- **2 Thessalonians 2:13** — Salvation includes sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth.
- **Hebrews 10:14** — Christ’s offering perfects those who are *being* sanctified.
- **Hebrews 12:5–11** — God’s discipline yields “the peaceful fruit of righteousness.”

**Transformation into Christ’s likeness**
- **Romans 8:29** — Believers are predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son.
- **2 Corinthians 3:18** — They are transformed “from one degree of glory to another” by the Spirit.
- **1 John 3:2–3** — Hope of seeing Christ purifies those who hold it.
- **Ephesians 5:25–27** — Christ sanctifies the church by the washing of water with the word, to present her holy.

**Means and pattern of the process**
- **John 17:17** — “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.”
- **Romans 6:19–22** — A shift from slavery to sin toward righteousness, with sanctification as the fruit and outcome.
- **Romans 12:1–2** — Bodies offered to God; minds renewed so life is transformed.
- **Galatians 5:16–25** — Walking by the Spirit rather than the flesh; the Spirit’s fruit replaces the works of the flesh.
- **Ephesians 4:22–24** and **Colossians 3:5–14** — Putting off the old self and putting on the new, shaped by knowledge of Christ.
- **1 Thessalonians 4:3–7** — God’s will is sanctification, spelled out especially as sexual holiness and honor.
- **1 Peter 1:14–16** — Holiness patterned on God’s own holiness.
- **2 Peter 1:3–11** — God’s power supplies what is needed; believers are to add virtue, knowledge, self-control, and love.
- **Titus 2:11–14** — Grace trains people to renounce ungodliness and live self-controlled, upright lives.

**Already and not yet**
- **1 Corinthians 6:11** — “You were sanctified” (positional, at conversion), alongside the many texts above that treat holiness as still in progress.
- **Hebrews 12:14** — Believers are to pursue the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.

Taken together, the process is Spirit-driven conformity to Christ, mediated especially by the word, involving both divine initiative and human effort, and aimed at complete holiness when Christ appears.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about the means of grace?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 10:17, Acts 2:42, 1 Cor 11:23-26, Matt 28:19
questions.response:
The phrase “means of grace” does not appear in Scripture, but the underlying idea—that God ordinarily conveys saving and sanctifying grace through appointed channels—is taught throughout the Bible. Classic Protestant theology identifies three primary ordinary means: the Word, the sacraments, and prayer.

### The Word
God’s word is the chief instrument by which faith is created and believers are built up.
- Romans 10:17 — faith comes by hearing the word of Christ.
- 1 Peter 1:23–25 — people are born again through the living and abiding word of God.
- Acts 20:32 — Paul commends the elders “to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up.”
- 2 Timothy 3:15–17 and Hebrews 4:12 — Scripture makes wise for salvation and is living and active.
- Isaiah 55:10–11 — God’s word accomplishes the purpose for which he sends it.

### The Sacraments
Baptism and the Lord’s Supper are visible signs and seals of the covenant of grace, through which Christ communicates the benefits of redemption to believers.
- Baptism: Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38; Romans 6:3–4; Galatians 3:27; Colossians 2:11–12; Titus 3:5; 1 Peter 3:21.
- Lord’s Supper: Matthew 26:26–28; 1 Corinthians 10:16–17; 11:23–26. Participation in the bread and cup is described as a real sharing in the body and blood of Christ.

### Prayer
Prayer is the means by which believers draw near to the throne of grace and receive mercy and help.
- Hebrews 4:16 — approach the throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy and find grace.
- Matthew 7:7–11; John 14:13–14; Philippians 4:6–7; James 1:5; 1 John 5:14–15 — God invites and answers the prayers of his people.

These means are effective not because of any inherent power in the acts themselves, but because the Holy Spirit works through them according to God’s promise (see, e.g., 1 Corinthians 2:4–5; 3:6–7; John 6:63). Scripture also shows that God is free to work extraordinarily apart from these means, yet he has bound himself to bless their faithful use.

questions.question: What Bible passages support covenant theology?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 17:7, Jer 31:31-34, Heb 8:6-13, Gal 3:29
questions.response:
Covenant theology reads Scripture as organized around God’s covenants, especially a covenant of works with Adam and a covenant of grace fulfilled in Christ. These are the passages most often cited for that framework. Interpretation is debated; dispensational and other readings treat some of the same texts differently.

### Adam and federal headship
- **Genesis 2:15–17** — life conditioned on obedience; often read as a covenant of works, even though the word “covenant” is not used.
- **Hosea 6:7** — “like Adam they transgressed the covenant” (wording and translation are disputed).
- **Romans 5:12–21** and **1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45–49** — Adam and Christ as representative heads, so that one’s act affects those “in” him.

### Historical covenants
- **Noah:** Genesis 6:18; 9:8–17 — an explicit covenant with Noah, his descendants, and creation.
- **Abraham:** Genesis 12:1–3; 15:1–21; 17:1–14 — promise, faith, and circumcision; treated as the root of the covenant of grace.
- **Moses / Sinai:** Exodus 19–24; Deuteronomy 5; 29–30 — the law given within the larger promise, often distinguished from the Abrahamic promise (see Galatians 3).
- **David:** 2 Samuel 7:8–16; Psalm 89 — a royal, everlasting line pointing to the Messiah.
- **New covenant:** Jeremiah 31:31–34; Ezekiel 36:25–27; Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25; **Hebrews 8–10** — the new covenant in Christ’s blood, written on the heart, fulfilling rather than discarding the earlier promises.

### One people, one promise, fulfilled in Christ
Covenant theology stresses continuity between Old and New Testament believers:
- **Genesis 3:15** — the first gospel promise after the fall.
- **Galatians 3:7–9, 15–29** — Abraham’s seed is Christ; those of faith are heirs; the law does not annul the promise.
- **Romans 4** — Abraham justified by faith, father of all who believe.
- **Romans 9–11** — Israel, the remnant, and Gentile inclusion in God’s purpose.
- **Ephesians 2:11–22** — Gentiles brought into the commonwealth and covenants of promise.
- **Hebrews 11** — Old Testament saints saved by faith in the promised Redeemer.
- **1 Peter 2:9–10** and **Galatians 6:16** — church language applied in ways covenant theologians connect to Israel’s calling (again, contested).

### Covenant of redemption (intra-Trinitarian)
Some Reformed writers also infer an eternal pact among Father, Son, and Spirit from texts such as:
- **Psalm 2:7–8; 110:1–4**
- **John 6:37–40; 17:1–5, 24**
- **Ephesians 1:3–14**
- **2 Timothy 1:9; Titus 1:2**

These are usually treated as theological inferences, not as a covenant named in the text.

### How the system is usually summarized from Scripture
1. God relates to people by covenant, not by bare power alone (Genesis 9, 15, 17; Exodus 19–24; Jeremiah 31).
2. Adam’s disobedience and Christ’s obedience are representative (Romans 5; 1 Corinthians 15).
3. The law at Sinai serves the earlier promise to Abraham and does not replace it (Galatians 3).
4. The new covenant fulfills the old promises in Christ (Jeremiah 31; Luke 22; Hebrews 8–10).
5. There is one way of salvation—by grace through faith—across both testaments (Genesis 15:6; Habakkuk 2:4; Romans 4; Hebrews 11).

A standard short statement of the view is the Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 7, which gathers many of these texts. For the main alternative, compare how dispensational writers handle Galatians 3, Ephesians 2–3, and Romans 9–11 as distinguishing Israel and the church more sharply.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about the Lord's Supper?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Cor 11:23-26, Matt 26:26-28, Luke 22:19-20
questions.response:
The Bible’s main teaching on the Lord’s Supper is in these places:

**Institution by Jesus**
- Matthew 26:26–29
- Mark 14:22–25
- Luke 22:14–20

**Paul’s fuller instruction**
- 1 Corinthians 11:23–34 — the clearest passage on what the Supper means and how it should be observed (remembrance of Christ’s body and blood, proclamation of his death, and self-examination)
- 1 Corinthians 10:16–17 — the cup and bread as participation in Christ and unity of the church

**Related practice in the early church**
- Acts 2:42 and Acts 20:7 refer to the believers “breaking bread,” which many understand as including the Lord’s Supper

John 6 (the bread of life) is sometimes linked to the Supper theologically, but it is not an account of Jesus instituting it.

questions.question: What passages address the doctrine of baptism?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, Acts 2:38-39, Rom 6:3-4, Col 2:11-12
questions.response:
Several New Testament passages are commonly cited in discussions of baptism. Traditions differ on mode, subjects (believers only vs. infants), and whether baptism is symbolic or sacramental, so these texts are listed by what they address, not as a single settled system.

**Command and practice**
- **Matthew 28:19** — Baptizing disciples in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
- **Mark 16:16** — Belief and baptism linked with salvation (textual status of Mark 16:9–20 is debated).
- **Acts 2:38–41** — Repentance, baptism in Jesus’ name, forgiveness, and the gift of the Spirit; about three thousand baptized.
- **Acts 8:12–13, 36–38** — Baptisms in Samaria and of the Ethiopian official.
- **Acts 9:18; 22:16** — Paul’s baptism; “wash away your sins, calling on his name.”
- **Acts 10:47–48** — Cornelius’s household baptized after receiving the Spirit.
- **Acts 16:14–15, 31–33** — Lydia’s household and the Philippian jailer’s household.
- **Acts 18:8** — Many in Corinth believe and are baptized.
- **Acts 19:1–5** — Disciples of John rebaptized in Jesus’ name.

**Meaning and effects**
- **Romans 6:3–4** — Baptized into Christ’s death; buried and raised with him to new life.
- **Galatians 3:27** — Baptized into Christ; clothed with Christ.
- **Colossians 2:11–12** — Buried with him in baptism; raised through faith.
- **1 Corinthians 12:13** — Baptized by one Spirit into one body.
- **Ephesians 4:4–6** — “One baptism” among the unities of the church.
- **1 Peter 3:21** — Baptism “now saves you” as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection—not as mere washing.
- **Titus 3:5** — “Washing of regeneration” (often read as baptismal, though the word “baptism” is not used).

**Jesus’ baptism and John’s baptism**
- **Matthew 3:13–17** (also Mark 1:9–11; Luke 3:21–22; John 1:29–34) — Jesus baptized by John; the Spirit descends.
- **Mark 1:4–5; Luke 3:3** — John’s baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins.
- **John 3:22–26; 4:1–2** — Jesus’ disciples baptize (Jesus himself did not).
- **Acts 1:5; 11:16** — John’s water baptism contrasted with baptism in the Holy Spirit.
- **Matthew 3:11; Mark 1:8; Luke 3:16** — John: “I baptize with water… he will baptize with the Holy Spirit.”

**Passages often brought into the debate**
- **John 3:5** — Born of water and the Spirit (baptismal reading is common but not universal).
- **Acts 8:14–17; 19:5–6** — Laying on of hands and the Spirit in connection with baptism.
- **1 Corinthians 1:13–17** — Paul baptized few in Corinth and stresses that Christ, not the baptizer, is what matters; he does not reject baptism itself.
- **Hebrews 6:1–2** — “Instruction about washings” (or baptisms) listed among elementary teachings.

Old Testament washings (for example Leviticus 14–16; Ezekiel 36:25–27) and the Red Sea crossing (1 Corinthians 10:1–2, “baptized into Moses”) are sometimes used as background, not as Christian baptism itself.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about church government and eldership?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Tim 3:1-7, Titus 1:5-9, Acts 14:23, 1 Pet 5:1-4
questions.response:
Scripture’s main teaching on church government and eldership is concentrated in a handful of New Testament passages. The terms “elder” (*presbyteros*), “overseer/bishop” (*episkopos*), and “pastor/shepherd” (*poimēn*) are used of the same office in overlapping ways.

**Appointment and role of elders**
- **Acts 14:23** — Paul and Barnabas appoint elders in every church.
- **Acts 20:17–35** — Paul addresses the Ephesian elders and charges them to shepherd the church, which God purchased with his own blood. Verse 28 uses “overseers” of the same men.
- **Titus 1:5–9** — Titus is told to appoint elders in every town; qualifications follow, and the elder is also called an overseer.
- **1 Peter 5:1–4** — Peter exhorts elders to shepherd the flock willingly, not for gain or by domineering, as examples to the flock, under the chief Shepherd.
- **James 5:14** — The sick are to call for the elders of the church.
- **1 Timothy 5:17–20** — Elders who rule well, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching, are worthy of double honor; accusations against elders require witnesses.

**Qualifications**
- **1 Timothy 3:1–7** — Qualifications for the overseer (character, household, ability to teach, not a recent convert).
- **Titus 1:6–9** — Parallel list, including holding firmly to sound doctrine so as to teach and refute error.

**Related offices and leadership texts**
- **Philippians 1:1** — The church is addressed with its overseers and deacons.
- **1 Timothy 3:8–13** — Qualifications for deacons.
- **Acts 15:1–29** (esp. vv. 2, 6, 22–23) — Apostles and elders together deliberate and decide for the churches.
- **Hebrews 13:7, 17** — Remember your leaders; obey and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls.
- **Ephesians 4:11–12** — Christ gives pastors and teachers (among other gifts) to equip the saints.
- **1 Thessalonians 5:12–13** — Respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord.

**How these texts are read**
Churches differ on polity—whether elders rule as a plurality in each congregation (presbyterian/elder-led), whether a single bishop stands over several churches (episcopal), or whether the congregation retains final authority under its elders (congregational). Those differences come from how these passages are weighed together, not from a single chapter that spells out one complete system. The consistent New Testament picture is local churches led by qualified elders/overseers who teach, shepherd, and exercise oversight, often alongside deacons who serve practical needs.

questions.question: What Bible passages teach about the second coming of Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Acts 1:11, 1 Thess 4:16-17, Matt 24:30, Rev 1:7
questions.response:
Several New Testament passages teach that Jesus will return visibly, personally, and in glory. Christians differ on the timing and details (for example, how these texts relate to the millennium), but the expectation of his return is widely shared.

**Jesus’ own teaching**
- **Matthew 24–25** (also **Mark 13** and **Luke 21**): The Olivet Discourse. Jesus speaks of his coming on the clouds with power and great glory, the gathering of the elect, and the need to stay watchful because the day and hour are unknown (**Matthew 24:30–31, 36–44**). **Matthew 25:31–46** pictures the Son of Man coming in glory to judge the nations.
- **John 14:1–3**: Jesus says he goes to prepare a place and will come again to take his people to himself.

**The apostles**
- **Acts 1:9–11**: After the ascension, angels say Jesus will return in the same way he was taken up.
- **1 Thessalonians 4:13–18**: The Lord descends, the dead in Christ rise, and believers are caught up to meet him.
- **1 Thessalonians 5:1–11** and **2 Thessalonians 1:6–10; 2:1–8**: The “day of the Lord,” judgment on those who oppose the gospel, and the revealing of the lawless one before Christ’s coming.
- **1 Corinthians 15:20–28, 50–58**: Christ’s return, the resurrection of the dead, and the final defeat of death.
- **Titus 2:11–13**: Believers wait for “the blessed hope—the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ.”
- **Hebrews 9:27–28**: Christ will appear a second time, not to bear sin but to save those who are waiting for him.
- **2 Peter 3:3–13**: Scoffers deny his coming; the day of the Lord will come, and believers should live holy lives in light of it.
- **1 John 3:2**: When he appears, believers will be like him, for they will see him as he is.
- **James 5:7–8**: Be patient until the Lord’s coming, which is near.

**Revelation and related hope**
- **Revelation 1:7**: He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him.
- **Revelation 19:11–16**: The rider on the white horse, called Faithful and True, comes to judge and make war in righteousness.
- **Revelation 22:12, 20**: “I am coming soon… Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!”

**Often linked Old Testament texts**
- **Daniel 7:13–14**: One like a son of man coming with the clouds and receiving an everlasting kingdom (quoted in the Gospels in connection with Jesus).
- **Zechariah 14:1–9**: The Lord’s coming and reign, often read by Christians in light of Christ’s return.

A short way many summarize the teaching: Christ will return personally and visibly (**Acts 1:11; Revelation 1:7**), raise the dead and gather his people (**1 Thessalonians 4; 1 Corinthians 15**), judge (**Matthew 25; 2 Thessalonians 1**), and renew creation (**2 Peter 3; Revelation 21–22**). For how a particular church reads the sequence of these events, a study Bible or a pastor in that tradition is the best next step.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about the final judgment?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 25:31-46, Rev 20:11-15, 2 Cor 5:10, Acts 17:31
questions.response:
The Bible teaches a final judgment in both the Old and New Testaments. Major passages include:

**Old Testament**
- **Daniel 12:1–2** — resurrection of the dead, some to everlasting life and some to shame and everlasting contempt
- **Ecclesiastes 12:14** — God will bring every deed into judgment
- **Psalm 96:13** and **Psalm 98:9** — the Lord comes to judge the earth in righteousness

**New Testament**
- **Matthew 25:31–46** — the Son of Man separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats
- **John 5:22–29** — the Father has given judgment to the Son; the dead will rise to life or to condemnation
- **Acts 17:31** — God has fixed a day to judge the world by a man he has appointed (Jesus)
- **Romans 2:5–16** and **Romans 14:10–12** — a day of wrath and righteous judgment; everyone will give an account to God
- **2 Corinthians 5:10** — all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ
- **Hebrews 9:27** — people are appointed to die once, and after that comes judgment
- **2 Peter 3:7** and **Jude 14–15** — judgment of the ungodly
- **Revelation 20:11–15** — the great white throne judgment, with books opened and people judged according to what they had done

Related themes also appear in passages such as **Matthew 12:36**, **1 Corinthians 3:12–15** (often read as a judgment of believers’ works), and **Revelation 22:12**.

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach about heaven and hell?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rev 21:1-4, Matt 25:46, 2 Thess 1:9, John 14:2-3
questions.response:
Scripture speaks of heaven and hell in many places. The main passages below are widely cited; Christian traditions differ on how literally to take the imagery and on whether final judgment means eternal conscious punishment, destruction, or something else.

### Heaven
- **John 14:1–3** — Jesus says he goes to prepare a place for his followers and will come again to take them to himself.
- **2 Corinthians 5:1–8** — An “eternal house in heaven”; to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord.
- **Philippians 3:20–21** — Believers’ citizenship is in heaven; Christ will transform their bodies.
- **1 Thessalonians 4:16–17** — The dead in Christ rise and the living are caught up to meet the Lord.
- **Matthew 6:19–21** — Store up treasures in heaven, where they cannot be destroyed.
- **Luke 23:43** — Jesus tells the thief on the cross, “Today you will be with me in paradise.”
- **Revelation 21–22** — A new heaven and new earth; the new Jerusalem; God dwelling with his people; no more death, mourning, or pain; the river and tree of life.
- **Revelation 4–5** and **7:9–17** — Worship before God’s throne; a great multitude from every nation.
- **Isaiah 65:17** and **66:22** — God creates new heavens and a new earth (background for later New Testament hope).
- **Matthew 25:31–46** — The righteous enter eternal life in the kingdom prepared for them.

Related ideas often linked with heaven: the kingdom of God (e.g., Matthew 5–7; Luke 17:20–21), resurrection (1 Corinthians 15), and being “with Christ” (Philippians 1:23).

### Hell and final judgment
Scripture uses several images—Gehenna, outer darkness, unquenchable fire, the lake of fire—rather than one technical definition.

- **Matthew 5:22, 29–30; 10:28; 18:8–9; 23:33** — Warnings about Gehenna; fear the one who can destroy body and soul there.
- **Mark 9:43–48** — Better to enter life maimed than to go into Gehenna, “where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched” (echoing Isaiah 66:24).
- **Matthew 13:40–42, 49–50** — The wicked thrown into a fiery furnace; weeping and gnashing of teeth.
- **Matthew 25:31–46** — Separation of the nations; some go to eternal punishment, the righteous to eternal life. Verse 41 speaks of “eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”
- **Luke 16:19–31** — The rich man and Lazarus: a great chasm; the rich man in torment, Lazarus comforted. (Often read as a parable; views differ on how much doctrine to draw from it.)
- **2 Thessalonians 1:6–10** — Those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel face everlasting destruction, shut out from the Lord’s presence.
- **Revelation 14:9–11** — Judgment imagery of fire and sulfur; “the smoke of their torment rises for ever and ever.”
- **Revelation 20:10–15** — The devil, beast, and false prophet in the lake of fire; death and Hades thrown in; anyone whose name is not in the book of life cast into the lake of fire (“the second death”).
- **Revelation 21:8** — The cowardly, unbelieving, and others listed have their place in the lake of fire, the second death.
- **Jude 7, 13** and **2 Peter 2:4–9** — Examples of judgment; some angels held for judgment; “blackest darkness” reserved for the ungodly.

### How these texts are often read together
- Heaven is pictured less as a vague “up there” and more as life with God—sometimes “in heaven” now in hope, and finally in a renewed creation (Revelation 21–22).
- Hell is tied to final judgment, exclusion from God’s presence, and severe imagery of fire, darkness, and destruction. Whether that imagery means unending conscious suffering or final destruction is debated (compare “eternal punishment” in Matthew 25:46 with “destruction” language in Matthew 10:28 and 2 Thessalonians 1:9).
- Many passages stress that judgment belongs to God and that the gospel’s aim is rescue and life, not speculation about the afterlife for its own sake (e.g., John 3:16–18; Romans 6:23).

For study, read the passages in context (especially Matthew 25, Luke 16, and Revelation 20–22) and compare a few translations. A study Bible or a standard systematic theology will show how different churches weigh these texts.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the doctrine of creation?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 1:1, John 1:3, Col 1:16, Heb 11:3
questions.response:
The Bible teaches creation most directly in **Genesis 1–2**, and affirms it in many other places.

**Primary account**
- **Genesis 1:1–2:3** — God creates the heavens and the earth in six days and rests on the seventh. The repeated refrain is that God speaks and it comes to be, and that what he made was good.
- **Genesis 2:4–25** — A closer account of the creation of the man and the woman, the garden, and human vocation.

**Other major passages**
- **Psalms** — e.g. Psalm 33:6–9; Psalm 104; Psalm 148 (creation by God’s word and ongoing care for what he made).
- **Prophets** — e.g. Isaiah 40:26–28; 42:5; 45:12, 18; Jeremiah 10:12; Amos 4:13.
- **Job 38–41** — God as the maker and sovereign of the created order.
- **New Testament** — John 1:1–3 (all things made through the Word); Colossians 1:15–17; Hebrews 11:3; Acts 17:24–26; Revelation 4:11.
- **Romans 1:20** — the created world as revealing God’s eternal power and divine nature.

Together these texts present God as the sole Creator of all things, creation as good and purposeful, and humanity as made in God’s image and accountable to him.

questions.question: What passages teach about God's providence?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 10:29-31, Rom 8:28, Eph 1:11, Dan 4:35
questions.response:
Several well-known passages teach that God actively cares for, sustains, and directs creation and human life—not as a distant observer, but as one who governs with purpose.

**Care for creation and people**
- **Matthew 6:25–34** — God feeds the birds and clothes the lilies; people are of greater worth, so anxiety is answered by trust in the Father’s care.
- **Matthew 10:29–31** — Not a sparrow falls apart from the Father; the hairs of your head are numbered.
- **Psalm 104** — God sustains the natural order: seasons, food, and the life of creatures depend on him.
- **Acts 17:24–28** — God gives life and breath to all; “in him we live and move and have our being.”

**Sustaining all things**
- **Colossians 1:16–17** — All things were created through Christ and “in him all things hold together.”
- **Hebrews 1:3** — The Son upholds the universe by the word of his power.
- **Psalm 139** — God’s knowledge and presence reach every place and every moment of a life.

**Guidance of human plans**
- **Proverbs 16:9** — People plan their course, but the Lord establishes their steps.
- **Proverbs 19:21** — Many plans are in a person’s heart, but the Lord’s purpose stands.
- **James 4:13–15** — Future plans should be held with the humility of “if the Lord wills.”

**Purpose even in hardship**
- **Genesis 50:20** — Joseph: what others meant for evil, God meant for good.
- **Romans 8:28** — For those who love God, he works all things together for good according to his purpose.
- **Ephesians 1:11** — God works all things according to the counsel of his will.

**Daily provision and mercy**
- **Psalm 23** — The Lord as shepherd: guidance, provision, and presence even in dark valleys.
- **Philippians 4:19** — God supplies what his people need according to his riches.
- **Lamentations 3:22–23** — Steadfast love and mercies that are new every morning.

Together these passages present providence as God’s ongoing rule and care: he sustains the world, knows and values people, directs outcomes beyond human planning, and can bring good even through what others intend for harm.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about the nature and practice of prayer?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 6:9-13, Phil 4:6, 1 Thess 5:17, John 14:13-14
questions.response:
Scripture teaches about prayer throughout both Testaments. Major places include:

**Jesus’ teaching**
- Matthew 6:5–15 and Luke 11:1–13 — the nature of prayer (not for show; addressed to the Father), the Lord’s Prayer, persistence, and confidence that the Father gives good gifts.
- Matthew 7:7–11; Luke 18:1–8 — asking, seeking, knocking, and persevering.
- John 14:13–14; 15:7, 16; 16:23–24 — praying in Jesus’ name, abiding in him, and asking according to his word.

**Apostolic instruction**
- Philippians 4:6–7 — prayer and thanksgiving instead of anxiety, with the peace of God.
- 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18 — rejoice, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything.
- Ephesians 6:18; Colossians 4:2 — praying at all times in the Spirit, with watchfulness and thanksgiving.
- 1 Timothy 2:1–8 — supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings for all people.
- James 1:5–8; 4:2–3; 5:13–18 — asking in faith, right motives, and the prayer of the righteous.
- Romans 8:26–27 — the Spirit helping our weakness and interceding.
- Hebrews 4:14–16 — drawing near to the throne of grace through Christ.

**Old Testament patterns and promises**
- Psalms (for example 5, 51, 86, 145) — praise, confession, lament, and trust.
- 1 Kings 8 / 2 Chronicles 6–7 — Solomon’s prayer and God’s response about prayer toward his name.
- Jeremiah 29:12–13; 33:3 — call on God and seek him with all your heart.
- Daniel 6 and 9 — regular prayer and confession.

Taken together, Scripture presents prayer as humble, faith-filled communion with God the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit—marked by adoration, confession, thanksgiving, and petition, offered continually and according to God’s will.

questions.question: What Bible passages relate to Sabbath observance?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Exod 20:8-11, Isa 58:13-14, Mark 2:27-28, Heb 4:9-10
questions.response:
Several well-known Bible passages address Sabbath observance, from creation and the Ten Commandments through the prophets and the New Testament.

**Creation and the commandment**
- **Genesis 2:2–3** — God rests on the seventh day and blesses it.
- **Exodus 20:8–11** — The fourth commandment: remember the Sabbath, keep it holy, and rest because God rested at creation.
- **Deuteronomy 5:12–15** — The commandment restated, linking rest to Israel’s deliverance from Egypt.
- **Exodus 31:12–17** — The Sabbath as a sign of the covenant; work is to cease.
- **Leviticus 23:3** — The Sabbath as a holy convocation and a day of complete rest.

**Prophets and later practice**
- **Isaiah 58:13–14** — Calling the Sabbath a delight and honoring it rather than pursuing one’s own affairs.
- **Jeremiah 17:21–27** — Warnings about carrying burdens and doing work on the Sabbath.
- **Nehemiah 13:15–22** — Nehemiah stopping commerce and labor on the Sabbath.
- **Ezekiel 20:12, 20** — The Sabbath as a sign that the Lord sanctifies his people.

**New Testament**
- **Mark 2:23–28** (also Matthew 12:1–8; Luke 6:1–5) — Jesus says the Sabbath was made for people, and that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.
- **Matthew 12:9–14** (Mark 3:1–6; Luke 6:6–11) — Healing on the Sabbath; doing good is lawful.
- **Luke 4:16** — Jesus’ custom of going to the synagogue on the Sabbath.
- **Luke 13:10–17; 14:1–6; John 5:1–18; 7:22–24; 9:1–16** — Further debates about healing and what is permitted.
- **Acts 13:14, 42–44; 16:13; 17:2; 18:4** — Paul and others teaching in synagogues on the Sabbath.
- **Colossians 2:16–17** — Not letting anyone judge you regarding a Sabbath day; such things are called a shadow of what was to come.
- **Hebrews 4:1–11** — “Sabbath rest” as a rest that remains for God’s people, tied to entering God’s rest by faith.

Jewish and Christian traditions read these passages differently—especially whether the seventh-day Sabbath continues unchanged, is fulfilled in Christ, or is observed on Sunday. The texts above are the main ones those discussions usually start from.

questions.question: Where are the Ten Commandments given in Scripture?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Exod 20:1-17, Deut 5:6-21
questions.response: The Ten Commandments are given in **Exodus 20:1–17** (God speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai) and restated in **Deuteronomy 5:6–21**.

questions.question: Where does Jesus teach the Lord's Prayer?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 6:9-13, Luke 11:2-4
questions.response:
Jesus teaches the Lord’s Prayer in two places in the Gospels:

- **Matthew 6:9–13**, during the Sermon on the Mount (the fuller, more familiar form).
- **Luke 11:2–4**, in a shorter form, after the disciples ask him to teach them to pray.

questions.question: What passages address the sacraments in Reformed theology?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, 1 Cor 11:23-26, Acts 2:38-39, Rom 6:3-4
questions.response:
In classic Reformed theology there are two sacraments instituted by Christ: baptism and the Lord’s Supper. They are treated as signs and seals of the covenant of grace. The passages below are the ones Reformed confessions and theologians most often use.

### Sacraments in general
- **Genesis 17:7–14** and **Romans 4:11** — circumcision as a covenant sign and seal; used as the pattern for New Testament sacraments.
- **Exodus 12** and **1 Corinthians 10:1–4** — Passover and the wilderness “baptism” and spiritual food as Old Testament types.
- **Matthew 28:18–20** and **1 Corinthians 11:23–26** — Christ’s institution of the two New Testament sacraments.

### Baptism
- **Matthew 28:19** — institution: baptizing in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
- **Romans 6:3–4**, **Galatians 3:27**, **Colossians 2:11–12**, **Titus 3:5**, **1 Peter 3:21** — union with Christ, cleansing, and the covenant sign that replaces circumcision.
- **Acts 2:38–41**, **8:36–38**, **10:47–48**, **16:14–15, 31–33** — apostolic practice, including household baptisms.
- For infant baptism (the majority Reformed view): **Genesis 17**, **Acts 2:39**, **1 Corinthians 7:14**, and **Colossians 2:11–12**, read with the household texts in Acts.

### The Lord’s Supper
- **Matthew 26:26–29**, **Mark 14:22–25**, **Luke 22:19–20**, **1 Corinthians 11:23–26** — institution: bread and cup as Christ’s body and blood, given for remembrance until he comes.
- **1 Corinthians 10:16–17** — communion (participation) in Christ’s body and blood, and the unity of the church.
- **1 Corinthians 11:27–34** — worthy reception, self-examination, and fencing the table.

**John 6:53–58** is often discussed, but many Reformed interpreters do not treat it as a direct institution of the Supper; they read it as faith in Christ, with the Supper as a later sign of that same feeding.

### Where Reformed documents take this up
- **Belgic Confession**, Articles 33–35  
- **Heidelberg Catechism**, Q&A 65–82  
- **Westminster Confession of Faith**, chapters 27–29 (and Larger Catechism Q&A 161–177)  
- **Second Helvetic Confession**, chapters 19–21  

Those chapters argue that the sacraments confirm the Word, do not work by bare performance of the rite, and are effectual to the elect by the Spirit through faith. Reformed Baptists share the two-sacrament framework and the Supper texts, but restrict baptism to professing believers and do not use the covenant-infant arguments above.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about church discipline?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 18:15-17, 1 Cor 5:1-13, Titus 3:10, 2 Thess 3:14-15
questions.response:
The Bible’s main teaching on church discipline is in a few New Testament passages that describe confronting sin, restoring the repentant, and, if necessary, removing someone from fellowship.

**Matthew 18:15–20** is the foundational text. Jesus outlines a stepwise process: go privately to the person who has sinned against you; if they will not listen, take one or two witnesses; if they still refuse, tell it to the church; if they refuse even the church, treat them as an outsider. The passage ties this to the church’s authority to “bind and loose” and to Jesus’ presence where two or three gather in his name.

**1 Corinthians 5** applies that idea to a public case of sexual immorality. Paul tells the church to remove the unrepentant person from fellowship (“hand this man over to Satan”), not to keep company with someone who claims to be a believer while living in open immorality, and to do this so the person might be saved and the church kept pure. He distinguishes this from relating to unbelievers in the world.

**2 Corinthians 2:5–11** shows the other side: when the disciplined person repents, the church should forgive, comfort, and restore them, so they are not overwhelmed by excessive sorrow and so Satan does not gain an advantage.

Other related passages:

- **Galatians 6:1** — restore someone caught in sin gently, watching yourself.
- **2 Thessalonians 3:6–15** — keep away from believers who live in idleness and disobedience to apostolic teaching; warn them as brothers, not as enemies.
- **Titus 3:10–11** — warn a divisive person once, then twice; after that, have nothing to do with them.
- **1 Timothy 5:19–20** — do not entertain an accusation against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses; rebuke those who persist in sin publicly so others may fear.
- **Romans 16:17** — watch out for those who cause divisions contrary to the teaching you received, and avoid them.

A broader theme of God’s fatherly discipline appears in **Hebrews 12:5–11**, but that is about God’s correction of his children, not the church’s formal process. Together, the passages above teach discipline aimed at repentance and restoration, carried out by the church, and reserved for serious, unrepentant sin rather than every personal offense.

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach about Christian liberty?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gal 5:1, 1 Cor 8:9, Rom 14:1-23, 1 Pet 2:16
questions.response:
Christian liberty in Scripture is freedom in Christ—from sin, condemnation, and bondage to the law as a means of righteousness—used to love and serve, not to indulge the self.

**Freedom in Christ**
- **John 8:31–36** — Those who abide in Jesus’ word know the truth, and the truth sets them free. “If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.”
- **Galatians 5:1** — “For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.”
- **2 Corinthians 3:17** — “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.”
- **Romans 8:1–2** — No condemnation for those in Christ Jesus; the Spirit’s law of life has set them free from the law of sin and death.

**Freedom from sin’s dominion**
- **Romans 6:14–18, 22** — Sin no longer has dominion; believers have been set free from sin and become slaves of righteousness, with the fruit of sanctification.
- **Romans 6:6–7** — The old self was crucified with Christ so that believers would no longer be enslaved to sin.

**Called to freedom, not license**
- **Galatians 5:13–14** — Called to freedom, but not to use it as an opportunity for the flesh; through love, serve one another. The whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbor.
- **1 Peter 2:16** — Live as free people, not using freedom as a cover-up for evil, but as servants of God.
- **1 Corinthians 6:12; 10:23** — “All things are lawful,” but not all are helpful or build up. Liberty is bounded by what edifies.

**Liberty and the conscience of others**
- **Romans 14:1–23** — In disputable matters, do not despise or judge a brother. Whatever is not from faith is sin; pursue peace and mutual upbuilding.
- **1 Corinthians 8:9–13; 10:24–33** — Take care that your liberty does not become a stumbling block. Seek the good of others, not your own advantage.

**The law of liberty**
- **James 1:25** — The one who looks into the perfect law of liberty and perseveres is blessed in doing.
- **James 2:12** — Speak and act as those who will be judged under the law of liberty.

**Not under law as a covenant of works, yet not lawless**
- **Galatians 2:4; 4:4–7; 5:18** — Freedom from the yoke some would impose; sons, not slaves; if led by the Spirit, not under the law.
- **Romans 7:4–6** — Dead to the law through Christ’s body, so as to belong to him and bear fruit for God, serving in the new way of the Spirit.

Taken together, the passages teach that Christian liberty is real, Christ-given, and Spirit-led: freedom from guilt and slavery to sin, freedom from using law-keeping to earn standing with God, and freedom exercised in love so that others are built up rather than harmed.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about marriage?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 2:24, Eph 5:22-33, Matt 19:4-6, Heb 13:4
questions.response:
The Bible’s main teaching on marriage is spread across several well-known passages rather than one single chapter.

**Foundational texts**
- **Genesis 2:18–24** — Marriage is presented as a one-flesh union: a man leaves his parents and is joined to his wife.
- **Matthew 19:3–9** (and **Mark 10:6–12**) — Jesus quotes Genesis and treats marriage as a lasting bond, with limited teaching on divorce.
- **Malachi 2:14–16** — Marriage is described as a covenant before God.

**New Testament instruction for husbands and wives**
- **Ephesians 5:22–33** — The longest direct teaching: mutual duties, with marriage compared to Christ and the church.
- **Colossians 3:18–19** and **1 Peter 3:1–7** — Shorter parallel instructions.
- **1 Corinthians 7** — Paul’s fullest discussion of marriage, singleness, sexual relations, and separation.
- **Hebrews 13:4** — Marriage is to be honored; sexual faithfulness is required.

**Related material**
- **Song of Solomon** celebrates marital love (often read allegorically as well).
- **Proverbs 5, 18:22, and 31** speak about fidelity and a good spouse.
- Passages such as **Genesis 1:27–28** and **Matthew 19:4–6** are often cited on the creation pattern of male and female in marriage.

Different Christian traditions weigh these texts differently, especially on divorce, roles, and remarriage. For the core biblical picture, start with Genesis 2, Matthew 19, Ephesians 5, and 1 Corinthians 7.

questions.question: What passages address the role of the civil magistrate?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 13:1-7, 1 Pet 2:13-17, Acts 5:29, Dan 2:21
questions.response:
The role of the civil magistrate is addressed mainly in these biblical passages, and in the classic Protestant confessions that expound them.

**Primary New Testament texts**
- **Romans 13:1–7** — The fullest treatment: civil authority is ordained by God, exists to punish evil and praise good, and is to be obeyed and supported (including by taxes) for conscience’s sake.
- **1 Peter 2:13–17** — Submit to every human institution “for the Lord’s sake,” whether emperor or governors sent to punish wrongdoing and commend what is right; honor all, fear God, honor the emperor.
- **Titus 3:1** — Be subject to rulers and authorities, ready for every good work.
- **1 Timothy 2:1–2** — Pray for kings and all in authority so that believers may lead a quiet and peaceable life.

**Related limits and background**
- **Acts 5:29** — Obedience to God over human authority when the two conflict.
- **John 19:11** — Authority is given from above.
- **Daniel 2:21; Proverbs 8:15–16** — God raises up and removes rulers; by him kings reign and princes decree justice.
- Old Testament patterns often cited alongside these include **Exodus 18**, **Deuteronomy 16–17**, and the prophetic critiques of unjust rulers (e.g., passages in Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Amos).

**Confessional summaries**
Reformed and Lutheran confessions gather these texts under the heading of the civil magistrate, notably:
- **Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 23** (“Of the Civil Magistrate”)
- **Belgic Confession, art. 36**
- **Augsburg Confession, art. 16**
- **Second Helvetic Confession, ch. 30**

Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2 are the passages most often treated as the direct New Testament statement of the magistrate’s God-given role: to maintain order, restrain evil, and protect the good, under God’s higher authority.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "God elects individuals to salvation based on His foreknowledge of their future faith and repentance."
questions.reference_answer: Election is unconditional, not based on foreseen faith Faith is the result of election, not its cause

required_points: Election is unconditional, not based on foreseen faith
Faith is the result of election, not its cause
scoring.rubric: Must reject the Arminian view of conditional election based on foreseen faith. Should affirm unconditional election per Reformed standards.

questions.response:
**From a Reformed perspective, that statement is rejected.** It describes conditional election (election based on foreseen faith), not the Reformed doctrine of unconditional election.

### What the statement claims
It says God looks ahead, sees who will believe and repent, and elects those people on that basis. Faith and repentance are treated as the ground or condition of election. That is the classic Arminian (and broader “prescient”) view, not the Reformed one.

### The Reformed alternative
Reformed theology teaches **unconditional election**: God chooses particular people for salvation according to His sovereign will and grace, not because of anything foreseen in them—including faith, repentance, or good works.

Faith is the **fruit** of election, not its cause. God elects, then effectually calls, and the elect come to faith. Election explains why anyone believes; foreseen faith does not explain election.

### Why Reformed theology rejects the statement
1. **Faith is God’s gift, not a human contribution that grounds election.**  
   If faith itself is given by grace (Ephesians 2:8–9; Philippians 1:29; Acts 13:48), it cannot be the prior condition on which God bases His choice. Making foreseen faith the basis of election turns grace into a response to something in the sinner.

2. **Scripture presents election as according to God’s purpose, not human response.**  
   Passages such as Ephesians 1:4–5, 11, Romans 9:11–16, and 2 Timothy 1:9 locate the reason for election in God’s will and purpose “before the foundation of the world,” not in foreseen belief. Romans 9 in particular stresses that election is not based on works or on anything the person does.

3. **“Foreknowledge” is not read as mere foresight of faith.**  
   In Romans 8:29, Reformed interpreters typically take “foreknow” in the sense of prior, covenantal love or choosing—not simply knowing in advance who would believe. Election, calling, justification, and glorification are then a chain God carries through for those He has set His love upon.

4. **The logical order matters.**  
   If God elects because He foresees faith, then human decision is logically prior to God’s choice. Reformed theology reverses that: God’s choice is logically prior, and faith follows as the result of regenerating grace.

5. **Confessional Reformed teaching is explicit.**  
   The Canons of Dort reject election “on the basis of foreseen faith.” The Westminster Confession likewise teaches that God elected “out of His mere free grace and love, without any foresight of faith, or good works, or perseverance in either of them, or any other thing in the creature, as conditions, or causes moving Him thereunto.”

### A fair distinction
The statement is a real and widely held evangelical position. Reformed theology does not deny that God foreknows who will believe, or that faith and repentance are necessary. It denies that those foreseen responses are **why** God elects. In the Reformed view, God foreknows faith because He has purposed to give it, not the other way around.

**Bottom line:** From a Reformed perspective, God does not elect individuals because He foresees their faith and repentance. He elects them freely, in Christ, according to His own purpose, and then grants the faith and repentance by which they are saved.

score_details.justification: The model clearly rejects the statement, correctly identifies it as conditional election, and thoroughly explains the Reformed doctrine of unconditional election. It covers all required points with excellent theological depth, referencing scripture and confessional standards, and distinguishes the Reformed view from the Arminian position effectively.
