questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "God's saving grace can be ultimately resisted by the free will of man."
questions.reference_answer: Effectual grace cannot be ultimately resisted God's sovereign call always accomplishes its purpose

required_points: Effectual grace cannot be ultimately resisted
God's sovereign call always accomplishes its purpose
scoring.rubric: Must reject the Arminian doctrine of resistible grace. Should affirm irresistible (effectual) grace.

questions.response:
From a classic Reformed perspective, that statement is rejected.

Reformed theology distinguishes the gospel’s outward call, which people do resist, from God’s effectual saving grace toward the elect, which is not ultimately resistible. The claim is not that sinners never oppose the Spirit, but that when God purposes to save, he renews the will so that the person comes freely and certainly.

### Why Reformed theology denies it
- **Bondage of the will.** Apart from regenerating grace, the fallen will is not neutral toward God. It is enslaved to sin and unable, of itself, to submit to him or embrace Christ (John 6:44; Romans 8:7–8; Ephesians 2:1–5; 1 Corinthians 2:14). “Free will” in the libertarian sense—an unregenerate ability to accept or finally refuse saving grace—is denied.
- **Effectual calling.** Those whom God has predestined he effectually calls by Word and Spirit: enlightening the mind, replacing the heart of stone with a heart of flesh, and renewing the will so that they are made willing (Westminster Confession of Faith 10.1; Canons of Dort III/IV). Saving grace does not merely invite; it accomplishes what God intends.
- **God’s purpose is not frustrated.** Election, redemption, and calling stand or fall together. If the elect could finally resist saving grace, God’s saving purpose would depend on an independent human decision and could fail—something Reformed theology denies (John 6:37–39; Romans 8:29–30; Philippians 1:6).

### The important nuance
Reformed writers do not say people never resist grace. Scripture itself speaks of resisting the Spirit (Acts 7:51), and many who hear the gospel reject it. The denial is narrower: **God’s saving, effectual grace toward those he intends to save cannot be finally overcome by the human will.** Resistance is real, but in the elect it is overcome. They believe most freely, yet that freedom is the fruit of grace, not its cause (WCF 10.1: “yet so, as they come most freely, being made willing by His grace”).

### Confessional contrast
The statement matches the Arminian teaching of resistible (prevenient) grace, which the Synod of Dort explicitly opposed. In the Reformed scheme it contradicts irresistible (or effectual) grace—the “I” of TULIP—and the related doctrines of total inability and unconditional election.

So, evaluated on Reformed grounds, the statement is false: saving grace may be resisted outwardly and for a time, but it cannot be ultimately resisted by those whom God has purposed to save.

It also addresses the required points of effectual grace and God's sovereign call, while adding a crucial nuance about resistance that further demonstrates its expertise. The 'Confessional contrast' is a strong addition, explicitly linking the statement to Arminianism and contrasting it with the 'I' of TULIP.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "A truly regenerate believer can fall away from grace and lose their salvation."
questions.reference_answer: True believers cannot lose salvation God preserves the elect

required_points: True believers cannot lose salvation
God preserves the elect
scoring.rubric: Must reject the possibility of losing salvation. Should affirm the perseverance and preservation of the saints.

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, that statement is false.

Reformed theology teaches the perseverance of the saints: everyone whom God truly regenerates will be preserved by God and will persevere in faith to the end. Salvation is not a status the believer maintains by ongoing performance and can forfeit; it is grounded in God’s electing purpose, Christ’s finished work, and the Spirit’s sealing and keeping. Classic expressions of this are the “P” of TULIP and the confessional teaching of the Canons of Dort (Fifth Head) and the Westminster Confession (ch. 17).

Typical biblical anchors include John 6:37–40 and 10:27–29 (the Father’s gift and the Son’s keeping), Romans 8:28–39 (no separation from the love of God in Christ), Philippians 1:6 (God completes what he begins), and 1 Peter 1:3–5 (an inheritance kept by God’s power). Regeneration is not a reversible human decision; it is a work of God that issues in a faith that endures, even through serious sin and seasons of weakness.

Reformed writers do not deny that people fall away. They deny that those who finally fall away were truly regenerate. Passages such as 1 John 2:19 (“they went out from us, but they were not of us”), the soils in Matthew 13, and warnings like Hebrews 6 are read as distinguishing temporary, non-saving profession from saving faith. Apostasy reveals that regeneration was never present, rather than undoing it.

Warnings and exhortations are still real. They are means God uses to keep his people, not evidence that the regenerate can be lost. A true believer may fall into grievous sin and for a time lose assurance and fellowship, but not union with Christ or final salvation. Restoration, not loss of justification, is the ordinary outcome of genuine repentance.

So the statement confuses apparent believers who apostatize with the truly regenerate, whom God preserves. On Reformed grounds, a person who is truly regenerate cannot fall away from grace in the sense of losing salvation.

It distinguishes between apparent and true believers effectively.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "Christ died equally for every individual person, intending to save all without distinction."
questions.reference_answer: The atonement is particular and definite Christ died especially for the elect

required_points: The atonement is particular and definite
Christ died especially for the elect
scoring.rubric: Must reject universal atonement in intent. Should affirm particular redemption while acknowledging sufficiency for all.

questions.response:
The statement is not consistent with confessional Reformed theology. Classical Reformed teaching rejects the claim that Christ died with an equal, saving intention for every individual.

**What the statement asserts.** It treats the atonement as aimed at every person in the same way, with a divine purpose to save all without distinction of persons. That is the view often called universal or indefinite atonement (in Arminian, Amyraldian, or hypothetical-universalist forms). Reformed confessions and the mainstream of Reformed dogmatics deny it.

**The Reformed alternative.** Definite or particular redemption holds that the Father gave a people to the Son, the Son died to secure their salvation, and the Spirit applies that redemption to those same people. Intention, accomplishment, and application are coextensive. Christ’s death does not merely make salvation possible for all alike; it actually redeems, justifies, and reconciles those for whom it was offered (John 10:11, 15; John 17:2, 6, 9; Eph. 5:25; Acts 20:28; Matt. 1:21; Isa. 53:10–12; Rom. 8:32–34).

**Distinctions Reformed theology insists on.**

- **Value and intention.** The cross has infinite worth and is sufficient to save any who come. Sufficiency is not the same as an equal intention to save every person.
- **“All” and “world.”** Scripture’s universal language often means all kinds of people—Jew and Gentile, every nation—not every individual without exception, and not an undifferentiated saving purpose toward each.
- **Offer and design.** The gospel is to be preached indiscriminately, and all who believe will be saved. A universal offer does not require a universal saving intention in the atonement. Faith itself is a fruit of Christ’s death for the elect, not a condition that makes an otherwise equal atonement effective.
- **What the cross accomplished.** If Christ bore the sins of every person with the same intent, Reformed theology asks why any for whom he died remain under wrath, and why faith, repentance, and perseverance are not secured for all. A merely potential redemption leaves the decisive difference in the sinner rather than in Christ’s work.

**Where the statement goes wrong, on Reformed terms.** “Equally for every individual” erases the particularity of the covenant of redemption. “Intending to save all without distinction” collapses the Trinity’s one purpose into a general wish that is not carried through. Reformed writers (Dort, Westminster, Owen, Turretin, and later confessional theologians) treat that as incompatible with an effectual atonement and with the doctrines of election and irresistible grace.

**A fair limit.** Some within broader Reformed circles (certain readings of Calvin, Amyraldian or hypothetical-universalist schemes) have said Christ died for all in some sense while the Spirit applies redemption only to the elect. Even those views do not usually mean an equal intention to save every person. Confessional Reformed theology—Canons of Dort, Head II; Westminster Confession 3 and 8—rejects equal, indiscriminate saving intent.

So from a Reformed perspective the statement should be denied. Christ died for his people, fully and effectually, and the gospel is freely offered to all, with the promise that everyone who believes will be saved.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "God gives prevenient grace to all people, enabling them to freely choose or reject salvation."
questions.reference_answer: Prevenient grace as an enabling universal gift is not a Reformed doctrine Effectual grace is particular, not universal

required_points: Prevenient grace as an enabling universal gift is not a Reformed doctrine
Effectual grace is particular, not universal
scoring.rubric: Must reject the Arminian doctrine of prevenient grace. Should distinguish effectual calling from a universal enabling grace.

questions.response:
The statement is the classical Arminian/Wesleyan account of prevenient grace, and Reformed theology rejects it.

**What it gets right, from a Reformed view.** No one believes apart from grace. Fallen people do not initiate their own salvation, and any ability to respond to the gospel is God’s gift, not a native human power. Reformed theology agrees that grace precedes faith.

**Where it parts company.** The disagreement is over what that grace does and to whom saving grace is given.

1. **Inability, not mere inability-until-enabled.** Reformed theology reads the unregenerate person as dead in sin and unable to submit to God (Eph. 2:1–5; Rom. 8:7–8; John 6:44, 65; 1 Cor. 2:14), not as neutral once a universal assist is supplied. The will is in bondage; it is not waiting for an equal chance to choose either way.

2. **Effectual grace, not merely enabling grace.** On the Reformed account, the grace that saves does not stop at making faith possible. It renews the heart so that the sinner freely and certainly comes to Christ (John 6:37; Acts 16:14; Ezek. 36:26–27). The Canons of Dort and Westminster Confession (chs. 9–10) teach effectual calling: God does not merely offer a capacity that the sinner may still refuse as the decisive cause of the outcome.

3. **Monergism, not synergism.** “God enables; the person freely decides” still makes the sinner’s choice the final difference between saved and lost. Reformed theology holds that regeneration precedes and produces faith, so the difference is God’s sovereign mercy, not a better use of a common grace (Rom. 9:16; Eph. 2:8–9; Phil. 1:29; John 1:12–13).

4. **Not given savingly to all.** Common grace and the outward gospel call are broad. The inward, saving work is particular—tied to election—and accomplishes what God intends (Rom. 8:29–30; Acts 13:48; John 10:26–29). A grace given equally to all, sufficient only to restore a libertarian choice, leaves God’s saving purpose contingent on human acceptance.

So from a Reformed perspective the statement rightly denies that sinners save themselves unaided, but wrongly relocates the decisive cause of salvation in a free human acceptance of a universal, resistible enablement. Grace, on this view, does not merely make salvation possible; it effectually brings the elect to faith.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "Man has libertarian free will that allows him to choose between good and evil apart from God's determining will."
questions.reference_answer: Fallen man's will is in bondage to sin True freedom comes through regeneration

required_points: Fallen man's will is in bondage to sin
True freedom comes through regeneration
scoring.rubric: Must reject libertarian free will in the fallen state. Should affirm compatibilist freedom and the bondage of the will.

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, that statement is false on both counts. Reformed theology affirms genuine human agency and moral responsibility, but it rejects libertarian free will and any choice made apart from God’s determining will.

**What the statement claims.** Libertarian free will means the power of contrary choice: in the same circumstances, with the same desires and character, a person could have chosen otherwise, and that choice is not determined by God (or by anything else). The statement adds that this power operates independently of God’s decree, so that good and evil are chosen outside his determining will.

**Why Reformed theology rejects it.**

1. **God’s will determines all that comes to pass.** Scripture presents God as working all things according to the counsel of his will (Eph. 1:11), directing the heart (Prov. 21:1), and ordaining even the free acts of sinners without becoming the author of sin (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). A choice “apart from God’s determining will” would place part of history outside his decree and providence. Reformed confession denies that.

2. **Fallen man cannot choose spiritual good.** The unregenerate will is not neutral between good and evil. It is enslaved to sin (John 8:34; Rom. 6:16–20), hostile to God, and unable to submit to his law (Rom. 8:7–8). No one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44, 65). So the claim that man can choose good apart from God’s grace—and apart from God’s will—contradicts total inability. What looks like “free” rejection of God is free in the sense that it is voluntary and uncoerced; it is not free in the sense of an undetermined power to choose spiritual life.

3. **Freedom is compatibilist, not libertarian.** Reformed theology distinguishes freedom from coercion and freedom from necessity. A person acts freely when he chooses according to his own desires and nature, without external force. That choice can still be certain under God’s decree and under the person’s character. Liberty does not require the power to choose contrary to one’s nature or independently of God. After regeneration, the renewed will freely and certainly embraces Christ—not because the choice floats free of God, but because God effectually works in the person both to will and to work (Phil. 2:12–13; Ezek. 36:26–27).

4. **Responsibility does not require libertarian freedom.** People are accountable for what they willingly do. Divine determination and human responsibility stand together in Scripture (Gen. 50:20; Isa. 10:5–7; Luke 22:22). Denying libertarian freedom does not make God the author of sin or excuse the sinner; secondary causes remain real, and the sinner sins according to his own will.

**Summary.** Man is a free agent: he chooses what he wants, and he is responsible. He does not possess libertarian freedom to choose good or evil apart from God’s determining will. Apart from regenerating grace he cannot choose spiritual good at all; under grace he chooses it freely, but never independently of the God who renews the will.

It addresses all key points, including the bondage of the will in fallen man and the nature of true freedom through regeneration, while also explaining God's sovereignty and compatibilist freedom.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "The Pope, when speaking ex cathedra on matters of faith and morals, is infallible and his teachings are irreformable."
questions.reference_answer: No human being is infallible Scripture alone is the infallible rule of faith

required_points: No human being is infallible
Scripture alone is the infallible rule of faith
scoring.rubric: Must reject papal infallibility. Should affirm Sola Scriptura as the only infallible rule.

questions.response:
The statement accurately summarizes Roman Catholic dogma (Vatican I, *Pastor Aeternus*), and from a Reformed standpoint it is rejected.

Reformed theology holds that God alone is infallible, and that he has given the church an infallible rule only in Holy Scripture. No bishop, council, or pope shares that attribute. The claim that a pope, speaking *ex cathedra* on faith and morals, is infallible and that his definitions are irreformable of themselves therefore contradicts the sufficiency and supremacy of Scripture.

### Confessional rejection
Classic Reformed standards say this directly:

- Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith and practice; councils may err and have erred, and their decrees bind only insofar as they agree with the Word (Westminster Confession 1.10; 31.3–4).
- The Pope of Rome is not the head of the church; that office belongs to Christ alone. The papacy is treated as a usurped authority, not an apostolic one (Westminster Confession 25.6; Belgic Confession 29).
- Nothing may be added to or set beside Scripture as necessary for salvation or as an irreformable rule of faith (Belgic Confession 7).

On that basis, an *ex cathedra* definition has no intrinsic authority over the conscience. It must be tested by Scripture like any other human teaching (Acts 17:11; Galatians 1:8–9). If it agrees with Scripture, it is received for that reason, not because a pope uttered it. If it does not, it is to be refused—even if Rome calls it irreformable.

### Why the claim fails on Reformed grounds
**No biblical office of an infallible pope.** Peter is prominent among the apostles, but the New Testament does not give him, or any successor, an unerring teaching charism. Peter himself is rebuked and stands corrected (Galatians 2:11–14). The “keys” and the promise of Christ’s presence are given to the church and its ministers under the Word, not to one see as an irreformable oracle (Matthew 16:18–19; 18:18–20; Ephesians 2:20). Apostolic authority was unique, foundational, and closed with the apostolic witness now fixed in Scripture.

**History does not bear the claim.** Popes and Roman definitions have conflicted with one another and with earlier consensus (for example, on the rebaptism of heretics, Honorius and Monothelitism, and later reversals or reinterpretations of disciplinary and doctrinal positions). An office that has erred cannot be the irreformable norm of faith. Vatican I’s definition (1870) is, on this view, a late doctrinal innovation, not the faith once delivered.

**It displaces Christ’s headship and Christian liberty.** To bind the whole church to a papal definition as irreformable *ex sese* (of itself, not from the consent of the church) places a human teacher between the believer and the Word. Reformed theology insists the church is *reformata et semper reformanda secundum verbum Dei*: always subject to correction by Scripture. An irreformable papal magisterium makes that principle impossible.

**Faith and morals are not a separate zone of papal sovereignty.** Reformed Christians agree that the church must teach what Scripture says about doctrine and life. They deny that the pope is the final, unerring judge of what Scripture means, or that unwritten tradition and papal definition can add binding content Scripture does not contain.

### What is not being claimed
This is not a denial that popes, like other teachers, may sometimes speak truly, or that Rome has preserved important catholic truths (Trinity, incarnation, and so on). Truth in a papal statement does not prove the office infallible. Nor does rejection of papal infallibility mean private judgment without the church: Reformed churches receive creeds, confessions, and councils as subordinate standards and as valuable witnesses. Subordinate is the point. They remain reformable by the Word; an *ex cathedra* decree, as Rome defines it, does not.

**Bottom line:** From a Reformed perspective the statement is false. Infallibility and irreformability belong to Scripture alone. Papal definitions, including those issued *ex cathedra*, are human judgments—useful when biblical, non-binding and to be rejected when they are not.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "Justification involves an infusion of righteousness that makes the believer inherently righteous before God."
questions.reference_answer: Justification is a legal declaration, not an infusion Christ's righteousness is imputed, not infused

required_points: Justification is a legal declaration, not an infusion
Christ's righteousness is imputed, not infused
scoring.rubric: Must reject the Roman Catholic doctrine of infused righteousness. Should affirm forensic justification by imputed righteousness.

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, that statement is false. It describes the Roman Catholic doctrine of infused righteousness, not the Reformed doctrine of justification.

Reformed theology teaches that justification is forensic: God declares the sinner righteous on the basis of Christ’s righteousness imputed (credited) to the believer, received by faith alone. It is a legal verdict, not a moral transformation that makes the person inherently righteous in themselves.

Key contrasts:

- **Imputation, not infusion.** Christ’s perfect obedience and satisfaction are reckoned to the believer’s account (Rom. 4:3–8; 5:19; 2 Cor. 5:21; Phil. 3:9). Righteousness is not poured into the soul so that justification rests on an inherent quality in the believer.
- **Ground vs. fruit.** The sole ground of acceptance before God is Christ’s righteousness, not any righteousness wrought in us. Renewal and growth in holiness belong to sanctification, which follows justification and is never its basis.
- **Simul justus et peccator.** The justified person is declared righteous while still a sinner in themselves. Inherent righteousness remains imperfect in this life and cannot stand before God’s judgment as the reason for acquittal.
- **Once-for-all declaration.** Justification is a completed act of God, not a process of becoming inherently righteous that must be maintained or increased to remain justified.

So the statement confuses justification with sanctification and replaces imputation with infusion. Reformed confessions (e.g., Westminster, Belgic, Heidelberg) reject that formulation and insist that we are justified by faith alone, through Christ’s righteousness alone, apart from works or infused grace as the ground of our standing before God.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "After death, most believers must undergo purification in purgatory before entering heaven."
questions.reference_answer: Purgatory is not a biblical doctrine Believers go immediately to be with Christ at death

required_points: Purgatory is not a biblical doctrine
Believers go immediately to be with Christ at death
scoring.rubric: Must reject the doctrine of purgatory. Should affirm the immediate presence with Christ for believers at death.

questions.response:
The statement is rejected by Reformed theology. Believers do not pass through purgatory; at death they are immediately received into the presence of Christ.

Reformed confessions state this directly. The Westminster Confession of Faith (32.1) teaches that the souls of the righteous are made perfect in holiness and received into the highest heavens, and that Scripture acknowledges no other place for souls separated from the body. The Belgic Confession (Article 37) and the Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 57) likewise teach that believers, at death, go at once to Christ, with no intermediate state of purifying suffering.

The doctrinal reasons are these:

- **Christ’s atonement is complete.** His one sacrifice fully satisfies divine justice for sin—guilt and pollution alike (Heb. 9:12, 26–28; 10:10–14; 1 John 1:7). Temporal punishment still owed after forgiveness is a category Reformed theology does not accept.
- **Justification is full and forensic.** Those united to Christ by faith are already declared righteous. Nothing remains to be paid off by the believer’s suffering after death (Rom. 8:1; 8:33–34).
- **Sanctification is finished at death, not by purgatorial fire.** The souls of believers are then made perfect in holiness by God, not by a period of penal purification (Heb. 12:23; WCF 32.1).
- **Scripture places the believer with Christ at death.** “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43) and “to be absent from the body” is “to be present with the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:8; Phil. 1:23) leave no room for a prolonged purifying detention. Hebrews 9:27 moves from death to judgment, not to an intermediate purifying realm.

“Most believers” does not soften the claim. On the Reformed view, every true believer—however imperfect at death—enters Christ’s presence at once. Purgatory, indulgences, and prayers or masses for the dead are therefore rejected as contrary to the sufficiency of Christ’s work and to justification by faith alone.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "Mary was conceived without original sin, remained sinless, and was bodily assumed into heaven."
questions.reference_answer: The immaculate conception and assumption of Mary are unbiblical All humans except Christ are born in sin

required_points: The immaculate conception and assumption of Mary are unbiblical
All humans except Christ are born in sin
scoring.rubric: Must reject Marian dogmas (immaculate conception, perpetual sinlessness, bodily assumption). Should affirm that all have sinned (Rom 3:23).

questions.response:
From a historic Reformed perspective, that statement is rejected. It packages three Roman Catholic dogmas—the Immaculate Conception, Mary’s lifelong sinlessness, and her bodily Assumption—that the Reformed churches have not received as apostolic doctrine, because they lack warrant in Scripture and conflict with what Scripture does teach about sin, Christ, and the church.

**Conceived without original sin.** Reformed theology holds that, apart from Christ, every descendant of Adam is conceived in sin and shares in Adam’s guilt and corruption (Ps. 51:5; Rom. 5:12–19). Mary is not an exception. She herself speaks of God as her Savior (Luke 1:47), which presupposes that she needed saving. The sinless one is Christ alone, conceived by the Holy Spirit. The Immaculate Conception (defined in 1854) is a later doctrinal development, not a teaching of Scripture or of the early ecumenical consensus the Reformers claimed to recover.

**Remained sinless.** “All have sinned” (Rom. 3:23) and the warnings of 1 John 1:8–10 are not set aside for Mary. Reformed Christians honor her as blessed among women, the virgin mother of the Lord, and a model of faith and obedience (Luke 1:28, 38, 42, 48). They do not treat her as sinless, immaculate, or a co-redeemer. To do so obscures both the universality of sin and the uniqueness of Christ’s obedience.

**Bodily assumed into heaven.** The Assumption (defined in 1950) is not taught in Scripture, and the New Testament is silent about Mary’s death and any translation of her body. Under *sola scriptura*, a doctrine may be believed with the certainty of faith only if it is taught by Scripture or deduced from it by good and necessary consequence. Pious tradition, however ancient in some quarters, does not bind the conscience. Reformed eschatology expects the resurrection of the body for all the dead in Christ at the last day, not a unique pre-resurrection assumption of Mary as an article of faith.

What the Reformed do affirm is narrower and, they would say, more biblical: Mary is the mother of God the Son according to the flesh (*theotokos* in the Chalcedonian sense), a virgin in the conception of Christ, highly favored, and an example of humble faith. She is a member of the church who needed the same grace in Christ that every believer needs—not a sinless mediatrix assumed body and soul into glory as a defined dogma.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "In the Eucharist, the bread and wine are transformed into the actual body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation)."
questions.reference_answer: Transubstantiation is rejected by Reformed theology Christ is spiritually present, not physically transformed in the elements

required_points: Transubstantiation is rejected by Reformed theology
Christ is spiritually present, not physically transformed in the elements
scoring.rubric: Must reject transubstantiation. Should articulate the Reformed view of spiritual presence in the Lord's Supper.

questions.response:
**From a Reformed perspective, that statement is rejected.** Classical Reformed teaching denies that the bread and wine are changed into the physical body and blood of Christ.

### What is denied
Transubstantiation—the claim that the substance of bread and wine becomes the substance of Christ’s body and blood, while only the outward appearances remain—is explicitly rejected in the Reformed confessions.

The Westminster Confession of Faith (29.5–6) calls the doctrine repugnant to Scripture and to common sense, says it overthrows the nature of a sacrament, and links it with superstition and idolatry. It affirms that the elements “remain truly, and only, bread and wine, as they were before.” The Belgic Confession (Art. 35) and Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 78) teach the same: the bread does not become Christ’s body.

Reformed theology also rejects the idea that Christ is physically or locally present in, with, or under the elements (as in Lutheran consubstantiation/sacramental union understood in a corporeal way), and it rejects any view of the Supper as a re-offering of Christ’s sacrifice.

### What is affirmed instead
The classical Reformed view (Calvin and the confessions, not bare memorialism) is often called a **real spiritual presence**:

- Christ is truly received in the Supper by believers.
- That reception is **by faith**, through the **Holy Spirit**, not by a change in the elements or a local descent of Christ’s body from heaven.
- The bread and wine are signs and seals of the covenant: they truly exhibit and convey what they signify to those who receive them in faith, but they remain bread and wine.
- Worthy receivers “inwardly by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually, receive and feed upon Christ crucified” (WCF 29.7).
- Unbelievers receive the outward elements only; they do not feed on Christ.

So the Supper is more than a bare symbol or mental reminder, but less than (and other than) a transformation of the elements into Christ’s physical body and blood.

### Typical Reformed reasons
- **Christ’s session**: Christ’s human body is in heaven. His presence in the Supper is by the Spirit, not by bodily ubiquity or a local presence on many altars at once.
- **The nature of sacramental language**: “This is my body” is understood as figurative sacramental speech (as with “I am the door,” “the rock was Christ”), not a metaphysical conversion of substance.
- **Paul’s language**: After consecration, Scripture still calls the element “bread” (1 Cor. 10:16; 11:26–28).
- **Once-for-all sacrifice**: Hebrews teaches that Christ offered himself once; the Supper commemorates and applies that finished work; it does not repeat it.
- **Faith as the instrument**: John 6 and the Supper narratives are read as teaching feeding on Christ by believing, not oral manducation of his flesh as such.

### How this sits among other views
| View | Relation to the statement |
|---|---|
| Roman Catholic transubstantiation | Affirms the statement |
| Lutheran | Rejects transubstantiation, but affirms a real bodily presence with the elements |
| Classical Reformed | Rejects the statement; affirms real spiritual reception of Christ |
| Memorialist (often associated with Zwingli) | Rejects the statement; stresses remembrance more than means-of-grace feeding |

**Bottom line:** Reformed theology judges the statement false. The Eucharist does not transform bread and wine into Christ’s actual body and blood. Christ is truly given to faith in the Supper, but the elements remain bread and wine, and his presence is spiritual, not a change of substance.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "The saints in heaven can hear prayers and intercede with God on behalf of believers on earth."
questions.reference_answer: Christ is the sole mediator Prayer to saints is not biblical

required_points: Christ is the sole mediator
Prayer to saints is not biblical
scoring.rubric: Must reject the invocation of saints. Should affirm Christ as the sole mediator (1 Tim 2:5).

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, that statement is rejected. Departed believers do not hear our prayers or act as mediators we may invoke.

Reformed theology affirms the communion of saints and the blessedness of those who have died in Christ. It does not treat them as channels of prayer. The decisive claim is Christ’s sole mediation: “There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5). Hebrews presents Christ as the high priest who always lives to intercede (Heb. 7:25; cf. Rom. 8:34). The Spirit also intercedes for believers (Rom. 8:26–27). Adding heavenly saints as hearers and intercessors we address divides what Scripture assigns to Christ alone and has no biblical warrant.

Scripture nowhere teaches that the dead hear the prayers of the living or that believers should ask them to intercede. The dead do not participate in earthly affairs in the way the practice assumes (Eccl. 9:5–6). Consulting the dead is forbidden (Deut. 18:10–12; Isa. 8:19). Passages sometimes cited—the cloud of witnesses (Heb. 12:1), the prayers of the saints in Revelation, or the rich man and Lazarus—do not establish a system in which the living pray to the departed. “Prayers of the saints” in Revelation are the prayers of God’s people, not a license to invoke Mary or other saints.

Classic Reformed standards draw the same line. The Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 94) requires that we trust in God alone and reject all idolatry and superstition. The Westminster Confession and related Reformed teaching reject the invocation of saints as contrary to Scripture and to Christ’s unique priesthood. Calvin’s critique in the Institutes is the same: honor the saints by imitating their faith, not by praying to them.

So the statement confuses two different things. Saints in glory worship God and share in Christ’s victory. They are not mediators who hear and relay the prayers of the church on earth. Prayer is to be offered to God alone, through Christ, in the Spirit.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "The Bible contains errors in matters of history and science, and is only authoritative in matters of faith and practice."
questions.reference_answer: Scripture is inerrant and infallible in all it affirms The Bible is fully trustworthy in all matters

required_points: Scripture is inerrant and infallible in all it affirms
The Bible is fully trustworthy in all matters
scoring.rubric: Must reject limited inerrancy. Should affirm the full inerrancy and infallibility of Scripture.

questions.response:
The statement is rejected by the historic, confessional Reformed doctrine of Scripture. Classic Reformed theology holds that the Bible, as God’s inspired Word, is true and authoritative in all that it affirms—not only in “faith and practice,” but also in its historical and other factual claims—while carefully distinguishing what Scripture actually teaches from what it does not claim to teach.

### Confessional and theological grounds
The Reformed tradition does not treat Scripture as a modern science textbook, nor does it deny ordinary features of human language (phenomenological description, approximation, different genres, ancient historiographical conventions). It does insist that whatever the biblical authors affirm is true, because God is their primary author and cannot err.

- The Westminster Confession (1.4–5, 1.9–10) presents Scripture as the infallible rule of faith and life, given by inspiration of God, and as the supreme judge in all controversies of religion. Its authority rests on God himself, not on a restricted domain of “spiritual” topics.
- The same conviction appears in the broader Reformed confessional heritage and in the Old Princeton / Warfield line: inspiration extends to the words of Scripture, and therefore to the truth of what those words assert. B. B. Warfield’s classic formulation is that the Bible is “the Word of God” in such a way that it is wholly trustworthy.
- The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978), affirmed by many confessional Reformed theologians and institutions, states the denial explicitly: infallibility and inerrancy are not “limited to spiritual, religious, or redemptive themes, exclusive of assertions in the fields of history and science.” Scripture is inerrant in all it affirms.

The view in the statement—often called limited inerrancy or “infallibility only for faith and practice”—is therefore a departure from confessional Reformed orthodoxy. It was characteristic of certain neo-orthodox and broader Protestant revisions in the twentieth century, not of the Reformed symbols or the mainstream of Reformed systematic theology.

### Why the restriction fails on Reformed grounds
1. **The doctrine of inspiration.** If all Scripture is God-breathed (2 Tim. 3:16) and if the human authors spoke from God (2 Pet. 1:21), then the truthfulness of God attaches to the whole of what is written, not to a subset labeled “faith and practice.” History and the real world are not religiously neutral; redemption itself is historical.
2. **Christ and the apostles.** Jesus and the New Testament writers treat Old Testament historical narratives as reliable (e.g., creation, the flood, Abraham, the exodus, David). A Reformed Christology does not permit us to correct the Lord’s view of Scripture.
3. **The unity of truth.** Reformed theology rejects a sharp sacred/secular split in which God can be trusted about salvation but not about the world he made and governs. Error in what Scripture affirms would undermine the ground of its authority in faith and practice as well.
4. **Proper interpretation still required.** Affirming inerrancy does not mean naive literalism. Reformed hermeneutics already accounts for genre, ancient cosmology expressed phenomenologically (“the sun rises”), round numbers, and the difference between what a text affirms and what it merely assumes or illustrates. The error in the given statement is not that it wants careful interpretation; it is that it concedes actual falsehood in matters the text presents as factual.

### A brief contrast
| View | Claim about Scripture | Reformed assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Confessional Reformed | True in all it affirms, including history; authoritative for faith and life because it is God’s Word | Historic position |
| Statement under review | Contains errors in history and science; authoritative only for faith and practice | Contrary to the confession and to the doctrine of plenary inspiration |

Some contemporary writers who identify as Reformed have adopted versions of limited inerrancy. That is a real diversity in the broader tradition, but it is a revision of the confessional position, not an expression of it. From the standpoint of the Reformed confessions and the classic doctrine of Scripture, the statement should be evaluated as false.

The structure, depth, and clarity are excellent.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "All people will eventually be saved because a loving God would never condemn anyone to eternal punishment."
questions.reference_answer: Universalism contradicts Scripture Eternal punishment is a biblical reality

required_points: Universalism contradicts Scripture
Eternal punishment is a biblical reality
scoring.rubric: Must reject universalism. Should affirm the reality of eternal judgment and the necessity of faith in Christ.

questions.response:
**From a historic Reformed perspective, that statement is false.** It is a form of universalism, and Reformed theology rejects it as contrary to Scripture and to the justice and holiness of God, not only to his love.

### What the claim assumes
The argument treats “a loving God would never…” as decisive. Reformed theology does not define God’s character by what we find emotionally acceptable. It starts from what God has revealed about himself. Love is essential to God (1 John 4:8), but it is not his only attribute, and it is not set against his holiness, righteousness, and justice. The cross is the place where love and justice meet, not where justice is cancelled (Romans 3:25–26).

### What Reformed confession and Scripture affirm
Reformed standards teach a final judgment with two outcomes: everlasting life for those in Christ, and everlasting punishment for the wicked. The Westminster Confession (ch. 33), for example, speaks of the righteous going into everlasting life and the wicked being cast into eternal torments. That tracks texts such as:

- Matthew 25:46 — “eternal punishment” set in parallel with “eternal life”
- 2 Thessalonians 1:9 — eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord
- Revelation 20:10–15 — the lake of fire as a final, not temporary, judgment
- John 3:16–18, 36 — salvation tied to faith in the Son; unbelief already under condemnation

Reformed theology also holds that salvation is by grace through faith, grounded in God’s electing purpose and in Christ’s definite, effectual work for his people (e.g., John 6:37–40; 10:11, 14–15; Ephesians 1:3–14; Romans 8:29–30). Not all believe. Scripture does not teach that every person will eventually be saved, whether in this life or after death.

### Why “love forbids hell” does not hold in this tradition
1. **Love is not opposed to justice.** A God who never judged evil would not be more loving; he would be indifferent to the wrong done to his glory and to his creatures. Punishment of sin is an expression of his holy character, not a lapse in it.
2. **The gospel already displays love without universal salvation.** God “desires” in the sense of taking no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11) and genuinely offers Christ in the gospel. That does not mean every person will repent and believe. Love invites; it does not, in Reformed teaching, override unbelief or empty hell by necessity.
3. **Hell’s duration matches the gravity of sin against God and the parallel with eternal life.** Reformed writers typically argue that “eternal” in Matthew 25:46 has the same force for punishment as for life. Softening one while keeping the other is special pleading.
4. **Universalism undercuts the urgency and particularity of the gospel.** If all are finally saved regardless, faith, repentance, and the church’s mission lose the necessity Scripture gives them (Mark 16:15–16; Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–17).

### Related views also rejected
Classic Reformed orthodoxy rejects not only strict universalism (“all will be saved”) but also the claim that eternal conscious punishment is incompatible with divine love. Annihilationism and “hopeful” universalism are likewise outside the confessional Reformed position, even when offered from pastoral concern.

### Pastoral note, still within the tradition
Reformed teachers often grant that the doctrine is severe and that we should speak of it with gravity, not glee. God’s patience, the free offer of the gospel, and the real sufficiency of Christ’s work for all who come to him are the proper answers to fear—not a denial that judgment is eternal. The loving act, on this view, is to warn and to point to Christ, not to assure people that condemnation cannot be final.

**Bottom line:** Reformed theology judges the statement to reverse the order of authority. It lets a human picture of love overrule Scripture’s teaching on sin, judgment, faith, and the finished work of Christ. A loving God can and does condemn the finally impenitent, and he saves all—and only—those who are his in Christ.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "The miracles recorded in the Bible should be understood as mythological or symbolic rather than as literal historical events."
questions.reference_answer: Biblical miracles are historical events God is sovereign over natural law

required_points: Biblical miracles are historical events
God is sovereign over natural law
scoring.rubric: Must reject the demythologization of miracles. Should affirm the historical reality of biblical miracles.

questions.response:
From a classic Reformed perspective, that statement should be rejected.

Confessional Reformed theology treats the miracles recorded in Scripture as real acts of God in history, not as myths later clothed in historical language. The Westminster Confession affirms that Scripture is the Word of God, given by inspiration, and that God is its author. On that view, when the biblical writers report the exodus, the raising of the dead, the virgin conception, or the resurrection, they are reporting what God actually did. To recast those reports as mythological or merely symbolic is to set aside the Bible’s own claim to speak truthfully about God’s works in time and space.

Several convictions drive that judgment.

**God acts in history.** Reformed theology does not treat God as a remote idea or a symbol of human religious experience. The God who creates, covenants, judges, and redeems is free to suspend or override ordinary patterns of nature. Miracles are not violations of a closed system that excludes God; they are extraordinary works of the God who already upholds all things. Denying their possibility usually rests on a view of the world Reformed theology does not share.

**The gospel depends on history.** Paul treats the resurrection as a public event whose denial empties preaching and faith (1 Corinthians 15). The cross and resurrection are not symbols of a general religious truth; they are the events by which sinners are justified and death is overcome. A merely symbolic resurrection cannot bear the weight the New Testament places on it. The same holds, in lesser degree, for the signs that attest God’s saving acts.

**Inspiration and trustworthiness.** If the biblical writers present miracles as things that happened, and if those writings are God-breathed, then reclassifying them as myth charges Scripture with a kind of error, or at least with a mode of speech it does not itself adopt. Reformed theologians have long distinguished literary forms—parable, poetry, apocalyptic imagery—from historical narrative. Jonah’s prayer is poetry; the feeding of the five thousand is narrated as an event. Typology is also real: the exodus signifies redemption, the bronze serpent points to Christ. But typology presupposes the event it signifies. Symbol does not replace history; it interprets it.

**The liberal alternative is a different religion.** The claim that miracles are mythological belongs to the tradition of modern criticism and demythologizing (Strauss, Bultmann, and their heirs), not to Calvin, the confessions, or later Reformed orthodoxy (Warfield, Hodge, Bavinck). Those writers did not deny that Scripture uses figures of speech. They denied that the miraculous core of redemptive history can be dissolved into symbol without losing the faith the church confesses.

A careful distinction is worth keeping. Reformed readers do not insist that every verse is flat prose chronicle. Poetry, vision, and parable must be read as what they are. Nor does affirming historicity require a crude literalism that ignores ancient literary conventions. What it does require is that events the text presents as God’s mighty acts—creation’s special works, the exodus, prophetic signs, the incarnation, the miracles of Jesus, the resurrection, and the apostolic signs—be received as having occurred.

So the statement reverses the Reformed order. Scripture is not a mythic vehicle for timeless ideas that the modern reader must extract. It is God’s true witness to what he has done, and the miracles are part of that witness. To call them mythological rather than historical is, on this view, not a deeper reading of the Bible but a refusal of it.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "The atonement is best understood as a moral example — Christ's death inspires us to live sacrificially rather than satisfying divine justice."
questions.reference_answer: The moral influence theory is inadequate The atonement is a penal substitutionary satisfaction of divine justice

required_points: The moral influence theory is inadequate
The atonement is a penal substitutionary satisfaction of divine justice
scoring.rubric: Must reject the moral influence theory of atonement. Should affirm penal substitutionary atonement.

questions.response:
The statement is not acceptable as a Reformed account of the atonement. It keeps a real but secondary truth and makes it do the work of the gospel’s center, while explicitly setting that center aside.

**What the statement gets partly right.** Scripture does present Christ’s suffering as a pattern for believers. Peter says Christ left us an example, that we should follow in his steps (1 Pet. 2:21–23), and Paul calls believers to the mind of Christ who humbled himself to death (Phil. 2:5–8). Reformed theology does not deny that the cross moves gratitude, repentance, and self-giving love. The Heidelberg Catechism even treats Christ’s death as both satisfaction for sin and the source of a new life of thankfulness.

**What it denies, and why that denial fails.** The decisive error is the “rather than.” Reformed doctrine holds that the atonement is, at its heart, Christ’s obedience unto death as the substitute who bears the penalty of sin and thereby satisfies divine justice. God’s love is not an alternative to his justice; the cross is where steadfast love and righteousness meet. Paul says God put Christ forward as a propitiation so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom. 3:25–26). Isaiah 53, 2 Corinthians 5:21, Galatians 3:13, and 1 Peter 2:24 all speak of sin, curse, and punishment being borne by another, not merely displayed as an inspiring story.

If the cross only inspires and does not satisfy, several things collapse:

- Sin remains an unpaid debt. Moral influence can stir the conscience; it cannot remove guilt before a holy judge.
- God’s justice is treated as something the gospel must get past rather than something the gospel upholds.
- Justification becomes moral improvement, or a changed feeling, rather than the imputation of Christ’s righteousness received by faith.
- The necessity of the cross is weakened. A lesser demonstration of love might have sufficed if no penalty had to be borne.

**How the tradition states it.** The Reformed confessions speak of satisfaction, not mere example. The Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 12–18, 40) says God’s justice requires that sin be paid for, and that only the God-man could bear the burden. The Belgic Confession (Art. 20–21) says Christ presented himself in our name before the Father to appease his wrath by his full satisfaction. The Westminster Confession (8.5; 11) teaches that Christ fully satisfied the justice of the Father and purchased reconciliation, so that justification is not by infusion of virtue but by imputing Christ’s obedience and satisfaction. Calvin’s line is the same: Christ’s death is a sacrifice that expiates and propitiates, not only a lesson in self-denial.

**A better ordering.** The moral power of the cross is real, but it is the fruit of an objective work, not a substitute for it. Christ died for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God (1 Pet. 3:18). Because justice has been satisfied, the Spirit can then conform believers to the pattern of that death. Example without satisfaction leaves the sinner still condemned, however moved. Satisfaction without a following life of gratitude would be a truncated discipleship—but that is not what the Reformed doctrine teaches. It refuses the false choice in the statement: Christ’s death both meets the demands of divine justice and, on that basis, calls his people to live sacrificially.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "Humans are born morally neutral and become sinful only through environmental influence and personal choice."
questions.reference_answer: Humans are born with original sin inherited from Adam The guilt and corruption of Adam's sin is imputed to all his posterity

required_points: Humans are born with original sin inherited from Adam
The guilt and corruption of Adam's sin is imputed to all his posterity
scoring.rubric: Must reject the denial of original sin. Should affirm the doctrine of inherited guilt and corruption.

questions.response:
**The statement is false from a Reformed perspective.** It denies original sin and total depravity, which are central to Reformed anthropology and soteriology.

### What the statement claims
It treats human beings as born in a state of moral neutrality (neither righteous nor sinful by nature), so that sin arises only later from outside influences and free personal decisions. That is closer to certain Pelagian, semi-Pelagian, or modern liberal views than to the Reformed confessions.

### Reformed teaching
Reformed theology, following Scripture and the Augustinian tradition, holds that:

1. **Original sin and inherited corruption**  
   All people (except Christ) are born already sinful—not merely capable of sinning, but guilty in Adam and corrupted in nature.  
   - Romans 5:12–19: sin and death entered through one man, and “by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners.”  
   - Psalm 51:5: “Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me.”  
   - Ephesians 2:1–3: we are “by nature children of wrath.”

2. **Total depravity (or radical corruption)**  
   The fall affects the whole person—mind, will, affections, and body—so that no part remains morally neutral or able, apart from grace, to please God or turn to him.  
   - Genesis 6:5; 8:21; Jeremiah 17:9; Romans 3:9–18; 8:7–8.  
   The will is not free in the sense of being equally able to choose good or evil toward God; it is enslaved to sin until regenerated (John 8:34; Romans 6:17–20).

3. **Confessional statements**  
   - *Westminster Confession of Faith* 6.2–4: by original sin we are “wholly defiled in all the faculties and parts of soul and body,” and from this corruption proceed all actual transgressions.  
   - *Canons of Dort* III/IV.1–3: all people are conceived in sin and by nature children of wrath, incapable of any saving good, and prone to evil.  
   - *Heidelberg Catechism* Q. 7 and Q. 8: we are so corrupt that we are wholly incapable of any good and inclined to all evil, unless regenerated by the Spirit.

Environmental influence and personal choice certainly produce *actual* sins, but they are not the origin of our sinful condition. They express a nature already fallen. Personal responsibility remains real—people sin willingly—but that willingness itself flows from a corrupted heart (Matthew 15:19).

### Why the distinction matters
If humans were born morally neutral, salvation could be framed primarily as moral education, better environment, or an unaided decision. Reformed theology instead insists that regeneration must precede and enable faith (John 3:3–8; Ezekiel 36:26–27), and that grace is monergistic: God must first make the dead alive (Ephesians 2:4–5). Denying innate moral corruption undercuts the necessity and sovereignty of grace.

**Summary:** Scripture and the Reformed confessions teach that humans are not born morally neutral. They are born in sin, guilty and corrupted in Adam, and only God’s regenerating grace can free the will and renew the nature.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "All religions offer equally valid paths to God, and Christianity should not claim exclusivity."
questions.reference_answer: Christ is the only way to God Religious pluralism contradicts Scripture

required_points: Christ is the only way to God
Religious pluralism contradicts Scripture
scoring.rubric: Must reject religious pluralism. Should affirm the exclusivity of Christ (John 14:6, Acts 4:12).

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, the statement is false on both counts. Reformed theology rejects religious pluralism and affirms the exclusivity of Christ as the only way of salvation.

**Why the claim fails**

1. **Christ alone (*solus Christus*).** Scripture presents Jesus not as one mediator among many but as the only one: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6); “there is salvation in no one else” (Acts 4:12). The gospel is not a preference; it is the announcement of what God has done in the incarnate Son.

2. **General revelation does not save.** Romans 1–2 teaches that all people know something of God through creation and conscience, and are therefore without excuse. That knowledge condemns; it does not reconcile. Saving knowledge comes only through special revelation—the Word, centered on Christ, received by faith.

3. **Sin and atonement are particular.** Reformed doctrine holds that human beings are dead in sin and cannot climb to God by sincerity, ritual, or moral effort (Eph. 2:1–9; Rom. 3:9–26). Reconciliation requires the substitutionary work of Christ. Religions that deny his person, cross, and resurrection do not offer an alternative route to the same God; they offer a different account of the human problem and a different remedy.

4. **Faith is faith in Christ.** Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. “Equally valid paths” relocates salvation from Christ’s finished work to the seeker’s religious sincerity—an idea the Reformers rejected as another form of works-righteousness.

5. **Confessional witness.** The Reformed confessions state this plainly. The Westminster Confession (10.4; 14) and related standards deny that people are saved by the light of nature, the law, or any religion apart from Christ. The Canons of Dort likewise tie salvation to the gospel of Christ, not to a generic theism.

**What this does not mean**

Exclusivity of salvation is not a license for contempt. Reformed theology also affirms:
- the image of God in every person, so neighbors of other faiths are to be loved and treated justly;
- common grace, so truth, beauty, and moral insight can appear outside the church without being saving truth;
- the duty to proclaim Christ, not to coerce belief.

Respect for persons is required; agreement that every religion is equally true or equally saving is not. Truth-claims conflict. Christianity’s claim is that God has spoken and acted decisively in Jesus Christ, and that this claim is either true or it is not—it cannot be one valid path among equals.

**Bottom line:** The statement confuses the universal offer of the gospel with a universal efficacy of all religions. Reformed faith holds that God is one, that he has revealed himself savingly in Christ alone, and that the church must not surrender that exclusivity for the sake of religious parity.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "God promises health, wealth, and material prosperity to all believers who have sufficient faith."
questions.reference_answer: The prosperity gospel distorts the biblical message God does not promise material prosperity to all believers

required_points: The prosperity gospel distorts the biblical message
God does not promise material prosperity to all believers
scoring.rubric: Must reject the prosperity gospel. Should affirm that God's purposes include suffering and that material prosperity is not promised.

questions.response:
The statement is false from a Reformed perspective. It is a form of the prosperity gospel, not the teaching of Scripture or the Reformed confessions.

Reformed theology does not treat health, wealth, or material success as covenant promises attached to the quantity of a believer’s faith. God’s fatherly care is real, and He sometimes grants temporal goods, but those goods are not guaranteed, not earned by “enough” faith, and not the measure of spiritual standing.

Several convictions drive that judgment.

**Faith is trust in Christ, not a technique for gain.** In Reformed teaching, saving faith receives Christ and His righteousness. It is not a force that obligates God to deliver prosperity, nor a work whose strength determines one’s circumstances. Tying blessing to “sufficient faith” turns faith into a performance, blames the sick and the poor for their condition, and obscures grace.

**The New Testament expects suffering, not uninterrupted prosperity.** Union with Christ includes sharing in His sufferings as well as His glory. The apostles, including Paul, knew poverty, illness, persecution, and unanswered requests for relief. Passages often used to promise wealth are either tied to the old-covenant land arrangement, are ordinary greetings or proverbs, or speak of spiritual life and final inheritance—not a universal material contract for every believer now.

**Providence is sovereign and wise, not formulaic.** God gives both plenty and want according to His purposes. Earthly loss can be fatherly discipline, a call to depend on Christ, a share in the church’s suffering, or simply life in a fallen world. Contentment in abundance and in need is the apostolic pattern, not the assumption that lack proves weak faith.

**Blessing is already and not yet.** Forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, and union with Christ are present gifts. Bodily resurrection, the end of sickness, and the renewal of creation belong to the age to come. Collapsing that hope into present health and wealth shrinks the gospel and misreads Christian hope.

**The confessions do not teach this.** The Heidelberg Catechism, Belgic Confession, and Westminster Standards speak of providence, contentment, the right use of earthly goods, and patient endurance under the cross. They do not teach that sufficient faith secures health and wealth for all believers.

God may prosper someone, and gratitude and wise stewardship are right. But “God promises health, wealth, and material prosperity to all believers who have sufficient faith” contradicts the Reformed reading of Scripture. It replaces the cross-shaped Christian life with a transaction God never made.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "Baptism is the means by which a person is regenerated and receives new spiritual life."
questions.reference_answer: Baptism is a sign and seal, not the cause of regeneration Regeneration is a work of the Holy Spirit

Regeneration is a work of the Holy Spirit
scoring.rubric: Must reject baptismal regeneration. Should affirm that regeneration is by the Spirit alone, with baptism as a sign.

questions.response:
**No. From a confessional Reformed perspective, that statement is false.**

Reformed theology treats baptism as a **sign and seal** of regeneration and of the covenant of grace, not as the means by which a person is regenerated or receives new spiritual life.

### What the Reformed standards actually teach

Baptism signifies and seals union with Christ, remission of sins, and regeneration. It does not cause them. The Westminster Confession (28.1, 28.6) calls baptism a sign and seal of “ingrafting into Christ, of regeneration, of remission of sins,” and then denies that its efficacy is tied to the moment it is administered. Grace is conferred by the Holy Spirit, according to God’s counsel, to those to whom it belongs—not by the rite itself.

The Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 69–73) and Belgic Confession (Art. 34) say the same thing in different words: as surely as water washes the body, Christ’s blood and Spirit wash the soul. The water does not regenerate. The Spirit does.

### How regeneration is understood

In Reformed doctrine, regeneration is the sovereign, monergistic work of the Holy Spirit—new spiritual life given in effectual calling (WCF 10; Canons of Dort III/IV). It is not produced by the sacrament operating by its own power (*ex opere operato*).

- For those who come to faith as adults, the Spirit ordinarily uses the **Word** (1 Pet. 1:23; James 1:18; Rom. 10:17). Faith, not baptism, is the instrument by which Christ and his benefits are received.
- Infant baptism (in Presbyterian and continental Reformed practice) admits a child to the visible covenant community and seals the promise; it does not itself bestow new life. Elect infants dying in infancy are saved by the Spirit as God pleases (WCF 10.3), not because the water regenerated them.
- Reformed Baptists (e.g., 1689 Confession) reject infant baptism altogether and still deny that baptism regenerates; it follows a credible profession and publicly signifies what grace has already done.

### What the statement actually resembles

“Baptism is the means by which a person is regenerated” is the doctrine of **baptismal regeneration**, associated especially with Roman Catholic teaching and, in a different form, with Lutheran sacramental theology. Confessional Reformed churches have historically rejected that view, even while insisting that baptism is a real means of grace—offering, signifying, and sealing what the Spirit gives—rather than an empty symbol.

Calvin can sound strong about baptism conferring grace, but he ties that efficacy to the Spirit and to faith, and he rejects the idea that the external rite itself makes someone spiritually alive.

**Bottom line:** Reformed theology says the Holy Spirit regenerates; baptism signifies and seals that grace. It is not the instrument by which new spiritual life is given.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "A person is born again at the moment they make a personal decision to accept Christ as their Savior."
questions.reference_answer: Regeneration precedes and enables faith The new birth is a sovereign act of God, not a human decision

required_points: Regeneration precedes and enables faith
The new birth is a sovereign act of God, not a human decision
scoring.rubric: Must reject decisional regeneration. Should affirm that regeneration is monergistic and precedes faith.

questions.response:
From a classic Reformed perspective, that statement reverses the order of salvation and misstates what regeneration is.

Reformed theology treats being “born again” as God’s sovereign, monergistic work, not as the result of a person’s decision. Scripture describes the unregenerate person as dead in sin and unable to come to Christ (Eph. 2:1–5; John 6:44, 65; Rom. 8:7–8). Regeneration is the Spirit giving new life and a new heart so that the person can and does believe (Ezek. 36:26–27; John 3:3–8; Titus 3:5). Faith is the fruit of that new birth, not its cause. Texts such as 1 John 5:1 are often read this way: the one who believes “has been born of God”—regeneration logically precedes faith.

So the moment of conscious trust in Christ is real and necessary, but it is not what produces the new birth. Effectual calling and regeneration enable the decision; the decision does not effect regeneration. “Accepting Christ” is the believer’s response to grace already given, not a human act that triggers the Spirit.

The statement fits a decisionistic or Arminian account better than the Reformed one. Reformed teaching would say instead: a person believes because God has regenerated them, not that they are born again because they decided to accept Christ.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "Man in his natural state has the full ability to obey God and achieve righteousness without divine grace."
questions.reference_answer: This is the heresy of Pelagianism Man is totally dependent on grace for any spiritual good

required_points: This is the heresy of Pelagianism
Man is totally dependent on grace for any spiritual good
scoring.rubric: Must reject Pelagianism. Should affirm total inability and the necessity of grace.

questions.response:
The statement is rejected by classic Reformed theology. It is the opposite of the Reformed doctrine of total inability.

From a Reformed perspective, fallen man still has natural faculties—mind, will, and the capacity for outward moral and civil acts—but he does not have the moral ability to obey God spiritually or to produce righteousness that God accepts, apart from grace. Sin is not merely a bad habit that leaves the will intact. It is a corruption of the whole person. The unregenerate person is “dead in trespasses and sins,” does not receive the things of the Spirit, and cannot please God in the flesh (Eph. 2:1–5; 1 Cor. 2:14; Rom. 8:7–8).

That is why the Westminster Confession says that man, by the fall, “hath wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation,” and cannot convert himself or even prepare himself for conversion by his own strength (WCF 9.3). The Canons of Dort teach the same: without regenerating grace, no one can turn to God. Faith, repentance, and obedience are gifts, not native powers.

The statement also confuses two different things Reformed theology keeps apart:

- Outward conformity and civil good, which unregenerate people can do under common grace, providence, and conscience.
- True spiritual obedience and righteousness before God, which requires regenerating and sanctifying grace.

Even those outward works, done from an unrenewed heart, are not righteousness in the justifying sense (WCF 16.7). Righteousness that stands before God is received by faith, not achieved by natural ability (Rom. 3:20–28). Sanctification likewise depends on the Spirit; the believer’s obedience is real, but it is grace-enabled, not self-generated.

Historically, the claim matches Pelagianism more than even semi-Pelagianism or Arminianism. Pelagius taught that man can obey God’s law without inward grace. Augustine, the Reformers, and the Reformed confessions treated that as a denial of both the seriousness of the fall and the necessity of grace. Reformed theology does not deny that man wills and acts. It denies that the fallen will, left to itself, can will spiritual good or earn righteousness.

So the Reformed evaluation is straightforward: man in his natural state does not have full ability to obey God or achieve righteousness without divine grace. What he needs is not assistance added to an already sufficient will, but new life.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "God does not have exhaustive foreknowledge of future free decisions; the future is partly open even to God."
questions.reference_answer: God has exhaustive foreknowledge Open theism contradicts God's omniscience and sovereignty

required_points: God has exhaustive foreknowledge
Open theism contradicts God's omniscience and sovereignty
scoring.rubric: Must reject open theism. Should affirm God's exhaustive omniscience and sovereign decree.

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, that statement is false and incompatible with confessional Reformed theology.

Reformed theology affirms that God has exhaustive, infallible knowledge of all things—past, present, and future—including the free decisions of creatures. The future is not partly unknown or “open” to God. God’s knowledge is not a passive watching of an unsettled future; it is grounded in his eternal decree and in his perfect knowledge of himself and of all he has ordained.

### Why Reformed theology rejects the claim

1. **God’s decree and knowledge go together.**  
   The Westminster Confession (3.1–2) teaches that God, from all eternity, freely and unchangeably ordained whatever comes to pass, yet in such a way that he is not the author of sin and secondary causes (including human choices) remain real. If God has decreed every event, he cannot be ignorant of any future free decision. Exhaustive foreknowledge follows from exhaustive sovereignty, not from a mere “crystal ball” view of the future.

2. **Scripture presents God as knowing the future completely.**  
   Classic texts include Isaiah 46:9–10 (“I am God… declaring the end from the beginning”), Psalm 139:1–6, 16, Acts 2:23 and 4:27–28 (the crucifixion as both foreknown and predetermined), and Ephesians 1:11 (God works all things according to the counsel of his will). Prophecy, election, and providence all assume that future human acts are known with certainty, not merely as possibilities.

3. **“Open” future language undercuts classical attributes of God.**  
   The statement is the core claim of open theism. Reformed theology treats it as a denial of omniscience (and, in practice, of immutability and aseity). If some future free decisions are unknown even to God, then God’s knowledge grows, his plans can be surprised or revised, and his promises and prophecies are at best highly probable rather than certain. That is not the God of Reformed confession.

4. **Human freedom does not require divine ignorance.**  
   Reformed theology rejects the libertarian assumption that a choice is free only if it is undetermined and therefore unforeknown. It holds a compatibilist view: creatures act freely according to their natures and motives, and those acts are nonetheless certain in God’s decree and knowledge. Responsibility does not require that the future be open to God.

### Summary judgment

| Claim in the statement | Reformed evaluation |
|---|---|
| God lacks exhaustive foreknowledge of future free decisions | Denied |
| The future is partly open even to God | Denied |
| (Implied) libertarian freedom limits divine knowledge | Rejected as a false dilemma |

So the statement is not a minor difference of emphasis. From a Reformed standpoint it contradicts the doctrine of God taught in Scripture and in the Reformed confessions: God knows the end from the beginning, and nothing future—including free human decisions—is hidden from him.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "The Son of God did not exist eternally but was the first and greatest being created by the Father."
questions.reference_answer: The Son is eternally begotten, not made Arianism was condemned as heresy

required_points: The Son is eternally begotten, not made
Arianism was condemned as heresy
scoring.rubric: Must reject Arianism/Socinianism. Should affirm the eternal deity of the Son, begotten not made.

questions.response:
**From a Reformed perspective, that statement is false and heretical.** It restates classical Arianism (and later forms such as Jehovah’s Witness Christology), which the church rejected at Nicaea and which the Reformed confessions explicitly deny.

### What the statement claims
It denies the eternal deity of the Son and treats him as a creature—the highest creature, but still made by the Father and therefore not God in the same sense as the Father. That is the heart of Arianism: “There was a time when he was not.”

### Reformed (and catholic) teaching
Reformed theology confesses that the Son is **eternally begotten, not created**, and is of one substance (*homoousios*) with the Father.

- **Nicene Creed** (received by the Reformed churches): the Son is “begotten of the Father before all worlds, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father.”
- **Westminster Confession of Faith** 2.3: in the unity of the Godhead there are three persons, “of one substance, power, and eternity: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Ghost.” The Son is “eternally begotten of the Father.”
- **WCF 8.2**: the Son, the second person, “being very and eternal God, of one substance and equal with the Father,” took on human nature. The mediator is not a created being who later became divine; he is the eternal Son who assumed flesh.

So the Son’s relation to the Father is **generation (begetting), not creation**. Begetting is an eternal, necessary act within the Godhead; creation is a free act by which God brings into being what is not God. The Son is not the first item in the created order.

### Scriptural lines Reformed theology presses
- **John 1:1–3**: the Word was with God and was God in the beginning, and all things were made through him—so he is not among the things made.
- **John 1:14, 18; 3:16**: the “only begotten” (*monogenēs*) Son, language of unique sonship, not of being manufactured.
- **Colossians 1:15–17**: “firstborn of all creation” is read as rank and heirship (preeminence), not as “first creature,” because the same passage says all things were created through him and for him, and that he is before all things.
- **Hebrews 1:3, 8–12**: the Son is the radiance of God’s glory and is addressed as God, whose years have no end—contrasted with angels, who are created ministers.
- **John 8:58; 17:5**: the Son’s preexistence is personal and eternal, sharing the Father’s glory before the world was.

“Firstborn” and similar titles are therefore titles of supremacy and inheritance, not proofs that the Son began to exist.

### Why the distinction matters
If the Son is a creature, even the greatest:
- he cannot be truly worshiped as God (which Scripture requires);
- he cannot fully reveal God or accomplish a redemption that reconciles us to God;
- the Trinity collapses into one God plus a supreme creature.

Reformed Christology holds the opposite: the one who saves is **very God and very man**—the eternal Son incarnate—so that his obedience, death, and resurrection have infinite worth.

### Bottom line
The statement denies the eternal generation and full deity of the Son. Reformed churches judge it contrary to Scripture and to the catholic creeds they affirm (especially Nicaea and the Westminster Standards). The orthodox formula is: the Son is **begotten, not made**; there was never a time when he was not.

All required points are thoroughly addressed.
